020b103b-b84e-52f0-a58e-80746cb6afa9.name: Incense burner
020b103b-b84e-52f0-a58e-80746cb6afa9.short_description: Incense burners were in high demand all around the Muslim world. Incense burners differ in shape and decorative repertoire, as well as quality. Some are fashioned in the form of cylindrical hoods, spherical units or composite architectural shapes. Royalty commissioned burners as gifts to shrines and for their palace and courts. This jade tripod incense burner from China is decorated with Arabic inscriptions inside three cartouches on the sides of its globular body.
020b103b-b84e-52f0-a58e-80746cb6afa9.bibliography: Wilson, M., Thomas, I. & Victoria and Albert Museum, *Chinese jades*, London: V & A Publications, 2004. National Palace Museum (Guo li gu gong bo wu yuan), *Exquisite beauty: Islamic Jades = Guo se tian xiang: Yisilan yu qi*, Taipei: National Palace Museum, 2007.

03194f3e-048b-5d3e-a6af-514f37ac800f.short_description: Massive Assyrian winged animals captured the imagination of Victorian England. Large scale reproductions of them were incorporated into “The Assyrian Court” at the Crystal Palace Exhibition.

0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.name: Reverent Baboon with Pharaoh figure
0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.description: The loud rejoicing of the Hamadryas baboon at the sunrise in its rocky habitat served as a model for the Egyptian celebration of the ascent and descent of the sun at the critical stages of its cycle. Baboons with upraised hands – the Egyptian gesture of reverence – became symbols for the “eastern souls”, the gods who cheer the sun at its appearance above the horizon. The king joins these gods in his role as sun priest.
0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.dates: 18th Dyn. Amenophis II, 1454-1419 BC; acquired in 1865/66
0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.dimensions: Height 130 cm, Width 42 cm, Diameter 61,5 cm
keywords: Maximilian of Mexico; Miramare; Egypt

0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.name: *Apollo and Daphne*
0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.description:
This sculpture is considered one of the masterpieces in the history of art.  
Bernini began sculpting it in 1622 after he finished *The Rape of Proserpina.* He stopped working on it from 1623 to 1624 to sculpt *David*, before completing it in 1625.  
With notable technical accuracy, the natural agility of this work shows the astonishing moment when the nymph turns into a laurel tree. The artist uses his exceptional technical skill to turn the marble into roots, leaves and windswept hair. Psychological research, combined with typically Baroque expressiveness, renders the emotion of Daphne's terror, caught by the god in her desperate journey, still ignorant of her ongoing transformation. Apollo, thinking he has achieved his objective, is caught in the moment he becomes aware of the metamorphosis, before he is able to react, watching astonished as his victim turns into a laurel tree. For Apollo's head, Bernini looked to *Apollo Belvedere*, which was in the Vatican at the time.  
The base includes two scrolls, the first containing the lines of the distich by Maffeo Barberini, a friend of Cardinal Scipione Borghese and future Pope Urban VIII. It explores the theme of *vanitas* in beauty and pleasure, rendered as a Christian moralisation of a profane theme. The second scroll was added in the mid-1700s.  
The group, like others created by Bernini in the Villa, was backed on to a wall, setting a mandatory point of view for the visitor entering the room, to fulfil the pictorial objectives and provide the surprising scenery, key components of the baroque style. As with other sculptures, it was placed in the centre of the room during the renovations of 1700. Bernini worked with the sculptor Giuliano Finelli, who provided the delicate detailing on the base, rocks and part of the leaves and tree.
0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.short_description: Bernini executed the group between 1622 and 1625. Such a pagan myth (by Ovid in *Metamorphosis*) in the cardinal's house is explained by a moral distich by Maffeo Barberini (Urbano VIII, 1623–1644) on the theme of *vanitas* “those who love to pursue fleeting forms of pleasure, in the end find only leaves and bitter berries in their hands.”
0b7d9d65-e30b-5a92-acf2-45ddb1343c5c.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

0bfcc099-89c3-58ef-bcd9-7607c73b68a5.name: *Angel with Trumpet*
0bfcc099-89c3-58ef-bcd9-7607c73b68a5.description:
Joseph Leonard Weber was a burgher of Buda from 1757. Probably born in Silesia into the Weber dynasty of sculptors in Svidnica, members of his family moved to Brno and Nagyszombat (Trnava). The Weber name can be found in the register of births in Buda from 1753 since all seven of the Weber children were baptised there.  
Weber's sculptural activity is documented from 1757 and includes the stone sculptures of *Faith*, *Hope* and *Charity* above the portal of St. Anne's church, dating from 1765, and the statue *St. Florian* on the facade of St. Florian Chapel, as well as the figures that decorate the organ and those on the high and side altars of the chapel (1761–1766).  
Almost the entire interior decoration of St. Florian Chapel, Buda is by Weber, made between the 1760s and 1770s. On 20 June 1761, Weber was paid 86 forints for the sculptural decoration of the chapel's organ.  
In the 1920s the chapel was rebuilt twice and the interior furnishing was dispersed. The sculptural ensemble of the organ, the white painted figures of King David playing the harp, two angels with trumpets, one with drums and several *putti*, came to the Municipal Museum of Budapest (today Budapest History Museum).  
The angel has an adolescent body and curly hair. He is playing a trumpet and has a puffed-out face; he stands *contrapposto*, with exact anatomy. His clothing consists of a light drapery fixed with a ribbon at his left shoulder. The abstract decorative shaping of the drapery was a Rococo stylistic feature of southern German origin. By around 1760, this feature was already a widespread motif used by the sculptors of Pest and Buda, and carried over to Hungary via the art of Károly Bebo, Lipót Antal Conti, Antal Eberhard and József Hebenstreit. It is still evident even during the Neo-Classical era.
0bfcc099-89c3-58ef-bcd9-7607c73b68a5.short_description: Weber’s ascendants were sculptors in Silesia, who moved from Svidnica to Brno and Nagyszombat (Trnava). It was while a citizen of Buda in 1761 that Weber worked on the sculptural decoration of the St. Florian Chapel. The Rococo music-making angels once decorated the organ.
0bfcc099-89c3-58ef-bcd9-7607c73b68a5.obtention: From the St. Florian Chapel in Buda

0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.name: Stone relief of a lion.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.description:
The area of Bab al-Faraj refers to the north and northwestern area of old Aleppo.  
Bab al-Faraj (Gate of Deliverance), also known as Bab al-Faradis (Paradise Gate), was built by the Ayyubid king al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi (d. AH 613 / AD 1216) as part of his expansion and refortification of the city. Today, the Bab al-Faraj area is almost completely destroyed. Some traces of the wall were revealed in archaeological excavations by the Syrian Directorate of Antiquities, including a round tower that can feasibly be identified with the Burj al-Tha'abin (The Tower of the Serpents). Both serpents and lions were common decorative and talismanic features on city gates and city walls, long used as symbols of protection and of power.  
This lion, one of a pair, was carved in relief each from a single large block hewn in an inversed t-shape form. The rather affable beast is carved in profile as if walking, with uplifted paws and a long curving tail over the body. Although rather schematic, details such as the eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth and some muscular details along the shoulder have been accentuated by deeply cut lines.  
Such lions are extremely common in AH 6th- and 7th- / AD 12th– and 13th–century architectural decoration in Anatolia and Mesopotamia, often appearing as a pair on city walls, gates, and other places of fortification. In Aleppo a pair of lions, albeit in a quite different style, protect the entrance tower of the Ayyubid Citadel. A second further and much more similar pair of lions can be found along the western city wall, still integrated. A third pair of lions on the northern city wall is only documented by photography.  
Not all the existing lion pairs are necessarily in their original location nor are they necessarily attributed to the same date.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.short_description: This stylised animal carving was found in the Bab al-Faraj (Gate of Deliverance) area in the northwest of Aleppo. Although it is difficult to establish the exact dating of this piece, it is known that the gates of Aleppo were fortified by the Ayyubid king al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.dimensions: Height 50 cm, length 104 cm, width 15.3 cm.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.method_for_datation: It is difficult to date this object definitively: some scholars have proposed a Mamluk attribution, identifying the lion as the blazon of Sultan Baybars (r. AH 658–75 / AD 1260–77). While Baybars did use his famous lion emblem on coins and numerous architectural constructions, he is not known to have repaired or renovated any of Aleppo's fortifications or city walls. It is far more probable that the lions belong to the Ayyubid period and the major construction works of al-Malik al-Zahir Ghazi.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.method_for_provenance: The carved lions were not found *in situ*, and therefore their attribution to the Bab al-Faraj is based on oral history. Given the local expertise in stone carving, it is probable that they were made in Aleppo, possibly as part of the Bab al-Faraj or the surrounding wall.
0cec6aaa-8c9c-5003-8b7b-39389edbe2cf.obtention: This lion is one of a pair discovered in the Bab al-Faraj area of Aleppo in the 1980s when extensive construction works took place. Archaeological chance-finds were moved to the Museum by the Syrian Directorate of Antiquities.

0e020cb4-5b0e-5b53-9a97-0e2adfd0f102.name: Large Red Line
0e020cb4-5b0e-5b53-9a97-0e2adfd0f102.description:
Ira Sapir (1995) specialised in glass and sculpture, obtaining his BFA from the California College of Arts and Crafts in 1978.  
He opened his own glass studio in 1979 in Oakland, California. During the 80s, he worked with blown glass as if it were a canvas to be painted, developing his well-known elliptical shape in minimalist colours. It was at this point that Torres Esteban contacted him in order to participated in the VICOINTER, 83 project.  
In 1985, he decided to take a break in his career. He later began to work with steel and copper, developing a weaving method using both materials. In 2003 he began to carry out installations dominated by steel as a sculptural material.

0e020cb4-5b0e-5b53-9a97-0e2adfd0f102.method_for_provenance: Feria de Cerámica y Vidrio in Valencia, 1983. VICOINTER, 83.

102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.name: Sitting lion.
102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.description:
Made of grey marble in a parallelepiped form that is sculpted, this object features a lion sitting on its hind legs rendered flat against the surface of a lower part of a segment of arch. The head of the animal is far larger than its body. Its eyes are globular and wide open, and its fully opened mouth reveals tightly clenched teeth, giving the face a ferocious air.  
The left flank of the animal is more densely decorated than the right. Fur in the form of curls hang from the left flank, to which the tail is also attached. The front legs are missing. The right flank lacks any ornamentation, which suggests that it was this side that was encased in the masonry while the left side was on show.  
The rounded shape of this piece leads to the conjecture that it formed part of a segment of a poly-lobed arch that belonged to an entrance door of a Hammadid palace.
102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.short_description: This marble piece is a sculpture of a lion with a disproportionately large head and a wide open mouth that was probably part of a doorway arch. Its tail is flattened against its left-hand side and the carved curls represent its fur.
102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.dimensions: Length 40.5 cm, width 24 cm, diameter 12 cm.
102b5a7a-7eb3-5088-8d91-c9be0bc5c5fa.method_for_provenance: The object was found on the site of the Qal'at Bani Hammad.

115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.name: Stone blazon.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.description:
In the Mamluk period, heraldry played an important role and was widely used on architecture, metalwork, textiles, glass and pottery. Its use was strictly the reserve of sultans and particularly of the officers who were awarded individual blazons, each according to their rank. While the early Bahri Mamluks used blazons which represented a distinct office held by an individual, the later Burji Mamluks combined several heraldic emblems which were commonly shared by a corps of *amirs* who served a distinct master.  
The stone roundel with the tripartite blazon from the Aleppo Museum represents a widely used composition from the late Mamluk period: it contains the symbol of the *jamdar* (master-of-the-robes) with a so-called “napkin” in the upper field, the stemmed cup of the cup-bearer (*saqi*) charged with the pen box of the *dawadar* (secretary) in the central field, flanked by what has been identified as a pair of powder horns. A second, smaller, stemmed cup is placed in the lower field.  
According to Meinecke (1972), this particular emblem was the most popular blazon of the late Burji period and is known to have been used by at least 47 *amir*s. Its first employment can be traced back to Sultan Qaytbay (AH 872–901 / AD 1468-96) when he was still an officer himself and he then conferred it upon his own followers. It was in use up to AH 922 / AD 1517 and came to represent something like the Mamluk “State blazon”.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.short_description: The use of royal emblems reached a high point during the Mamluk period. This carved stone roundel reveals a composition of symbols including those of the cup-bearer, the secretary and the master of robes.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.dimensions: Height 51.4 cm, width 55 cm, depth 18.7 cm.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by comparison with other similar pieces.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.method_for_provenance: Although the provenance is unknown, this medallion probably belonged to either Amir Uzdamur (also known as Özdemir), who ruled Aleppo twice in 884 / 1479 and between 889–99 / 1484–93, or the last Mamluk *amir*, Kha'irbak b. Bilbay. Both were closely connected to Sultan Qaytbay, leaving examples of this emblem on various buildings in the city: Uzdamur on his *caravanserai* (Khan al-Sabun), the Qastal al-Ramadaniyya, the Qastal Jami' al-Sharaf and the Jami' al-Sharaf itself; Kha'irbak on his mausoleum south of Bab al-Maqam and his *khan* in the *suq* not far from the citadel.
115adb41-ded2-5669-b97c-a902df406833.obtention: It is not known how the Museum came by this object.

16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.name: *A Member of Nagyszeben (Sibiu) Town Council*
16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.description:
This small alabaster portrait sculpture was found on a building site in Nagyszeben (Sibiu) in around 1880 and initially it was placed in the Hungarian National Museum. At the time, three coloured alabaster figures of two women and a man were in the Brukenthal Museum in Nagyszeben (Sibiu). All three are 28–30 cm in height, the man has a rounded beard and all three are wearing similar clothing (a long fur-collared, fur-lined braided coat, brocade jacket with a broad belt). The male figure – later in Germany (Gundelsheim, Siebenbürgisches Museum) – was identified long ago as Valentin Franck von Franckenstein (1643–1697), a Saxon count, government official, poet and scholarly historiographer, of whom several authentic portraits are known. The “Sachsencomes” were representatives of the descendants of mediaeval German settlers in multi-national Transylvania. A metal relief epitaph dedicated to Franck von Franckenstein was also transferred from the Lutheran church in Nagyszeben (Sibiu) to the Brukenthal Museum. This is attributed to the Lőcse (Levoča) goldsmith, Sebestyén Hann (1645–1713), who frequently worked for Franck. The female figures were identified as the first and second wives of the Saxon count, but the fourth figure in the series, preserved in Budapest, suggests another arrangement. This piece may also be the posthumous portrait of Franck's father, another Saxon count also called Valentin Franck, whose effigy was carved by Elias Nicolai (Lutheran church, Sibiu), or – more probably – of a younger member of the family.  
Instead of individual characterisations, the sculptor emphasises the social status and age of the subjects, presenting the slightly old-fashioned attire of Hungarian noblemen and women. Similar figures in the same rigid pose are known from Transylvanian tomb sculptures, constituting the link between the Late Renaissance and the Baroque styles of the 17th century. The material, yellowish alabaster with grey veins, was quarried in Transylvania and its varied uses in art reached its apogee in the 17th century.
16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.short_description: Marking the transition between the styles of the Late Renaissance and Baroque in Transylvania, this fine alabaster statue was made in the style of funerary sculpture. Its pair, a female figure, is still preserved in Nagyszeben (Sibiu).
16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.method_for_datation: by stylistic analysis and historical data
16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.provenance: Franck von Franckenstein family from Nagyszeben (Sibiu)
16a31ba5-4c16-5a18-9197-2cffb96b8f18.obtention: Franck von Franckenstein family from Nagyszeben (Sibiu); in 1881 transferred to the Hungarian National Museum, Budapest; from 1936/39 transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest; from 1974 in the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest.

1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.name: *Adoring Angel*
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.description:
Georg Raphael Donner was one of the most prominent and influential Central European sculptors of the first half of the 18th century. He developed his individual Neo-Classical style at a distance from the Baroque tradition, relying on models from antiquity and 16th-century Italian sculpture. His first monumental works were made for Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral, commissioned by Prince Primate Imre Esterházy.  
First of all he worked on the decoration for the Chapel of St. John the Almsgiver, executing the archbishop's sepulchral statue (1729–32). Later, he created the sculptural group of St. Martin and the beggar, as well as two adoring angels for the new high altar in the cathedral (1733–1735). This significant work is characterised by the perfect harmony between the sculpture and architecture; the idea and the form. The crowned canopy of the altar was originally carried by enormous free-standing fluted columns. The central figural group featured St. Martin seated on the back of a rearing horse. He shares his flowing cloak with the beggar lying on the ground. St. Martin is wearing a Hungarian noblemen's outfit and has the facial features of the archbishop. The beggar of heroic stature is looking at the saint with Christ's face, but the saint does not recognise him immediately. An external viewer of the altarpiece cannot recognise Christ's face either, because it is seen in semi-profile. Two huge kneeling angels join the scene on either side, their adoration directed towards the disguised Redeemer. Despite minor differences in movement, hand gesture and in the arrangement of drapery, the adoring angels are practically symmetrical; they are dignified celestial creatures, although their finely modelled, strong bodies are very real. Their pose expresses intimate and perfect veneration.  
The beauty of the modelling is enhanced by the subtle grey hue and silken lustre of lead, which also lends an earnest, reserved and elegant appearance to the statues. With these statues, Donner reached an initial peak of his oeuvre. The altar was dismantled in the 1860s when the cathedral was rebuilt in the Neo-Gothic style. The main group of the equestrian statue today is in the side aisle of Bratislava Cathedral, and the two adoring angels are part of the permanent collection at the Hungarian National Gallery.
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.short_description: The most important patron of the Viennese sculptor was Primate Imre Esterházy in Pozsony (Bratislava). The high altar of Pozsony (Bratislava) Cathedral was one of Donner's most significant works, but after it was demolished in the 19th century, the group of St. Martin and the beggar can be seen in the nave today, while the two huge angels were taken to Budapest in the 19th century.
1d0c0bff-d4e8-59b7-bd8f-5d6f7251d877.obtention: St. Martin’s Cathedral, Pozsony (Bratislava); purchased by the National Museum, Budapest in 1875; transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest in 1976

1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.name: Coat of Arms of the Erdödy Counts
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.description:
The coat of arms has an elongated triangular composition. In the middle is a a horse-head-shaped shield quartered with a heart in the centre: (1) on gold, a black, displayed, crowned eagle; (2) and (3) a blue bar with two six-pointed gold stars one beside the other; (4) on gold, a crenellated castle with a window and a door, in the heart of the shield: on red a stag rearing to the right from a halved gold wheel. Crest: above the shield, a gold crown from which grows gold acanthus leaves and an angel. Bearers of the arms: on each side is an angel with gold wings and one foot stepping sideways. The “background” is richly decorated with acanthus leaves, which in this case take over the function of the mantle.  
The Croatian aristocratic family of Hungarian origin, known as the Bakochs, came from the village of Erdöd. From the 16th to the 19th centuries, the Erdödy family played a leading role in Croatian history, acquiring many estates, bestowing five Croatian *bans* (viceroys) and one bishop, and playing an influential part in Croatian political life. They were particularly famous for fighting against the Ottomans.  
Among their many estates, Klanjec castle – built in 1603 and locally known as Novi Dvori Klanječki – is worthy of special mention.  
The Erdödy coat of arms was produced in the sculpture workshop of the Ljubljana, later the Zagreb master sculptor and woodcarver, Ivan Komersteiner, whose arrival in Croatia marked the final advent of Baroque art.  
In the south apse of Zagreb cathedral there is a similar memorial arms by Ivan Komersteiner produced in 1693 for *Ban* Nikola Erdödy who liberated much of Croatia from the Turks.  
Nikola Erdödy built a chapel in the west wing of Klanjec castle dedicated to St Francis Xavier, which he decorated with wall paintings. It is possible that the family arms shown here is from the castle, or perhaps even that it was on an altar commissioned by the Erdödys, who were known to be great donors.  
The Erdödy arms, probably the work of an unknown sculptor from Ivan Komersteiner's workshops, has retained the basic characteristics of Ivan's style, seen particularly in the use of luscious and fleshy acanthus leaves and angel figures as ornamentation.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.short_description:
Coat of arms of the Erdödy Counts, it comprises a shaped triangular composition around a crowned, quartered shield in gold-blue, with a red heart at the centre, and the family’s symbols. Two guardian angels support it, while there is a third, smaller, angel above the crown. Behind the shield and above the crown are gold acanthus leaves.  
The Erdödys were Croatian aristocrats of Hungarian origin, a family of high nobility that were influential in Croatian political life. The coat of arms is probably the work of the unknown sculptor from the Ivan Komersteiner's workshop. Komersteiner was one of the most important sculptors of continental Croatia at the end of the 17th century.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.method_for_datation: From characteristics of morphology, style and typology, and comparison with other works by the unknown master from the Ivan Komersteiner workshop.
1f6cda19-3462-52f3-8af4-485020daf089.obtention: In 1946, following World War II, the artwork was secured by the Commission for Collecting and Preserving Cultural Monuments, Antiquities and Libraries (KOMZA). In 1952, following the proposal of the Commission for the Liquidation of KOMZA founded by the Ministry of Education, it became the property of the History Museum of Croatia (today the Croatian History Museum).

1fe23b95-31f5-5b9a-b2ab-2854193671c7.name: *The Outcast*
1fe23b95-31f5-5b9a-b2ab-2854193671c7.short_description: This sculpture by António Soares dos Reis was made in Italy and it rapidly became an icon of romanticism, as it symbolises a young man who has been forced into exile.  The classic contours of the human body, the position of the model and the remarkable sculpture led to the recognition of the author as one of Portugal’s main exponents of sculpture and this piece a National Treasure.

208acb08-f9ab-592b-b800-800ffe643ab6.name: She the fresh
208acb08-f9ab-592b-b800-800ffe643ab6.description: In 2014, Rostislav Materka (1982) presented this piece as an entry into the competition organised by the European Glass Experience. According to the artist, the concept that governs the creation of this piece was following “the basics of craftmanship”. Specifically, it drew on the technical abilities of the craftspeople in workshops in the Czech Republic. The challenge was to create the piece without moulds or other external aids, in search of the shape created as a result of the physical properties of the glass itself. Once this shape was achieved, the artist managed to reshape it by sculpting, redefining its visual appearance. It can be said that he upturned the initial idea.

22f76b8b-02d4-572f-a730-9fa0910f176e.name: Vuelos I
22f76b8b-02d4-572f-a730-9fa0910f176e.description:
It is one of the greatest exponents of contemporary glass sculpture in Spain. Self-taught, Javier Gómez took his first steps in the world of glass in 1971, when he began working in the family workshop, which he would leave behind shortly later to focus exclusively on his art.  
Javier Gómez has worked with sculpture for more than 30 years, during which he has never stopped experimenting with sheet glass, using simple, overlapping sheets that are cut, polished and bonded. He sometimes includes expressive elements, such as cracking, sandblasting, or small trapped air bubbles, in addition to cold cuts, in order to achieve eroded and degraded surfaces, where light intentionally condenses causing unexpected plastic effects.  
His main source of inspiration has always been nature. He needs the calm of the surroundings in his hometown, Pedro Bernardo (Ávila), home to his studio, in order to work. His sculpture is forever in distant conversation with the orographic beauty of Valle del Tiétar, the landscapes and the birds that surround him. His art can be classified within the abstract genre, however certain organic resonances appear to belong to a distant universe that he has created himself.  
Not only a sculptor, Javier Gómez has been committed to driving and promoting contemporary glasswork in Spain. His most ambitious project was the 1997 creation of the Museo de Arte en Vidrio de Alcorcón, MAVA, thanks to the legacy of Takako Sano (+2006) and the support of the Local Council.  
The piece, Vuelos I, corresponds to the second stage of his work, from 1999 until the present day, when he moved away from the dynamic appearance of the first phase, in search of a new means of expression. He gravitated closer and closer to block sculpture, with a solid and resistant appearance in which the sheets of “floating” glass are held and the colour is incorporated into the pieces, based on shades of black, red, pink, blue, etc. Perfectly polished pieces with a translucent finish, colour scheme tinged by the light. The edges have a more translucent appearance, compared to the more intense central areas.

2681aa7c-6872-5aaf-afc2-c1e0626603b4.name: Fragment of a frieze.
2681aa7c-6872-5aaf-afc2-c1e0626603b4.description:
Fragment of frieze made of *timchent* (local plaster), sculpted with epigraphic, geometric and floral decoration composed of two registers separated into three frames. The first frame consists of repeated, perforated circles, while the other two consist of plaster fillets separated by a milled edge composed of alternating small squares and voids. The epigraphic decoration that adorns the first register consists of an inscription of the word '*baraka*' (benediction) in *kufic* characters, repeated three times, the third instance of which is incomplete. Right from the beginning of the Hegiran era, the word *baraka* was used as an inscription for ceramic plates, jars, copper utensils, architectural elements, etc.  
The second register consists of a pattern of lozenges. Below, a small fragment of foiled and stylised leaf can be seen, which probably belonged to a third register of floral decoration.  
The sculpture was executed with the aid of a iron blade acting on the *timchent* while it was still soft. According to H. Saladin, this local plaster derived from limestone peculiar to the region was 'applied onto cob or roughstone walls'.  
The geometric ornamentation of this panel is reminiscent of what the Romans and the Byzantines from North Africa engraved onto reliquaries, architectural elements, altars, etc.  
This fragment formed part of one of the long friezes that ran along the top of the wall right across the room in order to delineate the ceiling from the decoration that adorned the rest of the wall.
2681aa7c-6872-5aaf-afc2-c1e0626603b4.short_description: Frieze fragment with epigraphic, geometric and floral decoration split into three sections set apart by three frames. The first has a *kufic* inscription, '*baraka'* (benediction), repeated three times. The second is decorated with lozenges and the third, almost completely lost, was decorated with floral motifs.

2681aa7c-6872-5aaf-afc2-c1e0626603b4.method_for_provenance: The fragment was discovered in a palace in Sedrata following the report published in the *Comptes rendus de l'Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres* in 1952.

26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.name: Fountain mouth.
26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.description:
A lion, ochre in colour, sculpted in stone as if lying on its four legs. The head, huge and rounded, is disproportionate in relation to the body. The face shows two globular eyes surmounted by thick eyebrows, a large muzzle and an open jaw full of teeth that protrude onto the cheeks. A mane in the form of leaves gently overlapping each other and forming a sort of pinecone, stretches along the back. The tail lies along the right flank. The lion's paws appear thin. The very stylised whole demonstrates rather clumsy execution.  
This lion formed the mouth of a fountain, from which water spouted.
26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.short_description: Fountain spout in the shape of a lying lion noteworthy for the clumsiness of its execution: disproportionate head, protruding eyes, thick eyebrows, mouth open around excessively long teeth and thin paws. The mane resembles a pinecone and the tail is flattened against its right-hand side.
26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.dimensions: Height 12.5 cm, length 25.5 cm, width 10.5 cm.
26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.method_for_datation: Found in the site of the Qal'at Bani Hammad.
26d6637f-84b8-536e-b789-91910110aa5a.method_for_provenance: Golvin specifies that this fountain mouth was offered to the museum of Setif by P. Massiera, who brought it from the site of the Qal'at Bani Hammad.

27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.name: *The Adoration of the Shepherds*
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.description:
This bas-relief is part of a series which includes four horizontal and four oval scenes, all are in their original frames.  
Three shepherds approach to adore the Child. The Madonna, St. Joseph and the angels, occupying the middle of the scene, point to the object of interest, Jesus. Piò moulds the tender scene to create a soft and delicate three-dimensional picture, similar to his contemporary painters.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.short_description: This sculpture is a good example of the baroque technique of Bolognese terracotta. Terracotta bas-reliefs were intended as proper paintings, framed and hanging from the walls, but lacking colours. The figures are scattered on different planes; in the foreground they are nearly three dimensional while the background figures are drawn more two dimensionally.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.holder: Museo Diocesano di Arte Sacra di San Giovanni in Persiceto
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.method_for_datation: The date is inscribed on the surface of the bas relief. The origin is described by the biographer of the artist, Zanotti.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.obtention: The bas-relief was originally made for the oratory of the Suffragio in San Giovanni in Persiceto. It was moved to the oratory of the Holy Sacrament and later to the church of the Madonna della Cintura. In 1948 it was moved again to the Collegiata (the main church) of San Giovanni in Persiceto. The museum of the church was opened to the public and it was exhibited there.

28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.name: Part of an 'Angel’s concert'
28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.description: The coloured relief 'Angel’s concert' was created as an object of worship. The outer shape follows an erratic course, very likely caused by a missing part of the relief, and with the representation of a swelling cloudscape. Two dressed angels emerge out of the clouds that form the background. One of them is playing the lute and both are singing to the music, accompanied by a winged cherub. The angels are carved out to knee-length while only the cherub’s winged head is shown. Eye-catching, showing chubby and rosy cheeks and an unusual tufty hairstyle with some hair standing up, this relief may be regarded as typical of Hans Krumpper’s style. The relief stands as a very early example for the cheerfulness of the Baroque era, with flocks of church angels marking the climax after 1650.
28b857f3-2101-565b-a2b0-139be4166d04.short_description: The precious Early Baroque relief of a cheerful angel’s concert within a cloudscape was obviously created as an object of worship. One of the two angels plays the lute, while the other beneath holds the song book.

2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.name: The Builders
2a226eef-1a17-51ae-9e21-911b78e227e7.short_description: Arturo Dazzi was the son of the owner of a marble quarry and remained attracted to this raw material throughout his life. He attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Carrara and then won two national contests. The group of *The Builders*, as stated by the artist, was made for his final examination during the four years he spent at the Pensionato Nazionale di Scultura between 1904 to 1907. For this reason, the sculpture is very complicated and needed a lot of study and work in order to be completed. Nonetheless it gave great satisfaction to the artist: exhibited in 1907 in Italy and in 1909 in Munich the group was awarded both times with gold medals. The work shows an idealized version of the social “verism”, or truth, a concept common among young Italian sculptors of the time, and shows the influence of the painting of Constantin Meunier, *Enlèvement d’un creuset brisé*, done in 1884.

2a8712ba-8b88-5ee9-9129-b2c6ecca6096.name: Rectangular Composition
2a8712ba-8b88-5ee9-9129-b2c6ecca6096.description:
David Magán (1979) trains at the Escuela de Artes y Oficios de Madrid, where he specialises in both woodwork and steelwork. His relationship with glass began in 2003, after having attended a stained glass course, in addition to other glass courses at the Escuela de la Real Fábrica de Cristales. He has since experimented with multiple techniques born of a profound artistic investigation.  
He has collaborated in exhibitions and fairs around the world, including Korea, London, Colombia, Belgium or Denmark. His work has also been selected for various Visual Arts exhibitions and competitions, the most recent being the “European Glass Experience”, headed by the City of Venice, in collaboration with the Museo Vetratio di Murano, the Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio de la Granja and the Glass Museum of Riihimaki in Finland.  
His work is defined as a geometric abstraction, developed using translucent sheets of coloured glass, suspended in the air, where movement and light fuses the colours. Light is what truly drives his work, with its ability to modify the sculpture and the space that surrounds it, creating an atmosphere filled with colour, shadows and reflections.

2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.name: Bas-relief in carved marble.
2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.description:
In the right-hand section of the bas-relief is a seated figure wearing a richly embroidered tunic. The heavy crown on his head defines him as a sovereign or military leader. With his right hand he lifts a cup to his lips. To his right a musician plays the flute. The man's head is covered with a veil and the sleeves of his tunic are decorated with bands containing geometric motifs. His eyes are almond-shaped and very prominent.  
This bas-relief is one of those rare gems of Ifriqiyan art representing people and their daily life. The artist is totally unconcerned with anatomical detail. The musician's face does not betray age, type or expression. This work probably has its roots in a very ancient North African tradition. Some art historians hold that the style recalls various funeral stelae which the Romano-Africans dedicated particularly to Saturn and to Caelestis. Common features are the frontal poses, their rigidity, the indifference to spatial considerations and the prominence of the eyes. The similarities of this piece to several carvings in wood and ivory from the Spanish Umayyad, the Egyptian Fatimid and the Eastern Abbasid eras are astonishing, especially the face of the flute player, the costumes and the veils. The crown has been described as Norman by some experts. Similar crowns have been found on ivory panels from Fatimid Egypt and also on Mesopotamian pottery from the same era.
2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.short_description: This bas-relief is one of the few Ifriqiyan pieces depicting an animal scene. A person dressed in a rich, embroidered tunic is sat on the right side of the bas-relief. He is wearing a crown on his head, suggesting that he is a king or military leader. To his right, a musician is playing the flute.
2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.method_for_datation: The bas-relief was discovered at Mahdiyya, capital of the Fatimids and then of the Zirids during the 4th–5th / 10th–11th centuries, which tends to establish its dating in that era. This is corroborated by the large number of human figures and scenes from daily life produced in Ifriqiya at the same time.
2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.method_for_provenance: The Ifriqiyan origin of the decoration suggests the object was carved *in situ* re-using an old piece of Italian marble.
2ce846c0-44cf-593b-a417-5ec441dd4212.obtention: Following its chance discovery at Mahdiyya, the piece was acquired and shown at the Bardo Museum.

2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.name: Tomb of Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.description:
The Tomb of Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel is based on a traditional French model seen in, for example, the Tomb of Cardinal Richelieu at the Sorbonne in Paris. Laprade introduced a new typology to Portugal: a tomb with an architectural background filled with allegorical figures. The inclusion of funerary symbolism and its association with the allegories of Life and Death are adjusted to fit in with the Baroque spirit. At a time when abstract and formal caskets in cases were the norm this was an innovation in Portugal. The tomb was created in the artist's studio in Coimbra.  
In terms of the architectural composition, the pilasters are transformed into Atlantes representing crying women who stage the sorrow of death with veils that partially hide their faces. The mournful tone of these figures contrast with the graceful angels that flit about in an oval-shaped plaque carrying with them the coat of arms of D. Manuel. At the top and bottom of the beam, are *putti* seen together with symbols of Life and Death. The tympanum is decorated with the figure of Time – an allegory of Death – accompanied by an angel that holds the bishop's crosier. The close of the tombstone arch is furnished with a Phoenix – symbol of the Resurrection and celestial Life. The sense of movement is remarkable in the flowing sideways of Time's clothes and the curvature of the prostrate body of D. Manuel. The naturalist portrait of D. Manuel, with one hand on his chest gazing at the image of Our Lady, suggests that he is waiting for the final verdict. Watching over the scene is the macabre skeletal figure of a magistrate wearing a bay-leaf crown – symbolic of the transition from life to death – wearing an amulet with a *Memento Mori* distich.
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.short_description: A limestone tomb showing the deceased, Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel, prostrate accompanied by the allegorical figures of Justice, Fortitude, Faith, Charity and Time, and the religious scene of the Appearance of Our Lady of Penha de França in bas-relief.
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.owner: Vista Alegre Atlantis, SA – Fábrica de Porcelana da Vista Alegre

2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.place_of_production: Chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França, Vista Alegre, Ílhavo
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.obtention: In 1812 José Ferreira Pinto Basto, founder of the Vista Alegre Porcelain Factory, bought Quinta da Ermida to which the lease of the Chapel at Vista Alegre had been assigned. The entire Vista Alegre Estate did not belong to him until 1817. The Museum is guardian of the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha de França, at Vista Alegre.

308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.name: Small gazelle in bronze.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.description:
This bronze object is composed of three superimposed elements: a small gazelle joined to a rectangular pedestal on top of a ball with a shaft, above a small sphere surrounded by a four-petal corolla. Rivets fix all these elements to the shaft, which holds the different components and serves as an axis. The gazelle, the support, the ball and the shaft are solid cast. The animal has an arched neck and a thin layer of gold covers its body. The tops of its legs are decorated with geometrical knotwork and a woven design on their inner side whereas the inside of the neck is decorated with dots. The small rounded tail is stamped with a cruciform pattern. The gazelle's elegance and its decoration are reminiscent of Umayyad bronzes from Córdoba.  
The hollow sphere is not decorated and it is formed by two welded elements. The corolla is made out of flat strips cut into four wide lanceolate petals, gilded with serrated edges. The outside of the strips are decorated with a floral pattern with smooth palms and Marinid-style foliage.  
The two parts of this small bronze do not appear to belong to the same period. In all probability the upper part, gazelle and shaft, was made in Córdoba during the Caliphate period. The sphere and the four-petalled corolla would have been added in the Marinid period, possibly to use it at the top of an aquamanile.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.short_description: This elegant object, representing a small gazelle on top of a sphere surrounded by a corolla of petals, would have been placed on top of an aquamanile. Its two halves come from difference periods: the Caliphate of Córdoba and the Marinid era.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.dates: Hegira late 4th and 8th centuries / AD late 10th and 14th centuries.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis and comparison with Umayyad and Marinid pieces.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.provenance: Dual provenance: the upper part was from Córdoba and the lower part was made in Morocco.
308e03ea-6946-5a0c-a2aa-392943b0f903.bibliography: Hassar-Benslimane, J., 'Note à propos d'un bronze arabe trouvé au Chellah (Rabat)', *Bulletin d'archéologie marocaine*, Vol. X, 1976, pp.173–84.

32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.name: Equestrian figurine.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.description:
A figurine of a bearded horseman with Asian Turkoman facial features, long braided hair and a helmet. Around the right front hoof of the horse is a snake that is climbing towards the rider from his left. The snake is shown opening its mouth to bite the rider through his armour, but he repels it with his shield. He carries a straight sword lifted into the air, ready to strike. There is a grooved cylindrical column coming out of the stomach of the horse that probably supported the statue, keeping it upright. The horse wears blue reins that are executed in relief. The reins continue around the horse's mouth and hang in front of its neck, then, like a harness, run across the sides of the horse's body down to the lower part of its hind legs.  
The object is glazed in off-white and blue and, therefore, can be compared to the laqabi-style ware of Persia, also known to have been produced in Raqqa. Laqabi ware is often seen as luxury bowls and dishes with moulded decorations. Production probably centred on the city of Kashan in Persia. Raised areas were often coloured in bright- blue, yellow, green, purple and pink to differentiate them from the white or off-white background.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.short_description: Known as the 'Horseman of Raqqa', this masterpiece of Syrian polychrome underglaze sculptural ceramics clearly displays the influence of the Central Asian military elite on artistic taste and local production.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.method_for_datation: The object is similar to wares produced in Persia during the Seljuq period in the 12th century; a period that saw significant trade activity and migration between Abbasid domains and those of the Seljuq and other Turkoman peoples.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this object is difficult to determine because there was substantial trade activity in ceramics between various centres of production and wealthy consumers. Therefore, it is impossible to determine whether it was made in Persia and imported to Raqqa, or made in Raqqa after exposure to wares from Seljuq Persia. Its “Eastern” features and its similarity to the *laqabi* wares reveals a strong Persian influence in either case.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.obtention: Salim ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Haqq, Director General of Antiquities and Museums in the 1950s, referred to this figurine as the “Horseman of Raqqa” in the *Syrian Archaeological Annals*. It was found along with two others in a man-made pond during archaeological excavations in Raqqa. The pieces were then sold and taken to Paris where this figurine was deposited in a French bank. In 1949, after negotiations with the French government, the Horseman was returned to Syria and the National Museum of Damascus.

33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.name: Fragment of a basin.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.description:
Fragment of a basin sculpted in low relief, triangular in shape, both parts of which have been restored. Two of the sides are flat, the third is curved.  
The scene on the basin, of which only a part has survived, depicts hawking. The torso and part of the thigh of a horse rider can be distinguished, clothed in a pleated tunic belted around the waist by a large belt, and holding a white weapon in the right hand. Behind him, a falconer, whose face is mutilated and whose lower limbs have been amputated, and who is wearing a tunic that is open in front and tightened at the waist by a narrower belt, holds a dead hare. In his left hand, he holds up a falcon, of which only one foot and a bit of the tail can be seen above the horse's rump, the lower part of which is missing. A section of tree trunk, which could belong to a palm tree, appears behind the falconer.  
To the left of this scene lies an inscription consisting of two lines in *kufic* lettering. The first line is rather difficult to interpret ; the second reads as follows: ' …*ine wa arba'ou maya … amal ibn* …' (…four hundred…the work of Ibn…). '*ine*' cannot be translated as it is the last syllable of a number that could just as well be forty as seventy or even ninety.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.short_description: Fragment of a sculpted white marble ablutions basin, the two halves of which have been pieced back together. The bas-relief scene shows a falcon hunt. On the left-hand side there is an inscription in *kufic* characters. This object was originally from Andalusian Morocco.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.dimensions: Length 51.5 cm, width 21 cm, thickness 7.5 cm.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_datation: The object features a date which is missing the numerals representing single units and units of tens, and thus can only be placed somewhere between 440 and 489 (1048 and 1096).
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_provenance: Through comparing this bas-relief fragment to basins from al-Andalus, Marçais was able to attribute this fragment to a basin, which could have been used for ablutions, of the same origin.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.obtention: Gift of Edmond Doutté, who acquired it in Rabat in 1902, during an exploration in Morocco.

33919ff9-2350-55d3-9e18-73ae206b029a.name: Head V with square eye
33919ff9-2350-55d3-9e18-73ae206b029a.description:
Stanislav Libenský (1921-2002) and Jaroslava Brychtová (1924-2020) are key figures in the Czech Art Glass Movement, which drew the kiln casting technique (glass casted in a mould) to the forefront, in which geometric and monochrome pieces prevailed.  
Brychtová learned the techniques of cast, moulded and molten glass alongside his father, sculptor and founder of the Železný Brod Glass School, Jaroslav Brychta, in the 40s. In 1950 he led the architectonic glass department at the same school, where he met the director, Stanislav Libeský. Together they developed and perfected the glass fusion moulding technique, inspired by Czech cubism from the early 20th Century and metaphysical philosophy, within the purest abstraction where the light creates a fourth dimension to the sculptural work.  
Their work was highly valued by studio glass artists from the United States and Europe at international exhibitions, where their exhibited their work in the 60s and 70s. However, it wasn’t until the 80s that their work was recognised internationally as true pioneering works in the glass sculpting field.

33ca14b6-4b0a-5783-8318-06081aaaa3ca.name: *Truth*
33ca14b6-4b0a-5783-8318-06081aaaa3ca.description:
Sitting on rough-surfaced rock the figure of the smiling maiden holds an image of the sun in her right hand. She represents “Truth” according to Cesare Ripa's famous *Iconologia*, an encyclopaedic repertoire illustrating the personifications of abstract concepts, widely used by artists during the Baroque period to represent allegorical figures. A recent study has also shown that the marble figure of the maiden is a faithful sculptural representation of a painting by Correggio, *Allegory of Virtue*, which was in Rome at the time, incomplete, as part of the Pamphilj Collection. According to ideas expressed by the artist in his preparatory drawings, the statue was to be part of an imposing group showing a moral theme, *Truth Unveiled by Time*. It was intended to be overseen by an old man with a scythe, the symbol of Time, intent on lifting the cloth to reveal the radiant beauty of the maiden. The work was conceived during the pontificate of Innocent X Pamphilj (1644–1655). It was a particularly difficult time in the artist's life when he was unjustly accused of causing structural instabilities in Saint Peter's, resulting in the demolition of the bell towers that he had designed. Bernini, who never completed the sculptural group, arranged for the statue to remain at his home as a warning to his descendants. The different ways in which the marble is finished represent an important example of Bernini's extraordinary technical skills. The well researched contrast between the crystalline finish of the figure and the “non finish” of the rocks is also evident in the detail of the foot resting on the globe.  
The typically Baroque practice of using a metaphor of the personal to illustrate a universal warning is particularly noteworthy.
33ca14b6-4b0a-5783-8318-06081aaaa3ca.short_description: Bernini carved the sculpture for himself at a difficult time in his career (during the pontificate of Innocent X Pamphilj, 1644–1655) when he was accused of causing structural problems at St. Peter’s bell tower. The group, which was never finished, was to include the figure of Time. Bernini left the sculpture as an eternal warning to his heirs, with whom it remained until 1924.
33ca14b6-4b0a-5783-8318-06081aaaa3ca.method_for_datation: The sculpture was kept in Rome at Bernini’s home in Via della Mercede until 1852, before being moved to Palazzo Bernini in Via del Corso. In 1924 the heirs to Bernini’s estate transferred it permanently to the Galleria Borghese.

34f34c83-66aa-5e61-897d-108f4bf4dc50.name: *The Rape of Proserpina*
34f34c83-66aa-5e61-897d-108f4bf4dc50.description:
The work was commissioned by Cardinal Scipione Borghese from a young Bernini after he had completed *Aeneas and Anchises*. The group was then given to Ludovico Ludovisi, the new cardinal-nephew of Pope Gregory XV, who had succeeded Paul V Borghese in 1621. This commission was an act of high diplomacy by which Scipione hoped to win favour with the hostile cardinal, who was also an avid collector with a splendid suburban villa beside Villa Borghese.  
The subject shows Pluto, god of the underworld, abducting Proserpina, daughter of Ceres and Jupiter. The myth is related to the fertility of the earth and therefore could symbolise Scipione's desire for the rebirth of the Borghese family after the death of his father.  
The movement of the figures is a vortex of contrasting forms related to late Mannerist methods, permeated by an expressive theatricality that is typically Baroque.  
Bernini freezes the action at the height of the abduction, allowing him to best describe the tension in the bodies, stressing both the virile potency of the god and the sensual femininity of the nymph.  
In her futile struggle against the brutal violence, the nymph pushes her hand into Pluto's face in an attempt to free herself from his grip, while the god, thrust forward, clutches her with a triumphant expression beneath his thick beard.  
A tear on the girl's desperate face and Pluto's hands sunk gleefully into her thighs are two examples of extraordinary naturalism, a triumph of technique transforming hard marble into soft flesh,  
As in other works, Bernini seeks a painted style for the surfaces, applying different finishes to the flesh of the god and the nymph, and creating a hair effect for Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the underworld, using a gradine, a tool normally used in an intermediate stage of marble sculpting.  
The work, which belonged to the Ludovisi family, was acquired by the Italian State in 1908, and placed in Villa Borghese alongside other groups by the young Bernini that were commissioned by Cardinal Scipione.
34f34c83-66aa-5e61-897d-108f4bf4dc50.short_description: The sculpture shows Pluto and Proserpina in a twisting pose that is still linked to Mannerist art but which is combined with a Baroque theatricality. Executed between 1621 and 1622 the work was given by Scipione Borghese to Cardinal Ludovisi (*cardinal* *nepote* of Alessandro, the new pope Gregorio XV, 1621–1623).

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.name: Edward Jenner Inoculates his Small Son with the Smallpox Vaccine
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.short_description: Giulio Monteverde was an Italian sculptor who started carving wooden crucifixes before moving on to sculpture during his years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Genoa. In 1865 Monteverde moved to Rome to study at the Academy of St. Luke. The sculpture of Edward Jenner (1749-1823) represents the British physician and naturalist inoculating for the first time, on his own son, the smallpox vaccine that he invented. This work was initially rejected by the Academy of St. Luke, entrusted with selecting works of art for the International Exposition in Vienna, but then exhibited in it thanks to an influential friend. The plaster cast of Jenner won the gold medal in Vienna, and a similar success was had with the marble version presented at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 when it won the medal of honor. The bronze version shown in the picture represents Jenner administering the smallpox vaccine to his son, blending dynamism and details in the face of the scientist, clothes and objects.

39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.name: Basin.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.description: A large marble fountain-basin. The basin is basically a large hemisphere supported on a short foot and topped with a 12-sided rim, one side of which is blank and another of which has a section cut out to support the channel which brought water. Eleven of the sides carry an inscription giving the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor of Hama, al-Malik al-Mansur Muhammad ibn al-Muzaffar Mahmud ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Umar ibn Shahanshah ibn ‘Ayyub (also known by his shorter title of Mansur II Muhammad), who ruled from AH 641–83 / AD 1244–84. The exterior of the basin is carved with a bold design of two interlacing arabesque designs, each repeated six times in alternation and set off against a background of smaller floral decoration. Such a fine basin would probably have been placed in a prominent public mosque to serve the needs of congregants and to proclaim the glory of the ruler.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.short_description: A large marble basin for ablutions, carved on the exterior with prominent interlacing arabesque designs. The 12-sided rim is inscribed with the name and titles of the patron, the governor of Hama. Thus the basin served both the ritual needs of the community and the governor’s public image.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.method_for_provenance: The basin is inscribed with the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor in whose honour this object was made (see description above).
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.bibliography: Ayers, J., Oriental Art in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1983, p.111.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; religious objects; water; inscription

3b494886-dcbc-53f0-858a-e56bcd9a8635.name: Sculpturally conceived emblem
3b494886-dcbc-53f0-858a-e56bcd9a8635.short_description:
This work of art belongs to a group of emblems which is an artistic interpretation of an Arabic letter or word that brings the Sufi farther along his path to God when he remembers or repeats it in his devotions (*dhikr*).  
This emblem is a symmetrical composition with the word *al-shafi* (the Healer), one of Allah’s many names.
keywords: Calligraphy; Sufism; Symmetry; inscription; blazon; standard; procession

3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.name: *Crucifixion*
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.description:
The Dominican Monastery of St. Domingos de Benfica, founded in 1399 on the outskirts of Lisbon, was rebuilt in the second quarter of the 17th century during the government of Friar João de Vasconcelos (1624–1632). During this period Manuel Pereira was commissioned to make a series of sculptural devotional images among which were the *Crucifixion* and *Our Lady of the Rosary* – both located over the aisle altars – and *Saint Dominique of Gusmão* and *St. Peter the Martyr* in the main arch niches.  
Portuguese Manuel Pereira studied in Rome and lived in Spain where he received important commissions from the Madrid court, which at the time was the capital of the Iberian monarchy (1580–1640). Pereira worked in stone, wood and alabaster, and using these materials he conceived mainly devotional sculptures that visually imparted the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), aimed at heightening the inner conversion of the Christian. Manuel Pereira's sculptures are characterised by their dynamic composition, combined with the delicate treatment of the surfaces, which in their smallest details irradiate light, delivering a deep and intense psychology. These aesthetic values are present in the polychrome wooden sculptures of the *Immaculate Conception* in Toledo, *St. Ignatius of Loyola*, *St. Francis Xavier*, *St. Aloysus Gonzaga* and *St. Francis of Borja* commissioned by the Church of São Roque in Lisbon. One can include the *Crucifixions* in Cartuja de Miraflores in Burgos and St. Domingos de Benfica in Lisbon, where the realism and inner drama are remarkably intense. In the São Roque Benfica *Crucifixion,* based on an engraving by Pontius from a painting by Peter Paul Rubens, Pereira's Christ hangs lifeless and heavy from the cross, His face contorted, exhaling His last breath and His eyes closing slowly in agony.
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.short_description: The epitome of Manuel Pereira's sculpture lies in his Crucifixions among which this one, in the Church of St. Domingos de Benfica, is remarkably intense. Based on a composition by Rubens, Christ's heavy, lifeless body hangs from the cross, creating a deep and intense psychological tension that visually imparts the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), which in this context suggests that the body is elevated to eternity through the inner drama of the Passion.

3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.name: Window.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.description:
A window made of stucco, which contains pierced decoration filled with coloured glass. The decorations of the window are placed in two rectangular sections: one, larger, at the bottom and the other, smaller, at the top. The decoration in the lower section is composed of a pointed arch, within which are vegetal motifs including cypress trees, and decorative architectural components such as domes and minarets, which bear a strong Ottoman imprint. The upper section is composed of an inscription in *naskhi* script, which reads: 'Oh Muhammad'.This inscription is written against a background of geometric decoration and stylised-coloured flowers distinguished by their simplicity.  
Stucco windows appeared in buildings in the early Islamic era and were used in Amr ibn al-'As Mosque and in al-Azhar Mosque, during the Fatimid period. In the Mamluk and Ottoman periods stucco coloured-glass windows were used more generally. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo has a number of stucco coloured-glass windows in the collection that are embellished with a variety of decorations, which invests in them a special beauty particularly when the sun shines through them or when they are exposed to artificial light. Among the most beautiful is that with the registry number 9886.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.short_description: Stucco windows were known in different Islamic periods and were used in different buildings to filter the sunshine and soften its glare. When their pierced patterns were covered with coloured glass, the aesthetic effect was exquisite.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.method_for_datation: The window is dated based on the decorative architectural components, which have a definite Ottoman stamp. The window is also associated with construction of the Sariyat al-Jabal (Mosque of Suleyman Pasha) which was built in 935 / 1528.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.method_for_provenance: This window is associated with the Mosque of Suleyman Pasha, built in 935 / 1528 in the Citadel of Cairo and was probably made in Cairo, Egypt.
3cc3cd1b-6a98-54f3-8299-5ed61c1d3d3d.obtention: This object was transferred to the museum from the Mosque of Sariyat al-Jabal (Mosque of Suleyman Pasha).

47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.name: Niche.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.description:
Rectangular-shaped niche with a rounded back in the form of a shell, ornamented with fillets that end in roll mouldings. The façade of the bay, which is sculpted in bas-relief, is decorated with festoons, lozenges and circles, whereas the cornerstones are adorned with rosettes framed on either side with stylised leaves.  
The bay fits within a double frame: the first formed by a lozenge trellis, the second by a narrow fret band.  
The decoration of this panel evokes that sculpted by the Romans and the Byzantines from North Africa on shrines that were made of earth, as well as on architectural pieces, altars, etc., all of which attests to the continuity of the ornamental repertory.  
The sculpture was executed with a metal blade, worked on the *timchent* while it was still soft. According to H. Saladin (see Bibliography) this local type of plaster made from the region's limestone was 'applied to walls made of cobblestones or rubble'.  
The niche was built in the corner of a room at a certain height above ground-level. The upper part has undergone restoration work.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.short_description: Niche with a rounded back and a half-dome whose façade bears *naqsh-hadida* (sculpted plaster) decoration with simple geometric or floral rosette motifs in *timchent* plaster. Placed in the corner of a large room, it would have been used as a cupboard and also to help support the ceiling.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.dimensions: Height 77 cm, width 73 cm, depth 41 cm.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.method_for_datation: After the fall of the Rustamid dynasty, the Ibadids of Tahert escaped southward and founded a new town, Sedrata (296–467 / 909–1074). This fragment comes from a palace in that town. Alternatively, a fragment of frieze that was created for the same palace can be dated to the 5th / 11th century, as, according to Marçais, the *kufic* characters that feature could be from the '11th century and resemble those of Kairouan'.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.method_for_provenance: Report published in the *Comptes rendus de l'Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres* in 1952.
47f199fd-3322-5ab8-b00e-f35c60fd72f6.obtention: From an archaeological repository (excavations by Van Berchem, 1952).

485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.name: Narcissus
485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.short_description:
Erwin Eisch (1927-2022) was instrumental in founding the studio glass movement, which sought to make artistic statements with glass and move away from the functional and decorative uses that had previously constrained glass-making.  
  
This sculptural form of 'Narcissus' is one of a number of works that Eisch based around the mythological story of Narcissus, as told in several ancient sources. In all accounts the protagonist Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection and unable to pull himself away from the allure of it he eventually passes away to be replaced by a flower that now bears the same name. Eisch's 'Narcissus' sculptures are larger-than-life multi-part figural pieces in which the glass material acts as both human and mirror. the first version was displayed as part of a complex installation in a domestic interior featuring other mixed-media components by Eisch. The V&A's version is the third 'Narcissus' produced by Eisch, and was displayed in a mirrored glass box. This component no longer exists, but at the museum the figure is instead displayed in a showcase with a mirrored surface on which Narcissus lays.
485104a2-c65b-5c03-9552-8fe4f6bc4b16.author: Simon Spier

49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.name: *The Beheading of St. Paul*
49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.description:
*The Beheading of St. Paul* was commissioned by Virgilio Spada to a Bolognese sculptor, living in Rome, Alessandro Algardi. The statues were made in Rome and shipped to Bologna. They were intended to decorate the high altar of the Barnabite Church San Paolo Maggiore – St. Paul’s, patronised by the Spada family and to commemorate Virgilio’s father, Paul. Upon his death, in 1631, 6000 scudi was bequeathed for the construction of a chapel. In 1634 the Spada moved their residence from Rome to Bologna and Virgilio obtained permission from the pope for building the family chapel in Bologna, instead of Rome. After a few months the Spada made an agreement with the Barnabite fathers in Bologna. They were allowed to build the façade of the church and the high altar with its marble group and shrine. Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the projects for the shrine and the group was commissioned in 1634 to Alessandro Algardi. The altar was officially inaugurated in 1647. In 1648 Virgilio Spada commissioned a bronze bas-relief to Algardi for the frontal of the same altar, depicting the beheading of St. Paul.  
This beautiful group shows the executioner prepared to cut St. Paul’s head with his sword. The saint looks down and offers his head to the blow. There is a strong contrast between the movement of the executioner’s body and the static attitude of the saint. The bas-relief shows what followed after the execution according to tradition: the saint’s head bounces three times on the ground and creates three springs.
49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.short_description: The group depicts the moment of the beheading of St Paul. Typically, baroque is the juxtaposition between the Saint, already part a heavenly atmosphere, and the executioner with his cruel grimace. The artist succeeds in conveying the tension preceding the blow and the contrast between the saint’s serenity and the executioner’s tense mobility. The beautiful shrine framing the group creates a link with the architecture of the interior of the church.

493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.name: *Model for the Equestrian Sculpture of King Louis XIV*
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.description:
The terracotta model for the equestrian monument to Louis XIV was created by Bernini, already in his seventies, in late 1669 and 1670. The sculpture of the Sun King on horseback was ordered during a trip to Paris by Bernini in 1665, but we know from a letter sent by the artist to Minister Colbert, that it was not confirmed until 1669. The sculptor, who had studied his model carefully in Paris, decided to show him on the Mount of Glory controlling his galloping horse, his sceptre held horizontally; a symbol of regal equity. Although Bernini was not aware of the location intended for the sculpture, he arranged it – in accordance with Baroque taste – favouring a particular view point, in this case from the left, like the contemporary numismatics showing the king on horseback. This work can be traced back to several models both in ancient sculpture and modern painting and sculpture, most notably the model for the equestrian monument of Francis I by Leonardo (Budapest, Szépmuűvészeti Múzeum).  
The sculpture was transported to France in 1685, some years after Bernini's death and, as it did not please the king, it was then moved to Versailles. The work was transformed into Marcus Curtius by the French sculptor François Girardon and placed in a hidden corner of the gardens. The execution of the sculpture is actually quite ordinary: it was done by pupils of the French Academy in Rome and not directly by the artist and his prestigious Roman workshop. This makes the autography of this terracotta model of paramount importance, its bursting vitality reviving the splendour of the Berninian idea and his creative journey.  
The work was sold several times before ending up in the Contini Bonacossi Collection, from where it was given to the Galleria Borghese in 1923, a donation that was made permanent in 1926.
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.short_description: This terracotta was modelled by Bernini in Rome for an equestrian monument of Louis XIV, but the sculpture itself was executed by his pupils. The king, however, did not appreciate the work, and so it was transformed into Marcus Curtius by the French sculptor Francois Girardon, and transferred to Versailles (now at the Louvre).
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.obtention: Donated to the Italian state by the Contini Bonacossi family in 1926.

499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.name: *Kilga*, Jar-stand.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.description: This kilga or jar-stand, was carved from a single block of marble. It has a rectangular open top with legs carved in the form of crouching lions. Around the sides there are relief carvings of lions with an ornamental inscription containing good wishes for the owner. Lions were associated with rulers, suggesting that this object was intended for a palace rather than a religious building. Marble jar-supports of this type are unique to Egypt, used to filter the water of the Nile, thus making it fit to drink. Ibn Ridwan, a physician at the Fatimid court in Cairo in the AH 11th / AD 17th century, wrote: 'The best thing is not to use this water until it has been purified several times … the purified part is placed in a jar; only what seeps through the porosities of the jar will be used'.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.short_description: These marble *kilgas*, or jar-stands, are unique to Egypt. The basin of the stand was intended to support a stone or an unglazed terracotta jar. Being porous, the terracotta jars kept the water cool and also acted as a filter: water would seep through the body of the jar into the basin below.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.dimensions: Height 40 cm, width 39.5 cm, length 56.5 cm.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, the shape and style of decoration belongs to a group of similar objects that are associated with the Fatimid dynasty. The *kufic* script can be found in works of other media and architectural inscriptions from the 5th and 6th / 11th and 12th centuries.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.method_for_provenance: Historical sources mention the practice of water purification to filter water from the Nile; furthermore, this *kilga* was found in Egypt.
499ecee0-d098-5fd0-b896-0867f5949ae9.obtention: Donated by Dr J. M. Rogers in 1988.

4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.name: Model in plaster
4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.description: Following on the European fascination for the oriental world and for the famous Nasrid Palace of the Alhambra (Granada), a lot of reproductions of its remarkable architecture and decorations were made and spread. José Contreras was commended as restorer and decorator and his son, Rafael (1824–1890), was the leading pioneer of this trend in 1847. His work was continued by the grandson and by a huge number of plaster-cast workshops in Granada, and very likely, in other cities. His plasterworks were very successful in the International Exhibitions and were kept in private collections and museums like South Kensington (London). These delightful polychrome models, accentuated with a black frame, represents different rooms form the Alhambra Palace as the Comares Room, with its double horseshoe.
4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.dimensions: 68 x 41 cm; 72 x 53 and 54 x 49 cm
4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes, Cristina Giménez
keywords: Decorations; Design; models; Alhambra

4b67b99b-4bc9-5f80-b3eb-d2fe8c8f1154.name: Fountainhead
4b67b99b-4bc9-5f80-b3eb-d2fe8c8f1154.short_description: This animal, a hind or female deer, would once have stood beside a pool or fountain in one of the palaces of Umayyad Spain. A very similar piece, now in the Cordoba Museum, was discovered in the ruins of the caliphal pleasure-palace of Madinat al-Zahra, where the historian al-Maqqari mentions there being a marble basin adorned with fountain heads in the shape of different animals. The decoration on the hind’s body gives the impression that it is covered in a sumptuous, tasselled textile.
