4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.name: Lion from the Palace of Mushatta.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.description:
The scupture is of a lion lying on a thin rectangular plinth. The sculpture has been well preserved, except for its missing front paws and its, to all appearances, wantonly damaged face. The lion is crouching down on its back paws while supporting itself on the shanks of its front legs, so that the whole body is lying on the ground. Its head is raised and looks forward. The damage it suffered means that the carved details on the head can no longer be made out. A shallowly chiselled mane of short, outward-rolling curls frames the lion’s face from its ears down to the neckline, reaching over its shoulder and down along its back. Its ribs and the outline of its chest are characterised with flatly rendered indentations. Its hindquarters, over which its tail rests, are virtually round. The paws are especially long and wide, and lie close to the body. The pose of this sleek animal suggests that it is intently alert.  
It is possible that lion’s paws that have been discovered separately belong to this sculpture. However, they could also point to the existence of a second sculpture that was intended to complement this one symmetrically in the audience hall of the palace. Lions were an important iconographic element for rulers in Late Antiquity and the Sassanid period, which led to the Umayyad caliphs upholding and pursuing this tradition. This is made particularly visible by the two lions on the podium of the standing caliphs in Khirbat al-Mafjar, which demonstrate that this tradition flourished during the Umayyad period.  
Similar freestanding lion sculptures from the Umayyad period have yet to be discovered at other sites.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.short_description: This majestic lion was found inside the walls of the Palace of Mushatta in Jordan in 1903 in the vicinity of a building complex which may have been planned as an audience hall. Lions were associated with power and strength and were thus appropriate symbols of power in the palace of a Umayyad ruler.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.initial_owner: Probably Caliph al-Walid II (r. AH 125–6 / AD 743–4).
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.dimensions: Height 72 cm, length 122 cm, width 42 cm.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.method_for_datation: The provenance of the object was substantiated through its discovery during the salvage operation of Qasr al-Mushatta in 1903; therefore, it appears to be from the same period as the façade.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.method_for_provenance: The provenance was guaranteed through its discovery during the salvage operation in Qasr al-Mushatta in 1903.
4c2db764-43bb-574c-9e09-b5f486e451c3.obtention: Acquired as a gift from the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II to Emperor Wilhelm II, who presented it to the Royal Museums in Berlin in 1903.

4d98ef31-dc06-5d00-bccf-06eec1cb0a21.name: To What Exiled Country Are You Returning?
4d98ef31-dc06-5d00-bccf-06eec1cb0a21.description: Palestinian artist Ahmad Canaan’s sculpture combines the form of a boat with upright keys to evoke themes of exile, memory and resilience. The boat symbolises journeys and displacement, while the keys recall the Palestinian hope of return to lost homes. The hard metal and minimal design express both fragility and strength, turning the work into a visual object of collective memory and cultural resistance.

4e167204-1a3f-5a86-944d-ab0b42f8681b.name: Parthian Monument: the adoption of the Emperors
4e167204-1a3f-5a86-944d-ab0b42f8681b.description: During his reign, the Emperor Hadrian (figure right) adopted Antoninus Pius (centre left), who in turn adopted the 17-year-old Marcus Aurelius (left) and the eight-year-old Lucius Verus. A head stares from behind Hadrian’s left shoulder, presumably representing the guardian spirit of Aelius Verus, late father of Lucius. A bull is being offered to the gods as a sacrifice.
4e167204-1a3f-5a86-944d-ab0b42f8681b.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities
keywords: Ephesos

4ef3678b-8294-594e-939b-ef240304bdc5.name: *Infant Jesus as the Good Shepherd*
4ef3678b-8294-594e-939b-ef240304bdc5.description:
The ivory carved Indo-Portuguese representation of the Infant Jesus as the Good Shepherd is unique, blending the religious traditions of East and West. Carved in India from a single piece of ivory for a Portuguese patron, it features the Infant Jesus as Good Shepherd, a theme favoured by the Portuguese Empire, and handled here in a peculiar way, far from traditional iconographic models.  
The Infant Jesus sits on a three-tiered rocky mountain, each level of which contains a carved “grotto” within which is a scene from the Life of Christ; from bottom to top are the Adoration of the Shepherds, the Adoration of the Magi and the Baptism. Water cascades down onto the lower scenes.  
At the top, the Holy Trinity is framed by a tall fan-shaped Tree of Jesse, which acts as a backdrop to the entire piece. Below, the seated Infant Jesus plays an instrument similar to a mandolin. God the Father crowns the composition; wearing a triple-crown tiara with a cross He holds His crucified Son. Grapevines – from which heavy bunches of grapes hang – form the shape of a cross, symbolising the Eucharist, the wine from the grapes turning into the blood of Christ. The Holy Spirit is depicted as a dove flying above the Crucified Christ emblazoned on God's chest.  
St. Ignatius Loyola and St. Francis Xavier, founders of the Society of Jesus, flank the central niches of the two upper levels, where there are other saints and scenes from the Life of Christ: the Annunciation, Circumcision and Flight into Egypt. Artworks such as this were intended to reinforce the catechizing strategic mission of the Portuguese Church, framed by the principles of the Counter-Reformation.
4ef3678b-8294-594e-939b-ef240304bdc5.short_description: An ivory carved Indo-Portuguese representation of the Infant Jesus as the Good Shepherd. The Infant sits on a three-tiered rocky mountain featuring scenes from the Life of Christ. The Tree of Jessé, a symbol of the Holy Trinity, fans out as a background.
4ef3678b-8294-594e-939b-ef240304bdc5.holder: Museum and Library of the House of Braganza

*Encompassing the Globe*, catalogue, (ed. Jay A. Levenson) Smithsonian Institute, Washington, 2007.

keywords: Ivory; exotica; Indo-Portuguese work; Good Shepherd; Christian themes; carving; religious object; Jesuit; mission; religious orders

4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.name: Sphinx
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.short_description: This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in 1924 together with the cock in the David Collection and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world. They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads.
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.dates: Hegira 2nd half of the 6th century / AD 2nd half of the 12th century
keywords: Syria; Fritware; zangids; imaginary animal; zoomirphic imagery
materials: Cast, modelled, and carved fritware painted in an opaque white and a turquoise glaze

52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.name: Model of the Bologna Municipal Opera Theatre
52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.description:
This model is the faithful representation of the original project by Antonio Bibiena for the Municipal Opera Theatre of Bologna. It accurately documents the architectural structure and decorative elements of the interior. It is very important because most of these decorations were lost during the XIX century restyling.  
The longitudinal section of the model shows the large stall, the stage, its architectural frame and 4 tiers of boxes as well as the gallery. Tiers of separated boxes all around the hall were an original feature of the Bibiena design specifically meant for the baroque opera theatres. This feature was adopted in the most important European theatres.  
The three “architectural orders” employed on the different tiers reflect the Bolognese sober academic tradition in architecture. Wooden models like this one were made by craftsmen or sculptors following the drawings of the architect. This was common for important buildings, public monuments or cathedrals, since the Renaissance period.  
About 10 years later the theatre was finally opened to the public on the 14th of May 1763 with the representation of *The Triumph of Clelia* by C.W. Gluck.
52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.short_description:
This is the wooden model of the Teatro Comunale of Bologna, proposed between 1755-1763 by the famous architect Antonio Bibiena, one of the last members of the Bibiena Family.  
The construction of the new public theatre for the city was quite troubled and the project presented by the architect caused some polemics among the academic establishment. For that reason, the municipality asked for an accurate model of the building to be exhibited in the town hall so that all citizens could see it and express their opinion on it.
52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.holder: Museo Internazionale e Biblioteca della Musica
52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.owner: Museo Internazionale e Biblioteca della Musica
52384f24-9940-5834-bc9f-a6f4efa2c373.initial_owner: The Municipal theatre and its wooden model were commissioned by the Municipality of Bologna (Comune di Bologna)

54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.name: Jar-stand (*kilga*).
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.description:
Carved from a single block of marble, this jar-stand, locally called a *kilga*, consists of a hollow part, octagonal in cross-section, on four feet and a projecting basin in front. The basin is connected to the hollow part through an opening bridged by a tricuspid arch with two projecting lion-head bosses in the panel above. Four chamfers form shallow column-flanked niches showing a flat carved arch motif. *Muqarnas* (stalactite or honeycomb ornament) occupies the centre of the side panels. The two bosses at the side of the basin are repeated with two smaller ones at the upper edge of the side panels of the hollow part. The wide rim of the basin bears a *kufic* inscription carried over to the hollow part of the stand and continued in a band framing the side panels. On the right side the inscription is completely worn out. On the left side the text is in good condition, though the content is unknown. The feet are decorated with rimmed tongues and connected with tricuspid arches.  
The stands were intended as supports for large unglazed terracotta water-jars. The porous material of the body allowed water to seep from the bottom of the jar. The water filtered in this process could be ladled from the projecting basin as needed for drinking. Jar-stands of this specific form seem to be unique to Egypt from Fatimid into Mamluk times. The striking shape of the jar-stand might be a combination of several earlier Egyptian traditions for purification, storage, cooling and drawing of water. The dependence on the Nile for drinking water required treatment of the water to make it potable. The alabaster jars that are sometimes seen together with the stands, could not be original since the non-porous stone does not let water through. Not one of the earthenware jars is known to have survived, however.
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.short_description: Jar-stand on four feet, carved from a single block of marble and decorated. It consists of a hollow part which was intended to support an unglazed terracotta water-jar. The water which was filtered through the earthenware could be ladled from the projecting basin.
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.dimensions: Height 31 cm, length 64 cm, width 32 cm.
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.method_for_datation: Dating of this kind of jar-stand is difficult. A comparative study of the decorative patterns and their parallels in architecture, for example, is lacking. Stands with *kufic* inscriptions are generally dated to the Fatimid period.
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.method_for_provenance: The object was acquired by F. R. Martin in Cairo. This type of jar-stand seems to be unique to Egypt because all surviving examples were found there.
54eca39b-22aa-51c8-a036-7621d45074f0.obtention: Bought by the museum from the collection of F. R. Martin in 1897.

55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.name: Human head.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.description: Face of a man in his prime. A part of the head and the right side of the face are damaged. The man wears a moustache and a very full beard. The curls of his beard end in circular, shell-like orifices. The iris of the eye is indicated by a fragment of iridescent glass, ovoid in shape. This work has its roots in an ancient North African tradition. It brings to mind numerous stelae dedicated particularly to Saturn, which share the frontal aspect, the beard and the importance accorded to the eyes. However, the statue does bear a strong resemblance to the bas-relief of the prince and the musician found at Mahdiyya. The face appears Oriental but the absence of clothing obviates any definite conclusions.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.short_description: This plaster sculpture shows the face of a man in the prime of life. The style and emphasis of the eyes, forehead and beard are reminiscent of numerous stelae dedicated to Saturn, and the piece also presents some similarities to a piece found in Mahdiyya.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.dimensions: Height 16 cm, width 12 cm, thickness 7 cm.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.method_for_datation: This stucco head was found, among other human and animal carvings, in the excavations carried out at Sabra al-Mansuriyya in 1978. It was found in a very ploughed-up area with no clear archaeological layering. The objects were scattered around in a random manner. One has the impression that someone had tried to eradicate or hide these figurative objects for no obvious reason except that there could be a connection with the changing religious mentality in Ifriqiya. This action could indeed coincide with the persecution of the Shi'ites during the troubles in 407 / 1016 or following the split between the Zirid emirate and the Fatimid caliphate in 440 / 1048–9. This date could be a *terminus post quem*. The *terminus ante quem* is just after the founding of Sabra in 337 / 948. Any further precision is rendered impossible due to the lack of a definite archaeological layer.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.method_for_provenance: The manufacture of these objects, which is unique in Ifriqiya and in the Maghreb, appears to have taken place in Sabra al-Mansuriyya and to have been commissioned by the Shi'ites.
55179813-b0e7-5c56-9d77-119429fc40fd.obtention: After its discovery at Sabra al-Mansuriyya, this piece was placed in the site storehouse. It was acquired in 1992 by the Museum at Raqqada. It will be displayed in the second section of the Museum, currently under construction.

556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.name: Ablutions basin.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.description:
This parallelepipedic tank marked with plain striations on the inside, the short sides and the corners, was beautifully adorned on the outside, and almost all of the decoration has survived on two sides. The design on the decorated face, whose inscription has been destroyed, is divided into two styles. The first one, rising from the base, consists of a large frieze of grooved foliage, dotted with buds and rosettes and wide-veined plain palms with calyxes, and double ones with acanthus leaves and buds. The second comprises a strip in relief with two lines of grooved intersecting knotwork, one curved and the other straight, bearing fleurons and veined palms. It is framed by an edge, set back, formed by vegetal knotwork accentuated with small stylised palm leaves in the shape of six-pointed stars.  
The short side is occupied by two identical animal scenes, sculpted on two vertical panels separated by an empty space. On each panel, there is an eagle spreading its tail, carrying two quadrupeds on its wings and two gazelles from its claws. Two winged ibex confronting each other on either side of a fleuron finish the scene in the lower part.  
Most of the ornamentation on the other two sides has been destroyed, leaving only the text in *kufic* characters sculpted in relief on the rim and the decoration of the framing ribbon on the large side, which consists of a frieze of aquatic birds and fish alternating on a plant background.  
The surviving elements of the inscription that crowned the entire rim of the tank include the last digit of the hegira date (300), and the name of the patron, 'Abd al-Malik, *hajib* (chamberlain) of Hisham II.  
The design and animal scenes of this beautiful example of Caliphate artwork are reminiscent of the tank at al-Mansur and would appear to be from the same Madinat al-Zahira marble workshop in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.short_description: This basin is the work of a marble workshop in Madinat al-Zahira, Córdoba, the princely city built by al-Mansur. It was brought to Marrakesh by 'Ali ibn Yusuf and placed in the ablutions room of the Great Mosque.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.dimensions: Height 70 cm, length 155 cm, width 82 cm, depth 50 cm, thickness of sides 10 cm, thickness of base 20 cm.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_datation:
1\. The inscription, partially destroyed, sculpted on the upper rim of the tank reads '(the year) three hundred, in the name of God! God's blessing. Victory and divine assistance to the Hajib \[followed with his honours\] Abu Marwan 'Abd al-Malik ibn Amir (…), this is part of what he commissioned (…)'.  
2\. We know that 'Abd al-Malik was appointed *hajib* of Hisham II between 381 and 398 / 991 and 1008) by his father al-Mansur.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_provenance: Although it was discovered in the Ibn Yusuf Madrasa in Marrakesh, which belongs to the Sa'did period (10th / 16th century), the name of the patron and the comparative study with the al-Mansur basin in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid suggest that it was originally from Madinat al-Zahira in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.obtention: As state property from a historical monument.

58b9817a-c39c-5ed0-9922-32e3e0ccbd6a.name: The bronze statue representing 22 countries of member of Universal Postal Union
58b9817a-c39c-5ed0-9922-32e3e0ccbd6a.short_description: The Universal Postal Union was created in 1874, initially under the name "General Postal Union", as a result of the Treaty of Bern signed on 9 October 1874. The UPU is a specialized agency of the United Nations that coordinates postal policies among member nations, in addition to the worldwide postal system. Transportation freedom is guaranteed with this treaty.
keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service

5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.name: *Angel I*
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.description: This monumental figure of an angel is part of the sculpted decoration of the Minorite Church in Znojmo, only fragments of which have survived. The sculpture with its preserved polychromy, gilded robe and wings has retained its expressive air despite the loss of its former link with the architecture of the altar retable. Despite its larger-than-life size it features precise carving, full volume and a reduced means of expression: an elegant gesture of the hand and decoratively sculpted locks. The face has Heinz’s original trademark modelling of the nose, arches above the eyes and, in particular the chin. The figure testifies to the sculptor’s sense of monumentality. Heinz was among only a few sculptors in Moravia whose starting point was the Czech Radical Baroque style. His first experience as a sculptor was under the tutorage of Jan Sturmer in Olomouc and then in the circle of Matyáš Bernard Braun; he also collaborated with Severin Tischler. The decoration of the garden and funeral chapel in Velké Losiny Chateau exhibits the influence of Baltasar Permoser. Heinz first lived in Olomouc and travelled in Moravia. In 1755 he joined the Dominican Monastery in Znojmo. Whilst there he produced statues for the grounds and decorated altars predominantly in the Znojmo area (Lechovice, Louka, Šatov).
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.short_description: The *Angel* figure testifies to the sculptor's sense of monumentality for retable compositions. Heinz was among only a few sculptors in Moravia whose starting point was the Czech Radical Baroque style. The sculpture features precise carving, full volume and a reduced means of expression.
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.obtention: The sculpture comes from the decoration of a Franciscan (originally Minorite) Monastery. Around 1843 part of the interior was transferred to the Church of St. Anne, Znojmo, from whence it passed to the Museum of South Moravia, located on the premises of the former Minorite Monastery.

5e131b15-3042-5b4a-bc07-e72c9fb0b7fb.name: Figures in Turkish style
5e131b15-3042-5b4a-bc07-e72c9fb0b7fb.description: In these two porcelain figures, it is showed through the clothes, and combined with the Rococo style of the bases. Produced by many European manufactures at the time, this kind of objects could be easily found in rooms as the *fumoir*, usually decorated in an Orientalist style to recreate exoticism.

5fafc343-ccfd-52d3-8bd4-f2f311ffa1cf.name: *Bust of Clement XII*
5fafc343-ccfd-52d3-8bd4-f2f311ffa1cf.description:
Pietro Bracci produced a large number of works, mainly portraits. He was one of the most important late Baroque sculptors of the 18th century in Rome, and was involved in the creation of the Trevi Fountain. He was trained in the Baroque tradition based on the work of Gian Lorenzo Bernini and classical equilibrium.  
There is no documentary evidence linking the bust to the sculptor, nor any explicit references in the work-log that Bracci was in the habit of keeping after 1725, but the attribution is generally accepted by scholars.  
It is dated around the time of the pontificate of Clement XII Corsini, which lasted from 1730 to 1740, although it is possible that the bust was made after his death.  
The ageing face of the pope is sculpted faithfully, reproducing the lines infused with deep expressiveness and intelligence, key characteristics of the artist's portraits. The pontificate's vestments are finely decorated and tied at the chest, while the fur-trimmed cloak and underlying *mozzetta*  
(a short elbow length cape worn by Catholic clergy) are sculpted to achieve an elegant volume of folds that create a play of light and shadow.  
There are other busts of the pope, although full information is not available for all of them. Of particular interest is the one currently in Ravenna, which may have been intended for the pontificate's tomb in Laterano, and the bust of Clement XII, currently exhibited in the Galleria Nazionale di Arte Antica, which was acquired in 1927.  
The portrait of the pope in the Galleria Borghese was donated to the museum in 1910 by the Istituto dei Ciechi at the Baths of Diocletian.
5fafc343-ccfd-52d3-8bd4-f2f311ffa1cf.short_description: Pietro Bracci follows the Baroque tradition seen in Bernini's psychological portrait, *Cardinal Scipione Borghese*. Bracci was one of the sculptors involved in the creation of the Trevi Fountain.

621e7f00-7493-56e2-823c-2c4e19a49512.name: Fragments of plaster.
621e7f00-7493-56e2-823c-2c4e19a49512.description:
This panel is composed of two plaster fragments that have been sculpted with decorative motifs consisting of interweaving bands punctuated by blue painted pearls against a red background. These bands form eight-cornered stars, inside which appear flowers that feature three petals.  
This type of decoration is quite common in the palaces of the Qal'at Bani Hammad. The paintwork on the majority of fragments has worn off through time.
621e7f00-7493-56e2-823c-2c4e19a49512.short_description: Two plaster fragments sculpted with motifs consisting of interlaced bands punctuated by blue painted pearls on a red background. The bands form eight-pointed stars containing three-petal flowers. This type of covering was used to decorate the dome at the Palace of the Sea (Dar al-Bahr).

623ac570-c51d-5c93-af68-2dca3ce23ce0.name: Suspended Together
623ac570-c51d-5c93-af68-2dca3ce23ce0.description: Manal Al Dowayan’s Suspended Together can be used to question the assumption that the existence of roads, routes, and transport systems automatically means freedom of movement. Created in 2011, the installation refers to a period when Saudi women needed permission from a male guardian in order to travel. The suspended white doves suggest flight, mobility, and freedom, yet their stillness reveals a condition of restriction. In this sense, the work is especially relevant for discussing travel and infrastructure from a gendered perspective: even when roads exist, not everyone has equal access to movement. The piece reminds viewers that mobility is not only a matter of physical routes, but also of law, social permission, gender, and power. For this reason, the work can be used to expand a discussion of travel in the region beyond railways and roads, toward the unequal social conditions that determine who is allowed to move.

6857e440-8f5f-5412-a588-b0da5f2afb45.name: *Bust of the Cardinal Scipione Borghese*
6857e440-8f5f-5412-a588-b0da5f2afb45.description:
In 1605 when Paul V became Pope, he immediately made his nephew Scipione a cardinal, despite his young age, quickly promoting him to a position comparable to secretary of state. This enormous power allowed the cardinal-nephew to create a splendid home and a marvellous art collection over a decade, in an unorthodox manner.  
The bust portrait of Scipione by Gian Lorenzo Bernini was sculpted for his first major patron in 1632, after a creative hiatus of nearly seven years as a sculptor, during which he developed a new concept in portraits, more representative of the vibrant Baroque style.  
The spontaneous and intense pose, the arrangement of the bust with the head turned in a slight movement, the attentive gaze and the mouth open in an expression of vague wonderment combine to create a highly expressive, almost colloquial relation with the viewer.  
The cloth folds in the *mozzetta* (a short elbow length cape worn by Catholic clergy) and the detail of the small unfastened button showing us the live body beneath the clothes are an integral and involving part of the piece.  
The marked confidence displayed by this excellent example of a Baroque style of which Bernini was a master gives an intimate and human dimension to the sitter, despite his official status.  
With the bust almost finished, a hairline fracture opened up in the marble around the forehead, due to the stresses of the sculpting tools. The sculptor was forced to produce a second version of the bust at very short notice. This shows how little attention Bernini paid to his choice of marble, something that was of fundamental importance for other sculptors, such as Michelangelo. Despite the crack, the Cardinal requested that both works be delivered to him, keeping both in the Galleria Borghese.
6857e440-8f5f-5412-a588-b0da5f2afb45.short_description: Cardinal Borghese, the pope’s nephew, was a passionate collector and looked after the cultural policy of the papal court. He had a sensitive instinct for artistic quality and gave a boost to the birth of the Baroque. Bernini renders the Cardinal life-like; the transience of human feeling and the expression of inner emotions are part of the Baroque aesthetic.
6857e440-8f5f-5412-a588-b0da5f2afb45.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

6ac7d68d-dd1a-5e3a-afaa-4d2652475c9f.name: Concavity. Deppari; Projection Series
6ac7d68d-dd1a-5e3a-afaa-4d2652475c9f.description:
Toshio Iezumi (1954) began to work with glass in 1983, at the Tokyo Glass Art Institute. It was at this time that he began to work with glass sheets. His sources of inspiration are very broad, from the bronze originating in Ancient China to the most recent works of Constantin Brâncuşi and Donald Judd.  
Upon graduating in 1985, Iezumi developed and perfected the technique for which he is known today. He began sticking the sheets of glass using a special adhesive cured by UV light, creating an initial block with a similar shape to a cube. It should be noted that the sheets are not placed at random. The sheet which will be furthest away from the spectator tends to be a mirrored sheet. This is a way in which to play with the reflective properties of the glass itself. Thermal glass can be interspersed or finished among the normal sheet glass in order to play with the refraction of light from the different types of glass. He then grinds and sculpts this block until the desired shape is achieved. After this initial grind using a diamond blade, a pneumatic machine is used to sand and polish the piece. This step involves seven sub-steps in order to achieve a pure, delicate finish (with a pneumatic water fed grinder with a grain of between 60 and 1000, finished with a felt disk in cerium oxide). After hours of work he achieves the depth, optic effects and the degree of transparency desired for his work.

6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.name: Funerary panel
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.short_description: This small panel, rectangular in shape, bears a decoration carved in bas-relief on one of the two faces, which suggests that it was designed to be embedded in the wall of a religious monument. The panel is almost complete and in a good condition. The lower corners and the upper right corner are missing. There are gaps on top. A niche design occupies the central section of the panel, framed on three sides by an epigraphic band. The niche is composed by a pointed horseshoe arch resting on two lateral columns with pyramidal bases and vase-shaped capitals. A short inscription, divided on two lines, is engraved inside the arch. The two inscriptions are engraved with a thin, shallow stroke, and executed in a late *kufic* style with slightly bilobed apexes, provided with diacritical marks. The text of the frame, on one line, contains an epitaph and reads on the right side: *\[hadha\] qabr al-Hakim al-Faqih Ahmad b.*, on the upper side: *Sulayman al-Shuruti*, and on the left side: *rahmatu llah ʿalayhi wa-salla llahu ʿa*\[…\]. These are translated as: '\[This is\] the tomb of al-Ḥākim al-Faqīh Aḥmad b. // Sulaymān al-\[…\] // May God’s mercy be upon him and may blessings of God be upon \[…\]'. The text inside the arch reads: *Allahu akbar*. The text enclosed in the outer frame is preserved in its entirety, except for the first and last words, which have been lost. The epitaph is undated and dedicated to a law scholar (*faqīh*) whose nisba has not yet been deciphered. Note that the invocation at the end of the text contains an expression (*salla Allah ʿala…*) that is usually intended for the Prophet.
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.method_for_datation: The shape and size of the panel, as well as the palaeographic features of the two texts suggest a date no earlier than the late 16th century. A close comparison with the other similar panels with niche designs found in Ghazni is missing. The other specimens are ascribed to a more ancient period, between the 11th and 13th centuries, and differ both in the shape of the niche and in the writing styles and (and above all) in the content of the texts. In no case, in fact, is there an epitaph.
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.method_for_provenance: This funerary element was documented by the Italian Archaeological Mission in 1966, reused in one of the walls of the Ziyārat Ramak, located a few kilometers from the city of Ghazni (MAIA, Inv. No. IG0063; Neg. Nos. 3823/2,3; Fig. a).
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.bibliography: Massulo, Martina, “Marble Tombs From Ghazni (Fifteenth-Eighteenth Centuries): Morphological and Epigraphic Remarks”, *Eurasian Studies*, 13 (2015): 54-67.
6bbafa48-66dc-52f4-bf7a-3cc4fe5e25c9.author: Roberta Giunta
keywords: Funerary slab; marble; epitaph

6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.name: The Victims of Labour
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.short_description: Vincenzo Vela studied at the academy of Fine arts of Brera and at the age of 22 he won an Academy of Venice competition. The artwork is an homage to the workers who died during the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel between 1872-82, which had implemented new cost-lowering techniques that also caused numerous incidents and loss of life. Work conditions were very unhealthy: temperatures over 30 degrees, gas exhalations and no air shafts. Even the accommodations were unhealthy and dirty. When the workers went on strike for the inhumane conditions, police shot at protesters, killing four workers. The miners in *The Victims of Labour* are depicted carrying the body of a dying classmate on a stretcher out of the tunnel. A self-portrait of the sculptor is recognisable in the classmate’s face. The harsh modelling of the workers’ bodies, almost deformed, makes the scene even more powerful. The artist affirmed he had no commission for this work which was a passion project. In 1895 it was cast in bronze on request of the Ministry of Education; in 1900 it was sent to the Universal Exhibition in Paris.

6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.name: *St. John the Evangelist*
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.description:
St. John the Evangelist, gospel author and apocalyptic visionary, holds the Book of Revelations, with seals. At his feet is an eagle, one of his attributes. The eagle's mighty flight and the ancient belief that the bird could shade (or stop) the sun contributed to its coming to symbolise the soul and a mystic vision of God. Much of the animal symbolism of the Evangelists is derived from the Old Testament vision of Ezekiel (Ez 1:10). The eagle was attributed to John by the Church Father Hieronymus.  
The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. The cloak, running from the left shoulder around the right hip opens into a mighty relief train that fills the space between the book and a pedestal on the right, the outline of the figure thus appearing compact. Schweigl ornamented the soft surface of the statue with folds and incisions in the hem of the cloak. The soulful face corresponds with traditional representations of St. John the Evangelist, his fine facial features off-set with locks of wavy hair. The visual effect of the sculpture is enhanced by the treatment of its surfaces: gold plate combined with matt and gloss finishes.  
The artist's development included being apprenticed to his father who came from Tyrol. After studying at the Vienna Academy and following his father's death, Schweigl took over the family workshop in Brno. The workshop, which also functioned as a private art academy, produced sculptures for the whole of Moravia, part of Silesia. A series of sculptures for the Church of St. James was one of Schweigl's first independent commissions. He wrote several manuscripts on art and artists in Moravia intended for pedagogical schools, which laid the foundations of art history research in Moravia.  
In a later phase, Schweigl employed the St. John figure in a statue of the saint for a side altar in Vranov Church near Brno.
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.short_description: The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot placed forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. It was one of Schweigl’s first independent commissions. His writing on art laid foundations for art history in Moravia and his workshop’s output covered Moravia and parts of Silesia.

During Re-Gothicization in 1865, the sculpture along with the rest of the contents, were transferred to the parsonage. It has been museum property since 1947.

6e327e6c-97a6-5021-bdda-e534a67a0765.name: Reserve head
6e327e6c-97a6-5021-bdda-e534a67a0765.description: The *Reserve head* is one of the major works of the Viennese collection, found in an early tomb in the burial grounds of Giza. Though stylized, the visage is still full of life, with simultaneously idealized and very regular features. Scholars still disagree about the purpose of this type of object. Traditional explanations proffer their use as surrogate heads for the soul (mummifying having then been only in its earliest stages).
6e327e6c-97a6-5021-bdda-e534a67a0765.dates: 4th Dyn. c. 2600 BC; acquired by Hermann Junker during his excavation in Giza 1912–1929

6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.name: *Aeneas and Anchises*
6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.description:
This is the first work that a young Bernini completed for Scipione Borghese, who already owned a Barocci painting of the same theme. The subject, taken from Virgil's *Aeneid*, was potent for the Cardinal because it confirmed a dynastic celebration, Aeneas being considered an ancestor of the Borghese family, while simultaneously representing the birth of Rome. Aeneas, fleeing Troy with his father Anchises and his son Ascanius, arrived in Lazio and founded the eternal city. As a result, this subject acquired by analogy an historical and theological value: Ancient Rome and the Roman Church. The flight of Aeneas was also related to the Christian idea of *pietas romana*, while the figure of the hero symbolised the political role assumed by Scipione during the papacy of his aging uncle (in Latin, *scipio*, the staff that bears, as Aeneas supports Anchises).  
The sculpture retains the compactness of the block shape on a vertical axis into which the contrasting movement of the figures is woven, taken from the previous late-Mannerist period in Tuscany. On account of its transitional style, it has long been assumed to be the joint work of Pietro Bernini, the famous sculptor of Pope Paul V, and his young son. However, recently discovered documents unequivocally ascribe the work to Gian Lorenzo.  
The definition of the muscles and the plasticity of the shapes demonstrate Bernini's awareness of Hellenistic art, as well as Raffaello and the Carraccis. The sculptor is undertaking a study of ancient art, integrating it into the new language of art, with its psychology and drama, which would later be known as the Baroque.  
Bernini paid attention to the tactile quality of the marble, finishing the surface with different tools. This allowed him to create contrasts between finishes, achieving the illusion of colour and assimilating the sculpture to a painting.
6f46e756-ebc7-53f0-b7ab-a41b14c33d87.short_description: The artist pays attention to the tactile quality of the marble surface to obtain the illusion of colour. Aeneas's escape from Troy had an historical-theological meaning: the concept of *imperium* is moved to the Roman Church. The theme symbolises the *pietas romana* and Scipione's political role.

6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.name: *Sleep*
6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.description:
According to the payments made, the sculpture was commissioned between 1635 and 1636 by the nephew of Paul V, Marcantonio Borghese, with the mediation of Marcello Provenzale. It shows a *putto* with light, butterfly wings sleeping deeply. On his head, beside his arm and along his body are opium poppies, which allude symbolically to sleep, as does the small dormouse curled up on the rock. The subject relates to the literary description in Cesare Ripa's *Iconology* (1603), essential reading for artists in the 17th and 18th centuries, who drew on it constantly to compose allegorical subjects. The dormouse was considered to represent sleep or the “third phase” of the night, the “black” phase.  
The choice of the valuable and extremely hard Belgian marble (or “touchstone”) was probably due both to iconographic considerations and the artist's desire to show his skill in rendering soft flesh and the limp abandon of the limbs. The work, highly inspired by ancient sculpture, was thought to be an archaeological find in the early 18th century. Placed in Villa Pinciana and extolled by contemporary sources, the room housing it was given the name “sleep room”. It was accompanied by two vases with handles formed by entwined snakes, also in black marble, made in 1638 by Silvio Calci of Viterbo (active in Rome in the first half of the 17th century), possibly also alluding to sleep. Therefore the whole composition can be interpreted as an allegory for sleep, or maybe death.  
Compared to Bernini's grandiose and theatrical style, which characterised the entire Roman Baroque period, Algardi's style is marked by a greater classicism and a more lyrical tone, attributes that were particularly appreciated in the final years of the 17th century.
6ff68fbe-d897-52f5-a9e9-6b04552c0b6b.short_description: The sculpture is an allegorical representation. Black marble was chosen because it is a colour associated with the idea of night and sleep. The work shows an attention to antique art and the work of Bernini.

70400fa1-9e1b-5253-b587-686c8eff3455.name: Head
70400fa1-9e1b-5253-b587-686c8eff3455.description:
Martin Janecký is one of the best-known Czech artists for his use of a technique based on modelling from inside a bubble of melted glass, known as “inside sculpting”. This technique requires great precision in order to control the thickness of the glass, its temperature and ductility, in addition to great skill in managing the tools. Martin works with the help of incredibly skilled assistants who work with him in perfect synchronisation. Janecký can be identified primarily for his head and hand sculptures,  
created with diverse attitudes, textures and tones.  
Martin began to work with glass at age 13 in his father’s factory. He graduated from the Glass School in Nový Bor in 1998, and it wasn’t until 2003 that he began to gain international acknowledgement following his trip to a glass symposium at the Corning Museum of Glass.  
He has been a guest artist at numerous glass schools, workshops and museums across the globe, demonstrating how he creates his sculptures. Some of these include the Corning Studio, Museum of Glass (USA), Pilchuck Glass School, Tacoma Museum of Glass, Stand Wood, Chrysler, Norfolk, Bronholm, Rietvel and at the Real Fábrica de Cristales de La Granja, where he created this piece during his stay in 2017.

72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.name: Marble balustrade.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.description:
A marble balustrade consisting of nine adjoining pointed arches identical in form and dimensions, and supported by coupled columns of which there are close to 20. The details on the columns as well as on the capitals differ from each other but each pair of columns and their corresponding capitals are identical. The spandrel, the area between the arches, is ornamented with a series of carved marble circles. The column capitals assume one of two forms: the first resembles a finely detailed and knotted Corinthian capital and the second inclines more toward simplicity, approximating a whirling pomegranate blossom. The arches are decorated with carved ornamentation in the form of a knight's blazon. The decorative details on the pillars are varied but are distinguished generally by a chain of number “7s” wrapped around the body of the column in a vertical or horizontal format. The arches rest on marble panels, each supported by a pair of capitals on top of the coupled columns.  
This balustrade was originally in the Aqsa Mosque, where it is likely that its function was decorative. It was then transferred to the Islamic Museum following the renovation of the mosque. It is possible that this piece is tied to, with regard to the material, craftsmanship and technique of carving, a Crusader frieze (also at the Museum), which was transferred from the Dome of the Rock. Perhaps this piece was crafted in the same workshop as an atelier renowned for its high-quality carved marble was active in the Haram al-Sharif during the same period.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.short_description: This is a marble balustrade composed of nine adjoining tapered arches, identical in form and dimensions. They are supported by pairs of close to 20 pillars. The balustrade is a product of the Crusader period (Romanesque style).  It is relatively simple in appearance and detail. It was placed in al-Aqsa Mosque for decoration.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.dimensions: Height 84 cm, length 348 cm, depth 12 cm.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.method_for_datation: This piece was dated by comparison of both its technique and artistic style with pieces produced in the same period in Palestine, which were acquired by the Islamic Museum.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.method_for_provenance: The registers of the Islamic Museum indicate that the piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum in 1938. The balustrade appears in photographs published by R. W. Hamilton in 1949 showing the interior of the mosque before the balustrade was moved to the Museum. It is plausible that it was made in Jerusalem since large architectural pieces were usually made on site and a workshop was active in the Haram al-Sharif during the same period.
72cd6b04-4359-5c17-b1d0-29c1ddfe315f.obtention: The piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque in 1938.

736574db-9cd1-5e72-95d5-f1860d3596ad.name: *Mashrabiyya*
736574db-9cd1-5e72-95d5-f1860d3596ad.short_description: The *mashrabiyya* is a decorative architectural element characteristic of residences in the Arab world. It was generally used on windows or balconies on the second floor or above. As well as being a natural ventilation device, the *mashrabiyya* served the purpose of shielding the occupant from the vision of passers' by, whilst still allowing natural light to pass through the gaps. This particular piece is square shaped and made of limestone, sculpted in floral patterns.

keywords: Floral decoration; floral art; Architecture

736a018e-a855-56c6-a0e4-184b1dba4cd5.name: Male head
736a018e-a855-56c6-a0e4-184b1dba4cd5.description: South Arabia (Yemen) has always been famous for its incense. The cultivation and widespread trade of this desirable product turned Yemen into a very important region with a highly autonomous culture. This kind of head, sculpted on tombstones, portrayed the subject partly as abstract idealization and yet in a very naturalistic way.

737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.name: *St. Florian*
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.description:
The wooden statue of *St. Florian* has a counterpart, *St. Donatus*, both of which are one and a-half times life-size. Both pieces were transferred to the National Museum in Budapest on permanent loan from the town of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) in 1892. There is documentary data to confirm that *St. Florian* was part of the interior furnishing of the Parish Church of Our Lady, on which Stanetti worked between 1763 and 1764.  
In 1880 a landslide meant that the church was demolished and that the furnishing was taken out of the church and scattered among various locations. Most of the statues are now in Slovakian museums.  
It is known that the two gilded statues *St. Donatus* and *St. Florian* were originally placed independently in the nave. The two saints, which belong to the age of imperial Rome, had been revered since the Middle Ages as protectors from lightning, hailstorms and fire.  
The sculptures portray both saints as sturdy athletic men with reserved gestures, and their heroic poses are borrowed from stone sculpture similar to those erected near to vineyards and wheat fields. *St. Donatus* wears a wreath of leaves on his head and holds a bundle of lightning bolts to his chest; the sheaf of wheat that he originally held in his left hand is lost. Helmeted *St. Florian* has a burning house at his feet and a pail in his right hand. The flag from his left hand is lost.  
Dionysius Ignatius Stanetti, who made both sculptures, was a descendant of a noted Silesian dynasty of sculptors. His uncle, Johann (Giovanni) Stanetti perhaps toured Italy and was employed by the court circle in Vienna. Dionysius Stanetti moved to Hungary in the 1740s. He was married in Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) and was a burgher of the town until his death. Apart from the Late Baroque furnishings in the churches of the neighbourhood, he also created monumental public memorials: the Holy Trinity columns in Besztercebánya (Banská Štiavnica) and Körmöcbánya (Kremnica).
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.short_description: The Silesian, Dionysius Ignatius Stanetti, settled in Hungary. His sculptures from Upper Hungarian mining towns are well known. The church of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica) was demolished in the 1880s after a landslide and consequently the Baroque furnishings were scattered throughout the region. The two quality sculptures of *St. Donatus* and *St. Florian* were both deposited by Kremnica town in trust to Budapest.
737ab478-03ce-5011-915a-c7ab2ff80e33.obtention: Originally from the Roman Catholic Parish Church of Körmöcbánya (Kremnica), the two sculptural saints were initially deposited in 1892 at the National Museum in Budapest in perpetuity; in 1950 the sculptures were transferred to the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest, and in 1974 to the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest.

7aeb03eb-d2c3-50a9-9ca0-0776ebf921fd.name: Sarcophagus of the mourning women
7aeb03eb-d2c3-50a9-9ca0-0776ebf921fd.short_description: In the Sarcophagus of the Crying Women, found at the Royal Necropolis in Sidon like the Alexander Sarcophagus, nothing could be found other than the bones of its owner and a bronze belt buckle, since it had been robbed in an earlier time. From the partial traces on the marble that remained until today, it is understood that it had been dyed in blue and red initially. It is the best example of the group called by archaeologists "Sarcophagi with Columns", and it is considered as a final resting place, like the "Mausoleum of Halicarnassus" or the "Nereid Monument", rather than a tomb. Its architectural features were used in the architecture of the old building of the İstanbul Archaeological Museums. It is an example of Greek sculpture displaying Eastern influences. The shaved heads, bare feet, ragged clothes of the figures and their movements and expressions of sadness are features of Semitic societies. It is thought to be the sarcophagus of the King of Sidon, Straton (374-358 BC), who was said to have led a life of pleasure. The sarcophagus has the shape of an Ionian temple.
7aeb03eb-d2c3-50a9-9ca0-0776ebf921fd.dates: It is thought to be the sarcophagus of the King of Sidon, Straton (374-358 BC)
keywords: Sarcophagus Sidon; The Hellenistic Period; Istanbul Archaeological Museums

7eacd600-e860-593a-aed7-a9329d9d9011.name: Fragment of the Parthenon frieze
7eacd600-e860-593a-aed7-a9329d9d9011.description: The climax of the Greater Panathenaia, the chief festival of Athens, held in honour of Athena, was a procession which ended with the presentation of the newly woven *peplos* (a woman’s garment) to the tutelary goddess of the city. This is the subject of the frieze around the cella of the Parthenon, the temple on the Athenian Acropolis. This fragment depicts the garment being handed over in the presence of the goddess.
7eacd600-e860-593a-aed7-a9329d9d9011.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities
keywords: Athens; Acropolis; Franz Ferdinand

7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.name: Megaplanet
7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.description:
Artist Josh Simpson has been influenced by the Studio Glass movement since his career began in 1972. However, a creativity crisis in 1989 led to a U-turn in his career. He decided to take a break and delve into the world of Venetian glass in order to learn the Murrine and Filigree techniques. Inspired by his wife’s experiences and images of the Earth and Space, as captured by NASA, he embarked on the creation of his series of work, *Megaplanets*.  
These pieces are very challenging to create. They were born of the creation of the murrines and filigrees for each individual planet. These murrines were then stored for months until they were used. Upon creation of the Megaplanet, silver was melted with a small gob inflated piece of glass. He then continued to work with the marble, adding sheets of glass, one by one, as required. Sheets of gold or platinum, glass enamel, bubbles and many more are then added to these layers. The process takes around eight hours. It is then placed into the annealing furnace. Depending on the size of the Planet, this process can take months. This technique creates pieces similar to paperweights which recreate impressive landscapes.  
In 2003, the Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio organised an exclusive exhibition of his work. Following its closure, the artist donated this piece to the Museum.
7ec7333d-9cff-5b8d-b9c4-f322d00e2d87.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja

7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.name: Stone cenotaph.
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.description:
This large rectangular profusely decorated stone cenotaph belongs to a type that was widely distributed in Syria and Mesopotamia during the AH 6th / AD 12th century. The shape is reminiscent of a classical sarcophagus with a concave base, a cubic centre composed of two side stones, a front and a back stone, a solid convex lintel and a separate lid on the top (today some of the stones are broken). The decoration consists of a magnificent inscription in foliated *kufic* script taken from the Qur'anic verse “Ayat al-Kursi” (“Throne Verse”). The verse runs in bands around all four sides of the tomb, only interrupted by the carved vine-stem motif corner blocks. Two weave-like friezes decorate the base and the lintel of the cenotaph. Four small vertical cartouches are centrally located on each side of the cenotaph. These mention the deceased, Husayn b. Hasan al-Shukri, but no date.  
The form and decoration of this cenotaph belongs to the theme of classical continuity in stone carving, typical of Northern Syria during the early Zangid period. The intricate inscription has a close counterpart in the epigraphy of the Madrasa al-Shu'aybiyya, dated AH 545 / AD 1150, which is one of the last examples of the use of *kufic* script in monumental architecture in Syria before it was generally replaced by cursive *naskhi* and *thuluth* scripts.  
The cenotaph was found in the Cemetery of Salihin, one of the oldest and certainly the most prestigious funerary site in Aleppo. The cemetery lies to the south of the city and extends around Maqam Ibrahim, an ancient shrine containing a sacred rock associated with the Prophet Abraham, and thus an auspicious burial ground. It is now located in the National Museum of Aleppo.
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.short_description: Originally located in the most prestigious cemetery of Aleppo, the Cemetery of Salihin, which has legendary connections with Abraham, this cenotaph is one of the best surviving examples of AH 6th / AD 12th century Syrian stone carving and *kufic* calligraphy.
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.dimensions: Height 98 cm (with cover) 126 cm, length 190 cm, width 93.3 cm.
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.method_for_datation: The cenotaph was dated by stylistic criteria and by comparison with other finds. Another well-known but badly preserved cenotaph of the same type is exhibited in the National Museum of Damascus: the tomb of the Artuqid ruler Balak b. Bahram b. Artuq who fell against the Crusaders near Manbij in 518 / 1124 and was buried in Aleppo (Inv. No. 1051).
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.provenance: Salihin Cemetery, south of old Aleppo, Syria.
7f96985d-fe50-5ad6-9b89-32ac54812a59.obtention: The cenotaph was still *in situ* at the Salihin Cemetery when the area was surveyed by archaeologists Jean Sauvaget and Ernst Herzfeld during the 1930s and 1950s respectively.

81099b4c-753f-53ba-9785-217e53613a49.name: Madonna and Child
81099b4c-753f-53ba-9785-217e53613a49.description: It was not roses that guarded the sleep of the enthroned Madonna with the Child, but human bones. And her sleep lasted not for a hundred years, but for several centuries. The sculpture was piously buried in the charnel house of the church of Raron according to a custom prevalent in Europe at the time, and gradually vanished beneath the skulls and bones of the dead. The reason for burying the wooden figure was provided by the rebuilding of the parish church between 1510 and 1515. The Romanesque Madonna had fallen out of fashion and was no longer needed. The person who finally kissed her awake again was not Prince Charming, but a tradesman from the canton of Valais. During restoration work on the charnel house of Raron in 1924, he was told to clear out the bones – and so he stumbled upon several sculptures, including the most significant example of Romanesque art in Switzerland.
keywords: Madonna; Child; Sculpture; Raron; Vallais
materials: Carved in the round, limewood, polychromy

81262916-5478-5649-8cbf-3097f53ac172.name: *Archangel Gabriel*
81262916-5478-5649-8cbf-3097f53ac172.description:
The sculpture has a counterpart in a statue of Archangel Raphael, also in the collections of the Moravian Gallery. The angels were part of a Marian altar shaped as a column aedicule retable. The elegance of the columns and gracefulness of the individually approached movements stem from a free and full projection of the figures into space, if somewhat limited by the original altar architecture. In the dynamic meticulously modelled gown, the artist differentiated the fineness of the under-garment wrapping the body and worked into tiny folds, from the heavy folds of the upper attire encircling the figure in generous, carved-in wraps, creating a sweeping, melodious movement. The gesture of the angel’s right hand symbolises the Annunciation, the left hand is shaped to hold a lily, a symbol of the immaculate conception.  
Gothic churches in Bohemian and Moravian towns, refurbished in the Counter-Reformation period, were “re-Gothicized” in the late 19th century. Like this sculpture, their interior equipment passed on to smaller churches and museums. This is one of only a handful of preserved works by Richter, a remarkable but lesser-known sculptor from Olomouc. He created three altars for the Dome of St. Wenceslas in Olomouc (later transferred to Náměšt na Hané) and designed a monstrance for the church. Together with Josef Winterhalder Sr., he worked in Jan Sturmer’s Olomouc workshop.
81262916-5478-5649-8cbf-3097f53ac172.short_description: The gesture of the angel’s right hand symbolises the Annunciation, the left hand is shaped to hold a lily, a symbol of the immaculate conception. The sculpture is one of only a handful of known works by Richter, a remarkable sculptor from Olomouc.
81262916-5478-5649-8cbf-3097f53ac172.obtention: The sculptures are a part of what remains of the Baroque-period interior of the Dome of St. Wenceslas, Olomouc the major proportion of which was removed during “re-Gothicization” in 1893.

8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.name: Aquamanile in the form of a ram.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.description:
This standing animal sculpture has lost its front paws, ears and horns. With its long neck and head too small for its body, it exudes a feeling of great strength. On its breast is a crescent which seems to have a medicinal significance. Around its neck it wears a collar, decorated with an incised saw-tooth pattern, from which the crescent hangs. The eyes are circles sculpted around globular protrusions for the iris. This aquamanile was probably a fountain-head embellishing one of the local palaces or large houses. The water ran up a tube from under the ram's belly and emerged from the open spout of its mouth.  
This example can be included within a whole series of animal-shaped aquamaniles discovered in various Muslim countries, especially Egypt and Spain. They were generally deer, dogs or birds.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.short_description: Aquamaniles were probably used as fountain heads to decorate palaces and grand residences. This example belongs to a series of aquamaniles in the shape of animals, usually stags, dogs or birds, found in some Muslim countries including Egypt and Spain.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_datation: This aquamanile has definite affinities to other pieces found at Madinat al-Zahra, dating from the mid-4th / 10th century, and in Egypt, dating from the 5th century (11th). From the Ifriqiyan historical context and the simple decoration the piece can be dated to somewhere between the 4th–early 5th / 10th–11th centuries.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_provenance: This piece was a fortuitous discovery made at Beni Khalad probably during the 1930s. In spite of its resemblance to the aquamaniles of al-Andalus, its Ifriqiyan origin appears beyond doubt.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.obtention: This piece was presented to the Museum by the Friends of the Bardo in May 1941, where it has been on display since.

821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.name: Rosette.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.description:
Decorative rose patera or rosette in sculpted plaster composed of ten petals in blue on a red background. All that remains of the blue is a tiny trace on the edge of a petal. The central part would have been painted in yellow, as other plaster fragments discovered at the same place were painted in blue, red and yellow. The disappearance of the colour is due to the natural effects of light and air.  
This rose patera was no doubt just one element belonging to a plaster frieze that featured three colours (blue, red and yellow); or perhaps, as is affirmed by Marçais, it was placed on the cornerstone of an arch.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.short_description: Sculpted plaster piece representing a ten-petal rosette, originally painted blue, around a corolla, which may have been painted yellow, all on a red background. The colours have not survived well. This rosette would have been part of a multicoloured plaster frieze.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.method_for_datation: It was found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad, which dates from the 5th–6th / 11th–12th centuries, according to Kitab al-Istibsar: 'The Banu Hammad built some important constructions in the *qal'a* … including \[the palace\] known as Dar al-Bahr, at the centre of which was a vast basin'.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.method_for_provenance: From the report of the De Beylié excavation, 1909.

8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.name: Lower half of a sculpturesque high relief.
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.description:
This is one of a prominent group of sculpturesque high-relief representing human figures, animals, and vegetal motifs found in Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi. It consists of the lower half of a man sitting on a throne with his feet on a small stool. The stool is in the shape of a colonnaded portico that is supported by seven arches that rest on pairs of pillars. While other statues in the palace appear to be based on Sassanid prototypes, some prominent historians have also linked this figure with those at Qusayr Amra, which show clear Byzantine or Mediterranean influences.  
There is speculation that the figure represents Caliph Hisham bin 'Abd al-Malik who commissioned the building of the Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi complex. This is based on the fact that the statue exhibits luxurious clothing with traces of red, green and brown paint. The building under his feet symbolises his power and the extent of his rule. It is clearly intended to emphasise the glory and majesty of the ruler.  
Sculptures in stucco are part of the pre-Islamic Iraqi, Iranian and Central Asian tradition. Extremely high-relief pieces such as this, or even stand-alone sculptures in the round, are a new development in this tradition, although they can be compared to the relief sculptures found in Palmyrene tombs of ancient Syria.  
This sculpture was located on the second floor of the palace, along the interior façade that overlooks the courtyard colonnade.
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.short_description: Although fragmentary, this figurative carving in high-relief may have represented the Umayyad Caliph Hisham bin 'Abd al-Malik dressed in Persian-inspired royal garb and sitting on his throne.
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.initial_owner: Caliph Hisham bin 'Abd al-Malik (r. AH 105–25 / AD 724–43).
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.method_for_datation: This object, along with the rest of the palace complex, was dated according to the inscription on the lintel of the door of the *khan* adjoining the palace, which carries the date 109 (727).
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.method_for_provenance: The object was found and probably carved *in situ* at Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi.
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.provenance: Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi; 80 km southwest of Palmyra.
8473d6b1-ff39-54e8-aa27-a77f671d0068.obtention: The object was found during the archaeological excavation of Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi completed by the French Expedition of 1936 under the direction of Daniel Schlumberger.

86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.name: Panel from a cenotaph.
86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.description: A carved wooden panel, which once formed part of the cenotaph of Fakhr al-Din Abu al-Tahir Isma’il, an official in the service of the Ayyubid Sultan al-Malik al-‘Adil (r. AH 596–615 / AD 1200–1218). The surface of the panel is divided into smaller panels of varying size, with a long continuous one at the top and seven smaller ones below it. Each of the panels is carved into an abstract arabesque pattern. The spaces between these panels are filled with inscriptions, including verses from the Qur’an and benedictory phrases. Importantly, the date of the panel is given in the lower section. This panel is an interesting example of the re-use of materials in Islamic art, for it was carved on the back of a panel which bears decoration in the style of the Tulunid era (AH 254–92 / AD 868–905).
86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.short_description: A wooden panel which once formed part of the cenotaph of an Ayyubid official. Its surface is divided into smaller sections, each carved with an arabesque pattern. It was carved on the back of a panel which bears decoration in the style of the Tulunid period, some three centuries earlier.
86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.method_for_datation: The inscription gives the date as Rajab 613 / October–November 1216.
86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.bibliography: Lane-Poole, S., *The Art of the Saracens in Egypt*, London, 1886, p.122.
86731854-5b36-5a09-a5f5-43552aeb24a1.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; funerary object; carving

869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.name: Warrior relief.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.description:
A grey marble slab that is rectangular and nearly square, on which two figures of warriors are carved in high relief. The figures have been depicted within a frame delineated by a deep contour line. Their heads are shown in profile, their bodies from the front; they wear helmets with pointed tops, armour, and short boots. They are shown with one foot forward, as if attacking. The figure on the left has a sword in one hand and a shield in the other. The figure on the right is holding his sword in one hand while grasping the sword's scabbard in the other. Both figures are shown in military dress, and their garments, as well as the details of their bodies, are defined with carved outlines.  
  
The tree with split-palmette leaves on the right-hand side of the slab, as well as the vegetal forms used as fillers in the upper corners, shows the influence of Sassanid on Islamic decorative arts. The warriors' clothes and pointed helmets show similarities with those seen in medieval Crusader painting, offering valuable documentary evidence about military dress and equipment of the period.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.short_description: Konya was the capital of the Anatolian Seljuq Sultanate during the AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries and its citadel was decorated with rich figurative reliefs. This warrior relief not only depicts the military costume and arms of the period but also is an important document for the period.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.dimensions: Height 89 cm, width 91 cm, depth 10 cm.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.method_for_datation: Konya citadel, where it is thought this object originated, dates to the 6th / 12th century. For this reason the object is dated to the same century.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.method_for_provenance: It is known from several sources (e.g. the journals of the 19th-century French traveller Charles Texier) that the citadel at Konya, capital of the Anatolian Seljuqs, was adorned with figurative decoration in stone. This object is thought to have belonged to the citadel, which does not survive. It is thus probable that it was made in the vicinity of Konya.
869b86b6-4148-5cb5-9768-3fc1fa05ffdb.obtention: The relief was transferred to the Tiled Pavilion (çinili Köşk), Istanbul, in 1870 as part of the 19th-century initiative to collect artworks from across the country. The object was transferred to the Museum in 1941.

8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.name: Cock
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.description:
It was difficult to make and fire large ceramic figures like this one and the sphinx (Isl 56) with the technology of the day. They easily crackled or simply collapsed. The manganese, turquoise and blue glazes as well as the carved decoration are typical of laqabi ware, but while the glazes on a horizontal surface are kept in place by the carved decoration, this is not the case on an upright object like this one.  
  
Although both animals must be considered mythical creatures, the artist managed to depict the watchful and aggressive cock with all of this animal’s natural characteristics.
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.name: *Prince Livio Odescalchi*
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.description:
Prince Livio Odescalchi (1652–1713) belonged to the influential Italian Odescalchi family, a family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI.  
Emperor Leopold I Habsburg, in gratitude for the great financial aid granted him by Pope Innocent XI to meet the costs of the war against the Ottoman Turks, named his nephew Livio Duke of Srijem and granted him the Ilok estate as a fief and many other privileges. Livio himself had excelled in the battle to defend Vienna in 1683.  
He was a great collector and decorated his residences with fine artworks. He was also a patron of the arts.  
The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, is an outstanding work with realistic emphasis on individuality. Dramatic tension is achieved through the expression of the head turned to the right, and by the rich drapery enveloping the body falling in heavy semicircular folds.  
Monnot often worked for the Odescalchi family. He was an excellent master with a fine technique and a strong and characteristic expression reminiscent of Bernini.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.short_description: The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, shows Prince Livio Odescalchi, a member of the influential Italian family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI. The sculpture shows the influence of Bernini. Livio Odescalchi had links to Ilok and Slavonia by way of the deed of gift he received from Leopold I Habsburg, granting him the Ilok estate and surrounding lands and other privileges for merit in wars against the Ottomans.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.initial_owner: The Odescalchi family, owners of Ilok Manor
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.method_for_datation: Information about the work is due to the research of the Italian art historian, A. Bachi, an expert in Roman Baroque sculpture.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.provenance: Artworks including *Prince Livio Odescalchi* were moved to the newly formed Ilok City Museum in 1952, which transferred to Odescalchi Manor in 1968.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.obtention: Up until World War II, the Odescalchis owned Ilok Manor. As state property, it had several different uses but after refurbishment in 1968, it became a museum and this bust and other objects from the Odescalchi estate became part of the new permanent collection.

8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.name: St. Michael Archangel
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.description:
This statue was made for the library of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, near Bologna, and dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna but mainly worked in Rome after 1625. In the period of the full flourishing of baroque art he became the main interpreter of classicizing sculpture.  
In this bronze group depicting the struggle between St. Michael and the devil, Algardi leaves aside his usual stylistic moderation. The rhythm is frantic and agitated: the angel is tense as he strikes his final blow; the clothes hang to his legs, while his face and breast keep their beauty unchanged. The sculpture is influenced by the painting of the same subject painted by Guido Reni for the Roman church of S. Maria della Concezione. Compared with the airy elegance of the painting the sculpture appears more rhetoric and forced.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.short_description: This statue was made for the library of the convent of San Michele in Bosco, near Bologna. It dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna, but after 1625 he worked mostly in Rome. The struggle between the archangel and the devil compelled the artist to abandon his usual controlled style. He adopted a more complex and violent rhythm, while continuing to look for ideal elegance and beauty.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.initial_owner: Convent of St. Michael in the wood
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.method_for_datation: In his *Vite de pittori, scultori et architetti moderni*, published in Rome in 1672, Giovanni Pietro Bellori notes that Algardi made for Taddeo Pepoli, abbot of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, a statue depicting St. Michael Archangel trampling over the Devil. The statue was to be exhibited in the library, financed and promoted by the same abbot.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.obtention: In 1799, when religious orders were suppressed, the Accademia Clementina took care of the statue, once in the library of the convent; in 1871 it was moved to the Museo Civico and since 1985 it has been exhibited in the Museo Civico Medievale.

8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.name: Plaster relief.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.description: A section of a frieze depicting two horsemen in battle with a dragon and a lion. The wide upper border contains a geometric composition of interlocking stars and polygons, while the main background is filled with a floral composition including spiralling tendrils and palmettes. On this ground, two horsemen are depicted facing each other; the one on the left, shown charging, is slaying a dragon, while the one on the right kills a lion. Both the figures' clothing and facial types are characteristically Seljuq. The fidelity to nature with which the horses are depicted, as well as the way one horseman turns around in the saddle to thrust his sword into the lion, lend the scene an active air. The portrayal of a horseman slaying a dragon was a popular subject in Anatolia in the Seljuq period as well as before. Christian scenes of Saint George killing the dragon were depicted in a similar way.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.short_description: This plaster fragment from Konya Palace depicts a horseman accompanied by other horsemen fighting a dragon. Costumes and accessories and the way the figures are rendered all reflect the features observed in depictions of horsemen and hunting scenes very common in Anatolian Seljuq-period art.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.dimensions: Height 28 cm, width 53 cm, depth 4 cm.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.method_for_datation: Equestrian compositions and hunting scenes are widespread in the art of the Anatolian Seljuq period. Stylistic considerations suggest a date of the 7th–8th / 13th–14th centuries.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.method_for_provenance: The object was found during archaeological excavations at the Konya Palace; it is probable that it was made on site.
8d5bacd1-856d-5b16-8d3e-40994e3243e8.obtention: The object was brought to the Museum after being found during archaeological excavations at the Konya Palace in 1941.
