8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.name: *St. Gertrude*
8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.description:
St. Gertrude (626–659) was the daughter of Pepin I of Landen, the Prefect of the Palace of the Merovingian King Dagobert I of Austrasia. She was abbess of the Monastery of Nivelles (today in Belgium) founded by her mother Saint Itta of Aquitania. St. Gertrude is presented as a noble and independent woman who refused to marry because she wanted to be a nun. She devoted her life to the study of the Holy Scriptures and collaborated with the Irish saints Foillan and Ultan to assist the needy and promote Evangelisation.  
The Monastery of Arouca commissioned Jacinto Vieira to make a set of limestone sculptures of male Benedictine saints for the nave and a set of female saints for the choir, all of which were particularly venerated by the Cistercian Order. Almost unknown, Jacinto Vieira belonged to a group of Northern Portuguese sculptors, who, during the reign of King João V, sought to combine the national Portuguese aesthetics typical of the 17th century with the Italian aesthetic peculiar to the erudite Roman Baroque. Mainly an expert in sculpture in wood, Vieira managed to adapt his mastery in wood, acquired in the saint-making workshops, to stone sculpture.  
This image of St. Gertrude depicts her with an abbess' crosier and a medallion surrounded by a *gloria luminosa* filled with an inflamed heart with Baby Jesus, following the iconographic canons of the day and the austerity of the Cistercians. St. Gertrude stands out due to the elegance of her gesture, her contemplative facial expression and her mystical aura over the other nuns, all of them dressed with delicate pleated garments and habits with enormous sleeves, which are the main features of this set of sculptures.
8f66553f-e1b0-520b-9337-b61ebdf1701d.short_description: St. Gertrude was canonised in 1677 and is an emblematic character both of the Benedictine and Cistercian orders. *St. Gertrude* is one of a set of stone sculptures from the Monastery of Arouca depicting the saints worshipped by the Cistercian Order to enhance their role in promoting the Teachings of Christ according to the Counter-Reformation.

8f7d2a93-9bbc-5639-a80e-3049fce77e6c.name: Las palabras las lleva el viento
8f7d2a93-9bbc-5639-a80e-3049fce77e6c.description:
Alberto Gambale was born in Ferrara. He trained at the Academia de Bellas Artes de Bolonia, before embarking on an immense search and experience within the pictorial and sculptural field, discovering glass as the core material for his work. He perfected his work by way of many other courses with significant artists within the contemporary glass field, such as: Detleft Tonz, specialist in Tiffany glass; Gil Reinolds, German-American Bullseye Artist; Elimer Preder; the great, internationally renowned Italian-American artist, Narcissus Quagliata and S&K Higuchi, Japanese experts in molten glass.  
In 1992, he participated in the Polariscope programme, that took place at the Fundación Centro Nacional del Vidrio, in which glassworkers of various nationalities were involved. They all created a piece inspired by a common topic: water. Since, Alberto Gambale has maintained contact with the Escuela del Vidrio at the Foundation, providing several monographic courses, both in stained glass and alternative techniques.  
He currently works in his workshop in Ferrara, experimenting in the field of molten glass, as we can observe in this piece, in addition to teaching classes in different Glass Schools, such as the Escuela de Vidrio de Bolzano and the Escuela de Vidrio de la Real Fábrica de Cristales.
8f7d2a93-9bbc-5639-a80e-3049fce77e6c.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja

90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.name: *The Kiss of Judas*
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.description:
The sculpture represents a scene from the Gospel of St. Matthew (26:49) when Judas, one of the apostles, marks Christ with a kiss as the man who should be arrested and tried. As in the sculptures featuring Christ parting with Mary in the Heiligenkreuz Monastery Museum, Austria, and in the Bratislava City Museum, Slovakia, in *The Kiss of Judas* Giuliani concentrates – in the encounter of two figures – on the motif of instant motion typical of the work of Giovanni Bernini, a key baroque sculptor. The dramatic subject of Judas's treason is conveyed by means of the medium as a contrast in the approach to both figures: the figure of Christ is self-absorbed, resigned to his fate, characterised by calm gestures and static drapery flowing in large forms, while Judas approaches Christ in an expressively captured haste which the sculptor has portrayed, aside from Judas's step forward, by a dramatic gesture extended into space, as well as by Judas's clothes floating around the body as if blowing in a wind.  
The sculpture is unique, in that no associates or assistants participated in its creation, as was the case with Giuliani's sizeable works.  
Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice, and later in Munich under Andreas II Faistenberger. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy, in Moravia for the Kounics (Slavkov) and many times for the Liechtensteins (Lednice).
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.short_description: The sculpture depicting a dramatic scene of treason from the Gospel of St. Matthew exemplifies a typical baroque motif of instant motion. Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice and later in Munich. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy in Austria and Moravia.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.method_for_datation: The overall approach to shape in the figures is classic Giuliani. His authorship is confirmed by the execution of the faces as well as by the softly modelled and finely executed drapery of both figures, which complement not only the form but also become major interpretational elements of the content.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.obtention: The sculpture became part of the museum’s collections before 1962; its provenance is unknown.

91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.name: Carved figure of a mammal.
91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.description: This mammal looks like a cow with no horns or like a hippopotamus with no tail. The lower part of the two hind legs and of one of the fore-legs is also missing. Face on, the features are quite clear but highly simplified; just rough cavities for the eyes, a hole to indicate the nostrils and a hollowed-out line for the mouth. Seen from the back, the face is totally unrecognisable. The neck and the rest of the body are thick-set. It is unclear what this animal was used for. Could it have decorated the facade of a wall or have been part of a bas-relief? This is very difficult to ascertain because of the rarity of such objects in both Occidental and Oriental Muslim art. We do have clay figures of horses, camels and mules from Iran and Samarkand, but their function is well-defined. They were used as toys or ornaments and are completely different from Kairouanese figures, which are unique in Muslim art.
91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.short_description: This animal figure in stucco appears to be a bull with no horns or a hippopotamus with no tail. The purpose of this mammal is unknown, given the rarity of such objects in Islamic art. Kairouanese figurines are entirely different.
91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.method_for_datation: This stucco head was found, among other human and animal carvings, in the excavations carried out at Sabra al-Mansuriyya in 1978. It was found in a very ploughed-up area with no clear archaeological layering. The objects were scattered around in a random manner. One has the impression that someone had tried to eradicate or hide these figurative objects for no obvious reason except that there could be a connection with the changing religious mentality in Ifriqiya. This action could indeed coincide with the persecution of the Shi'ites during the troubles in 407 / 1016 or following the split between the Zirid emirate and the Fatimid caliphate in 440 / 1048–9. This date could be a *terminus post quem*. The *terminus ante quem* is just after the founding of Sabra in 337 / 948. Any further precision is rendered impossible due to the lack of a definite archaeological layer.
91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.method_for_provenance: The manufacture of these objects, which is unique in Ifriqiya and in the Maghreb, appears to have taken place in Sabra al-Mansuriyya and to have been commissioned by the Shi'ites.
91accd64-ec4c-56b4-b2f4-b293a427f8c4.obtention: After its discovery at Sabra al-Mansuriyya, this piece was placed in the site storehouse. It was acquired in 1992 by the Museum at Raqqada. It will be displayed in the second section of the Museum, currently under construction.

9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.name: Blessing Christ Child
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.description: The Christ child giving his blessing might originally have been part of a Madonna with Child. Iconographically and with great certainty the polychrome figure can be identified as the Infant Jesus according to the effortless gesture of his right hand raised in blessing. The almost-nude child is apologetically dressed only with a gold-plated waistcloth across the right thigh, with his arms spread. Finest proportions and the effects from the flesh-tint result in one of the most brilliant small sculptures of Hans Degler and can be compared with his work *Mary and the Jesus Child* donated to the nearby village church of Weilheim-Unterhausen in 1621. Short curls of hair, some of them above the forehead, and the drapery of the waistcloth were typical of that time. The closed lips in the facial expression of the child underline the graveness with which he looks onto the world.
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.short_description: It is assumed that, originally, the sculpture was accompanied by the Virgin Mary on whose lap the Infant Jesus was once seated with his outstretched arms.
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis of Hans Degler’s work.
9234bd90-3685-526a-a423-4819263bef3f.bibliography: Helm, R., “Segnendes Christkind”, *Stadtmuseum Weilheim i.OB 1882–1982*, Stadt Weilheim (City of Weilheim (ed.)), Weilheim 1982, p. 31f.

9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.name: *St. Onuphrius*
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.description:
José de Almeida, a highly important Portuguese sculptor of the Baroque period, made a qualitative leap that can be more easily explained by considering his career and his works that are extant. After studying in Rome under the patronage of King D. João V, he worked at Carlo Monaldi's atelier, and became a member of the St. Lucas Academy which awarded him several commissions. Returning to Lisbon he worked in stone but it was inconclusive due to qualitative irregularity. It is worth mentioning the following works: *St. John the Baptist* and *Queen St. Elizabeth* made for the Bemposta Palace chapel vestibule (finished by Barros Laborão); the *St. Paul* and the *St. Camillus de Lellis* for the porch and façades of the Necessidades Palace, together with his signed works, of which a fountain decorated by him is located in front of the Bemposta Palace chapel.  
His series of wooden Virgins include those at St. Mamede Church and the Old Church of Our Lady of Conception, and probably one at the Lady of the Rosary from the S. Domingo Church in Guimarães. Confusingly, they are attributed either to him or to Machado de Castro.  
Less known are the *The Steps of Passion* or *Processions*, a set of articulated and spindly figures from the brotherhood and the Church of Lady of Monte do Carmo in Lisbon. They exhibit remarkable modelling of the faces and hands, as well as perfect use of both plastic and luminous values, typical of someone with solid training. They represent the largest preserved sculptural cycle in wood made in the Almeida Workshop.  
*St. Onuphrius*, which aesthetically belongs to this group, is similar to sculptural representations of the previous century. The sculpture is made according to the aesthetic values of Roman sculpture while still retaining its Portuguese identity.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.short_description: In his masterpiece, *St. Onuphrius*, José de Almeida demonstrates his skill in rendering human anatomy; his ability to manipulate light and imbue drama, seen in the clothing and in the details of the hair and beard.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.initial_owner: Church of the Santíssima Trindade e Redenção dos Cativos, Lisbon
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.dimensions: H: 169 cm; l: 55 cm; w: 39 cm
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.method_for_datation: Cyrillo Volkmar Machado (1823) was the first author to refer to the *Saint Onuphrius*, and attributed it to José de Almeida. In 1914, Joaquim de Vasconcelos discarded this information and suggested it was the work of the sculptor Manuel Pereira. In 1950 and 1963, Reynaldo dos Santos returned to Cyrillo's attribution of José de Almeida which, since then, has been consecrated.
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.provenance: Church of the Santíssima Trindade e Redenção dos Cativos, Lisbon
9307f66a-0153-5428-9ef4-503ec9519720.obtention: *St. Onuphrius* was taken from the Sacramento Convent in Lisbon which was the depository for the objects taken from the extinct religious corporations. It was integrated into the sculpture collection of the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in 1913. According to a report dated 1833 it had been used in sculpture classes at the Academy of Fine Arts, having previously been removed from a chapel at the Holy Trinity Church and the Redemption of the Captives, in Lisbon.

94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.name: Lower part of a semi-naked female statue.
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.description:
The lower part of a semi-naked female figure found at Qasr al-Mushatta. Carved out of limestone, the figure has a drape over her thighs the edge of which she holds with her left hand along with a basket or bag. In her right hand she holds an unidentified object.  
  
The proportions of this female figure are curvaceous and voluptuous. Such figures obviously flouted Muslim principles and were not supposed to be seen by the public.
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.short_description: The lower part of a semi-naked female figure found at Qasr al-Mushatta. Carved out of limestone, the figure has a drape over her thighs. Such figures flouted Muslim principles and were not supposed to be seen by the public.
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.dates: Hegira first half of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.method_for_datation: Qasr al-Mushatta, where this figure was found, dates to the end of the Umayyad period (first half of the 2nd / first half of the 8th century).
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.method_for_provenance: The figure was found within the Umayyad palace of al-Mushatta.
94369548-7782-52b0-adae-f3a0d1f1caf6.obtention: The figure was found during the course of restoration work and an archaeological excavation that was carried out in 1962 by the Department of Antiquities of Jordan at the Umayyad palace of al-Mushatta; the object was then transferred to Jordan Archaeological Museum.

957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.name: *St. John of Nepomuk*
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.description:
The Czech martyr John of Nepomuk became one of the major Moravian saints at the turn of the 17th century. The general vicar of the Archbishop of Prague was murdered in 1393. As a saint, his cult spread all over the Czech lands and Roman Catholic Europe and even overseas. John of Nepomuk was worshipped even before his canonisation and beatification in Rome in 1729. Today, one still encounters pilgrimage sites, pictures and statues erected in his honour in many places in Moravia.  
Ignaz Lengelacher, sculptor to the Dietrichstein family, frequently devoted himself to St. John of Nepomuk as a subject for his work in Moravia, from the saint's figure on the Holy Trinity Column in Mikulov (1723–34) to his statue in Pouzdřany (1751).  
In terms of composition, the subject appears in Lengelacher's oeuvre in a number of versions, manifesting the artist's fertile imagination and the inventiveness of his approaches to a single saint. St. John is alone in Lengelacher's statues, standing or kneeling, or sometimes accompanied by the standing figures of angels holding characteristic attributes.  
Lengelacher paid particular attention to interpretation of the saint's mental state in the adoration of the cross which, as shown by the position of hands, he had initially been clasping in quiet, self-absorbed contemplation. The seriousness of the subject is accentuated by the strict emphasis placed on the plain physique of the statue. The cloud pedestal provides the figure with a compositional base and indicates a connection with the transcendent, as the figure is an apotheosis of a martyr, a patron saint of the Czech lands.  
After 1750, Lengelacher left for Bavaria and then went to Bruchsal in the Baden region, where he entered the service of the Bishop of Styria. In 1758 he is recorded as the sculptor to the enlightened and art-loving Margrave Karl Friedrich of Baden (c. 1811) in Karlsruhe, whose court also hosted, among others, Voltaire, Lavater and Goethe.
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.short_description: John of Nepomuk became one of major Moravian saints at the turn of the 17th century. His cult spread all over Catholic Europe and even reached overseas. Today one still encounters pilgrimage sites, pictures and statues erected in his honour in many places in Moravia.
957546c7-81b8-5a1c-88cb-b6935f998bc2.method_for_datation: Style analysis is supported by the sculpture’s origins as private property in South Moravia.

97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.name: *The Source*
97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.description: Mona Saudi sculpts abstract forms imprinted by feelings. Her perfect mastery of gesture allows her to work with dexterity in all materials. Although she has a particular fondness for marble, she also works with granite, pink Jordanian stone, and bronze. Two versions of *The Source* were realised: the first in bronze (AH 1405 / AD 1984), shown here, and the second in pink Jordanian stone in a larger format (AH 1407 / AD 1986). Circles emanating from the central eye, which symbolises the water source, bring movement to the work. The terms "eye" and "source" are the same word in Arabic.
keywords: Water; bronze; sculpture; Mona Saudi

982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.name: Monument to Luigi Ferdinando Marsili
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.description: This monument was commissioned by the Institute of Sciences of Bologna to commemorate one of its main founders, General Luigi Ferdinando Marsili in 1733, three years after his death. The monument is located in the right arm of the transept of the church of St. Dominic in Bologna which was refurbished a few years before by the architect Dotti. It is made of a very poor material, stucco, which is a mixture of marble powder and sand. Many Bolognese sculptors used stucco in the Baroque age to create true masterpieces for churches and noble residences. From the church wall hangs a great and rich curtain covering objects once beloved by the General; books, weapons, and artist tools. The upper portion is occupied by the slender figure of Fame, holding in her hand a trumpet and an oval medallion with Marsili’s profile. Under the diagonally projecting slab with its Latin inscription struggles Time, represented as an old man with a sickle. The baroque theme of Fame defeating Time is perfectly conveyed.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.short_description: This monument represents the baroque spirit in the use of allegories, in the employment of many diagonals crossing in the composition and in the dynamic movement transmitted to the sculpted curtain.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.method_for_datation: The monument date is established thanks to archive documents and to the Latin inscription.

98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.name: Statue of Jules Ferry
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.short_description: This symbolic statue of the French protectorate in Tunisia was located in the centre of the European quarter, between the cathedral and the official residence of the French government, on the Avenue Jules Ferry, today renamed Avenue Habib-Bourguiba. This bronze statue, reaching around three metres in height, is one of the last surviving elements of a monument which had been dedicated to one of the most important thinkers of French imperialism.

9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.name: *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian*
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.description:
These splendidly colourful Rococo statues of *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* came to the museum from the parish church of Egervár in the county of Zala. The patron of the church, Count Ignác Széchényi, commissioned a new large tabernacle with six carved figures for the high altar of the church, made in around 1730, in 1757. The Széchényi family already had connections with artists in Graz, the area where Philipp Jakob Straub chose to settle and work.  
Both statues are of saints believed to be protectors from the plague, and both express pain and suffering. *St. Roch*, dressed in pilgrim's clothes, turns his eyes heavenward. His lips parted in pain, he points to the wound on his foot. Next to him is the dog that allegedly brought him bread when he was suffering from the plague. Bound to a tree and wounded by arrows, the young martyr, *St. Sebastian*, is resigned to his fate. His head rests on his shoulder and tears drip from his closed eyes. *St. Roch*'s garments flutter in deep folds, providing the contrast of light and shade, while light glides softly on the sensuously beautiful body of *St. Sebastian*.  
The statues are promoted into the vanguard of Rococo sculpture in Hungary by the outstanding quality of modelling, the subtle and reserved colouring and the empathic rendering of emotions.  
Philipp Jakob Straub was born into the Württenberg family of sculptors and moved to Vienna with his brother, Johann Baptist Straub (later court sculptor in Munich), in 1727. Philipp Jakob Straub studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1730 to 1733, at which time he settled in Graz. In Graz he worked on commissions for the church, the aristocracy and the middle class, both in wood and in stone. On stylistic grounds, research attributes to him an extensive oeuvre in Styria where he introduced the influence of Bavarian Rococo sculpture and the practices of stone sculpture from the court in Vienna.
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.short_description: The high altar in the parish church of Egervár (c. 1730) contained tabernacle statues – two of which were *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* – and all of which were commissioned from Styria in 1757. Documents relating to count Széchenyi's relationship with the church and the artist helped to confirm the attribution of these works to Philipp Jakob Straub, a member of the South-German Straub family. Straub settled in Graz and brought fine Rococo sculpture to the Transdanubian region.

9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.name: Fountain basin.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.description: Oblong basin in grey marble. A sculpted decorative element consisting of two poly-lobed arches that end in serpentine motifs can be found at both ends of the cavity. The four cornerstones of the basin's edge are adorned with four full medallions. The cavity of this fountain consists of a hollow with a bordering edge. One of the two sides features an orifice that was once connected to piping. The basin's exterior form becomes narrower towards its base.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.short_description: This rectangular basin is decorated with sculptures consisting of two poly-lobed arches finished with snake motifs. There are four full medallions in the four spandrels around the basin. This basin was probably used to provide water to the Palace of the Sea (Dar al-Bahr).
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.dimensions: Height 26.5 cm, length 119 cm, width 52 cm, depth 17 cm.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.method_for_datation: Found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th–6th / 11th–12th centuries).
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.method_for_provenance: Discovered by De Beylié in the northwest corner of the great court of Dar al-Bahr.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.provenance: Dar al-Bahr, Qal’at Bani Hammad, Algeria.

9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.name: Basin
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.description:
This basin was discovered in pieces at the end of the 19th century in the centre of Seville. Restoration work has reconstructed the bands of inscriptions, as well as the decoration on three of its sides.  
The front is decorated with three tri-lobed arches, framed by alfiz (frame) panels supported on columns. Each arch contains a plant sprouting leaves, palmettes, pinecones and intertwining stems. The space between the arch and the alfiz panel shows the same type of decoration, and the whole thing is framed by an inscribed strip.  
The right-hand side shows a space divided vertically into three parts. The central area is undecorated, probably to allow space for the water to come out, and the other two sides show similar scenes: eagles, seizing deer with their talons, bear two lions face to face on their outspread wings, while beneath them two griffins facing each other complete the scene. This iconography, of Sassanid origin, refers to power, abundance and eternity.  
Only the inscribed band is preserved from the third side, a strip with ducks and fishes, and, underneath it, the remains of a lion attacking a deer.  
We know from the inscription that this basin was commissioned for the royal palace of al-Zahira on the orders of al-Mansur, prime minister and favourite of Hisham II, who was still a child when he became Caliph in AH 366 / AD 976, following the death of his father al-Hakam II. The unstoppable rise to power of al-Mansur started shortly after the accession of Hisham II. With the intention of establishing a parallel dynasty to the legal Umayyad one, al-Mansur built a palatine city called Madinat al-Zahira. This new city, rival to Madinat al-Zahra, was in the eastern part of Córdoba, but limited material remains have survived to the present day. The city was burnt to the ground in AH 399 / AD 1009.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.short_description: Emulating the Umayyad caliphs who built Madinat al-Zahra, the hajib of Córdoba al-Mansur built the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahira, and he commissioned this ablutions basin for it, as stated on the inscription. Animal-shaped spouts would have emerged from the attached side pillars, of which only traces have survived.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.dimensions: Height 68 cm, width 150 cm, depth 77 cm.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_datation: The inscription in *kufic* lettering says: '…Almanzor Abi Amir Muhammad ben Abi Amir and glory to God. \[This was\] ordered to be made for the royal palace of al-Zahira and was finished with the help and assistance of God under the direction of the great Amiri Fata in the year seven seventy and three hundred'. Consequently, the basin has been dated to 377 / 988.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_provenance: There are two other basins attributable to the same period and place, one of which can be found in the Alhambra Museum, Grenada, and the other in Marrakesh (Morocco). This latter was made for ‘Abd al-Malik, son of Al-Mansur. The three pieces have similar decorations of eastern origin on one of their sides.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.provenance: The missing royal palace of Madinat al-Zahira (Córdoba), Spain.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.obtention: The basin arrived at the National Archaeological Museum in stages. The two most important parts, the front and part of one of the sides, were bought on 22 November 1882. Another fragment arrived in 1923. Finally, on 30 July 1930, the last piece arrived from the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Seville.

9ba14117-d905-597a-95be-0025b3200e4e.short_description: Henry Salt and J.L. Burckhardt donated this colossal bust of Ramesses II to the British Museum in 1817 where it created a sensation and became known as the Younger Memnon. 9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.name: Marble plaque.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.description:
A marble plaque, approximately rectangular in shape, the apex of which is an ornamented crown. In the centre of the plaque is a mosque lamp, carved in high relief and suspended from the crown by thick ropes. Flanking either side of the lamp, at the bottom of the composition, there are engraved carvings of two candlesticks with tapering wicks. The neck and base of the lamp are embellished with vegetal motifs and braided bands; in the centre of the body is an inscription that states: 'God is the Light of the Heavens and the Earth'. Vegetal decorations appear above and below the carved inscription, which is contained within a rectangle and delineated by two beaded borders.  
Although, this form of decoration does not appear in any known Mamluk glass mosque lamps, nevertheless the general form and the carved inscription are distinguishing characteristics of Mamluk mosque lamps. The candlesticks, in relief, that appear on the plaque, are decorated with vegetal scrolls and diamond-shaped motifs. The background of the plaque is decorated with vegetal scrolls composed of grape clusters, heart-shaped buds and split leaves, in addition to a pair of stylised lotus blossoms below the lamp. Traces of brown paint also appear in the background.  
A number of Mamluk carved plaques, embellished in engraved decoration in marble, stone and plaster bear testimony to the widespread popularity of the sculptural arts (in wood and stone) during the Mamluk period. They also bear witness to the creativity and originality of the craftsmen in the design of vegetal and geometric compositions.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.short_description: This example of Mamluk-period marble engraving depicts a mosque lantern (*mishkah*), two candlesticks and an inscription saying 'God is the Light of the Heavens and the Earth'. Such marblework bears witness to the skill of the craftsmen in that era.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.method_for_datation: The object is known to date to the 8th / 14th century because it was made for the Madrasa Bedeiriyya in Cairo, built during this time period.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.method_for_provenance: This plaque was found in the Madrasa Bedeiriyya, which lies in the neighbourhood of the Madrasa Salihiyya al-Najmiyya in the Fatimid Street Al-Muizz Li-Din Allah in Cairo. The Madrasa Bedeiriyya was founded in 758 / 1357 by Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Bedeir al-'Abbas who worked as a lecturer of *fiqh* (jurisprudence) of the Shaf'i school. It is likely that the plaque was produced in Cairo for the *madrasa*.
9f13783f-37c2-5e26-9fc8-82aec3de2188.obtention: The plaque was found on site at the Madrasa Bedeiriyya. The Council for the Preservation of Arab Monuments undertook the preservation of the plaque in the eastern court of the mosque of al-Hakim bi Amrillah in 1880, where the first acquisitions of the Museum of Islamic Art were housed before they were transferred to the present Museum building in 1903.

a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.name: *Au bord du Nil* (On the Banks of the Nile)
a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.description:
Often called the father of modern Egyptian sculpture, Mahmoud Mokhtar united the art of his country's pharaonic past with the 20th century to convey the spirit of a newly independent Egypt. The artist aspired to create an artistic language that would reconcile contemporary Egyptian society with its cultural and historical identity.  
Throughout his career, Mokhtar drew inspiration from scenes of everyday life in Egypt's countryside and he frequently depicted the fallaha (peasant woman). Au Bord du Nil is a life-size statue that shows a fallaha wearing a tarha (traditional Egyptian veil) and holding a balas (jug used to transport water) on her head. The fallaha was a leitmotif in the artist's output, representing Egypt and the Nile Delta as an intrinsic part of the nation. The sculpture exemplifies Mokhtar's clean, bold and angular lines, evoking the ancient priestesses who walked the Nile's banks.  
  
*Au Bord du Nil* sends a clear, powerful message in response to the turbulent political climate of the 1930s (AH 1348), when Egypt was under British military administration. At the time, the Egyptian people's desire to reclaim national sovereignty had grown, prompting Mokhtar to transform the fallaha into a nationalist emblem.
a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: woman; water; bronze; Nile

a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.name: *Virgin Mary with Jesus*
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.description:
This standing Madonna with child is characterised by an S-shaped cloak encircling the figure from the left shoulder to the right knee, appearing blown by a sudden gust of wind. The cloak makes up a surprisingly rich yet compact outline for the carved statue. Madonna’s posture contrasts with the expressive air of the drapery. Her head slightly turned towards the child, she is only holding him with indicated touches of the hands, presenting Christ to the viewer in the manner of the Gothic Madonna and thereby emphasising the notion of the Eucharist. The motif of Baby Jesus playing with Madonna’s veil is of the same origin. With her physique, facial expression and plain clothes, the Madonna’s nature appears almost secular.  
Weber employed a similar compositional scheme, in a reduced form and mirror-like manner, in the figure of St. Rose of Lima on a side altar in the Dominican Church of the Holy Cross, Znojmo. The restrained expression of both figures is typical of Weber’s oeuvre, which found a relatively broad application in South Moravia (in Lechovice, Suchohrdly, Tasovice, Dyje, Znojmo). In the 1740s Weber worked for the Augustinian order in Brno (his son was a member of the order). Apart from his decoration of the Augustinian library (now to be found in Old Brno), an entrance portal with the figures of Moravian margraves has survived.  
Leonard Weber came from a large family of sculptors in Silesia and later settled in Slovakia. Sculptors of the same name, possibly a father and son, whose relationship has not yet been demonstrated, were also active in Budapest at the time.
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.short_description: The standing Madonna with child is characterised by an S-shaped cloak encircling the figure from the left shoulder to the right knee, appearing blown by a gust of wind. The restrained expression of the figures is typical of Weber’s oeuvre, which became relatively widespread in South Moravia.
a94ed934-07d9-5fb3-9373-ad09b02656d8.obtention: Acquired before 1950 from a private collection, Budkov Chateau.

a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.name: Bas-relief with bull.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.description:
A bas-relief of a bull carved in marble. The right-hand and lower parts of the carving are missing. The head of the bull is full-face and the body and the neck are in profile. The head looks, oddly, at a complete right angle to the neck. The features are strongly sculpted, with the nose suggested by folds ending in a cavity. The eyes are round, the iris well-carved and the lower eyelids stand out aggressively from the eyeballs. The forehead is two deep folds under a plaited mane.  
Only one horn remains, next to the ear, the other having been broken off. The body of the animal is harmonious but gives no impression of robust strength. From the position of the legs, the bull seems to be rubbing up against a tree composed of a trunk and a few branches. Behind the animal's body two buds and three open vine-leaves emerge. Each element has several lobes and is sculpted in a naturalistic style. The carving is set within a frame decorated with grooved arcs and points similarly to an 'egg and dart' design. The naturalistic manner of the carving has led some historians to attribute a Byzantine origin to the piece and suggest that it was re-used in the Aghlabid era. But, in fact, several similar pieces exist in Muslim art and the frontal muzzle is very frequently found. Moreover, we should not forget that Byzantine and classical influences are characteristic of early Aghlabid art.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.short_description: The decoration of this bas-relief is quite common in Islamic art, and is evidence of the survival of Byzantine and classical influences. The body of the animal, a bull, is sculpted harmoniously and the sculpture is framed by arcs and points similar to 'egg and dart' design.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.dates: Hegira, second half of the 3rd century / AD 9th century.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.dimensions: Height 38 cm, length 57 cm, thickness 11 cm.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.method_for_datation: This piece decorated one of the walls in the state rooms of the as-Sahn Palace on the Raqqada site, which was excavated between 1961 and 1969. We know that this second Aghlabid capital was built in 263 / 876, which puts a *terminus post quem* date on the bas-relief. The chronological period covers two centuries, up until the desertion of Raqqada at the time of the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. Not possessing an excavation file with information on the archaeological layer in which the object was found, we are unable to date it more precisely. However, the classical style of the decoration would suggest the second half of the 3rd / 9th century.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.method_for_provenance: An architectural decoration found *in situ*, the piece was probably carved at Raqqada, re-using some old marble of Italian origin.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.obtention: After its discovery at the Raqqada excavations in 1960 the bas-relief was conserved at the site storehouse until 1993. It was then transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada and displayed there.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.bibliography: *Ifriqiya: Thirteen Centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.174–6.
a955d465-0ca9-595d-bd2a-f998ffb85fd5.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Figurative decoration; carving; relief; animal decoration

ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.name: Sanctuary and Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.description:
The Cistercian Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques (the first King of Portugal) in 1153. Having just conquered the Arabs, Afonso Henriques wanted to commemorate his victory, and foundation of the monastery was part of his strategy to consolidate his authority in the new kingdom. The Monastery is considered to be one of the best preserved medieval monastery complexes in Europe besides being a bastion of the Portuguese nationality.  
Sanctuary: as part of the New Sacristy, this Chapel was called the “Mirror of Heaven” by the eminent Portuguese art historian, Reinaldo dos Santos, due to its supreme beauty and spirituality. Building began in 1670 when Frei Constantino Sampaio was Abbot of the Monastery (1669–1672).  
With an octagonal plan, the interior is fully covered with gilded wood and is lit by a ceiling lantern. This light, filtered and diffused, enhances the theatrical atmosphere of the gilded and polychrome Baroque octagonal structure, which includes six horizontal niches filled by 89 reliquary sculptures.  
Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard: the sculptural ensemble in terracotta represents the Transit of St. Bernard. It was built when Frei Sebastião de Sottomayor was the Abbot of the Monastery (1675–1678). The ensemble can be divided into two groups: at the lower level is a group of free-standing sculptures and another of high-relief figures inserted at the back of the altar. St. Bernard is shown in agony at the centre of the scene, while close to his feet Cistercian monks mourn his death. Close to St. Bernard’s head, the kneeling General Abbot and a group of musician angles glorify his death. At the top, surrounded by two musician-angels and cherubs, the Virgin welcomes the soul of St. Bernard with opened arms. The life-size sculptures are built in overlapping horizontal blocks.
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.short_description: The Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques in 1153. The monastery became powerful due to donations throughout the centuries and contains several treasures, namely the Baroque reliquary Sanctuary and the Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard.

b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.name: *The Opening of the Suez Canal*
b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.short_description: The artist Pietro Magni studied at the Academy of Brera, travelled to Rome in 1849 and battled for the Roman Republic. His first artwork as mentioned in the author’s biography is *The First Steps*, known though the photographs to have been on display at the International Exhibition in London in 1862. In 1863 the businessman Pietro Revoltella commissioned the artist to create a marble group showing the opening of the Suez Canal, now in the Revoltella Museum in Trieste. It shows how important the project was for the commissioner, confident that the new opening toward the East would offer economic advantages to his city. Unfortunately he died two months before seeing the Suez Canal completed. The sculpture shows a classical allegory with Europe uniting the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea, behind them the genius of commerce with winged feet indicating the canal the unifies Europe and Asia.

b3644b51-f021-58b2-9968-b330cbd36614.name: Jar-stand
b3644b51-f021-58b2-9968-b330cbd36614.short_description:
This jar-stand or *kilga* was carved out of one massive block of marble. It rests on four horn-shaped feet joined by single mihrab-shaped arches. The sides are carved with muqarnas, the third side and the corners with bold trefoils. The border of the lower part is decorated with an inscription repeating the phrase *al-baraka al-kamila* (perfect blessing).  
The upper part is designed to hold a water jar made of unglazed earthenware and a receptacle at its lower front side. The porous material of the jar cools the water through evaporation. The porous material of the unglazed jar served as a filter. The water was collected in the lower basin and had the quality of drinking water. *Kilgas* were found in well-equipped households or were part of public endowments such as public water fountains or mosques.
b3644b51-f021-58b2-9968-b330cbd36614.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
b3644b51-f021-58b2-9968-b330cbd36614.method_for_datation: Marble jar-stands of this particular design were characteristic for Fatimid and Ayyubid Egypt and are found nowhere else.

keywords: Jar-stand; kilga; marble

b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.name: Stucco stained-glass window.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.description:
A large arched rectangular stained-glass window with a wooden frame of 7.5 cm wide. It also has two interior frames of stucco that are each 5 cm wide. Together the frames contain the entire window. Flanking the two plaster frames is a decorative band that is 10 cm wide. The window has 10 decorative elements, consisting of one-, two-, three- or four-leafed blossoms. Circles with a fan-like circumference divide these units from each other.  
The principal decorative scheme of the window consists of an upper section and a lower one connected by a circle. In each section there are 14 circles; each of which has a circumference of 20 cm. The circles encompass vegetal decoration in the form of bifurcating branches, which surround the interior circumference of each section and meet above it. The decoration in the upper section includes the text of the *Basmala* (“In the name of God …”) and in the lower section, a verse from “Surat al-nisa'” “Chapter of the Women” (4: 125), which reads “Allah did Take Abraham for a Friend”. The epigraphic inscriptions are coloured in white glaze to accentuate them.  
The manufacture of stucco windows inset with stained glass requires a number of stages. The first stage is the preparation of a solid wooden frame to contain the finished window. Liquid plaster is then poured into the frame and left to dry completely. The window is then placed on an iron mount where an imprint of the decoration is made on the surface of the plaster. This can be done by transferring the design from a sheet of tracing paper with the use of a needle and lead filings, and then using a cutting tool. The carving is done directly on to the plaster by hand with the use of precision tools. The work is extremely exacting as the plaster is fragile, making the window vulnerable to damage. The carving is done at a level of deflection of 45 per cent, allowing light to fall at the centre of the mosque hall. The glass is slotted into the empty spaces from the back. Finally, the window is transferred from the workshop to the site where it is mounted. To produce a window such as this would take between nine and 12 months.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.short_description: The windows at al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock as well as other religious buildings are made from plaster and coloured glass. This window from al-Aqsa Mosque is adorned with vegetal, geometric and epigraphic decoration. The fragility of these windows has led to their being replaced almost every century.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.dimensions: Height 288 cm, width 166 cm, depth 9.5 cm.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.method_for_datation: The date of the object was established by analysis of its decoration, and by comparison with other similar windows that had already been reliably dated, some of which are preserved at the Islamic Museum, while others remain *in situ* at the Dome of Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production as a stained-glass stucco-window workshop is still operational at the Haram al-Sharif to this day. Furthermore, a window such as this would have been difficult to transport due to their extreme fragility, so it is likely to have been crafted *in situ*.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.obtention: The window was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum during restoration of the mosque after a fire in 1969.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.bibliography: Flood, F. B., “The Ottoman Windows in the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque”, in S. Auld and R. Hillenbrand (eds), *Ottoman Jerusalem*, London, 2000.
b3b65730-0a51-56dc-a29d-497a32b57535.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: stucco; stained-glass; vegetal decoration
materials: Wood, plaster (stucco) and stained-glass crafted using casting, carving and mounting.

b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.name: *Maria Immaculata*
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.description: This marble figurine, signed by Schletterer, corresponds with the popular type of Immaculate Virgin that evolved during the Catholic revival: the Virgin is at prayer atop a globe and a crescent moon, while she stands on the head of a serpent that symbolises evil. The slender female figure is modelled in a slight S-curve; her compact silhouette determined by the cloak. This feature, along with her charming face and the picturesque details such as the *putto* hiding beneath the drapery, derive from a Viennese variant of the arsenal of Late Baroque Venetian sculpture. The most notable representative of this trend in the imperial city of Vienna was Lorenzo Mattielli, while the leading master of the classical style was Georg Raphael Donner. Both artists influenced the oeuvre of the Tyrolese sculptor, Jakob Christoph Schletterer, who passed down his increasingly sophisticated classicistic style to subsequent generations during his long tutorship at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. In the main, Schletterer made altar sculpture and reliefs for monastic churches in Lower Austria, but sepulchral monuments are also known to be by his hand. His documented works in Hungary – the Virgin Column in Sopron made after Andrea Altomonte's plans in 1745, and the garden statues at Darufalva (Drassburg) from 1758 – suggest that he probably delivered other works to Transdanubia. This signed, white marble *Immaculata* from Esterházy Castle, today at the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest, is a more animated Rococo variant of the garden statue in Darufalva (Drassburg). In the collection of the Hungarian National Museum there is a similar Immaculata figurine, produced in Tata and transferred from the Cistercian abbey in Zirc, which also dates to the 1750s.
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.short_description: As a follower of Georg Raphael Donner and a professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, Schletterer’s monumental works are found throughout Hungary (Győr, Sopron and Drassburg). This small, signed sculpture belonged to the Esterházy family in Tata.
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.provenance: Count Ferenc Esterházy, Esterházy Castle, Tata
b72e7f3c-1702-565a-9c32-720167e16639.obtention: From the collection of Count Ferenc Esterházy at Esterházy Castle, Tata; Kuny Domokos Museum, Tata

b9e5d59c-90cf-5a1d-80ec-21247c2e8944.name: *St. Francis Xavier and St. Ignatius of Loyola*
b9e5d59c-90cf-5a1d-80ec-21247c2e8944.description:
Saint Ignatius of Loyola was the main founder and the first Superior General of the Society of Jesus, a religious order of the Catholic Church professing directly to the Pope a vow of obedience, as far as missionary duties were concerned. The early Jesuits were sent by Ignatius to pagan lands where they could work on the propagation and strengthening of the Catholic faith. Among them was St. Francis Xavier. He had studied at the same college as St. Ignatius in Paris and helped him plan the foundation of the Society of Jesus. St Francis was sent to Lisbon in 1540 principally because King D. João III wanted him to serve in India.  
In a short period of 10 years (1542–1552) he converted people from Goa, Ceylon, Malacca and Moluccas, where he established several missionary centres; he also established some others in central and southern Japan. He was buried in Goa where is body is still enshrined at the Basilica of Bom Jesus. He continues to be considered the greatest missionary since the Apostles.  
Christianity was expanded by St. Francis Xavier's work as a missionary and by his apostolic zeal. He became a model of holiness and an instrument of evangelisation against other confessional denominations.  
The floral and vegetal motifs that adorn these two sculptures have their origins in oriental art. Commissioned during Portuguese rule in Asia the sculptures are the result of the exchange of knowledge and ideas, techniques and materials from both cultures. The technical expertise reached by both Chinese and Japanese artists allowed their elite cosmopolitan styles to be linked together, and their patrons and the merchants who dealt with their work, to discover new art markets.
b9e5d59c-90cf-5a1d-80ec-21247c2e8944.short_description: According to the austerity of Counter-Reformation rules, the Society of Jesus ordered a simplified interior design for the Church of São Roque, which included the Asian-influenced painted wooden sculptures *St. Ignatius of Loyola* and *St. Francis Xavier*.

bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.name: *St. Thaddeus Jude*
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.description:
This sculpture portrays the saint in a state of self-absorption and contemplation. With the head slightly tilted towards the right shoulder, the shape is defined by a picturesque cloak inventively arranged on the chest to cascade over a plain, low pedestal. The rich folds of the gown are partially obscured by a medallion with a profile of Christ, while the iconography identifies the bust as St. Jude Thaddeus, a close relative of Jesus and disciple to Him. Jude Thaddeus brought a portrait of Christ’s face to the king of Edessa (the Image of Edessa). Jude died a martyr’s death in Persia or Phoenicia and is often represented by the attribute of the club that killed him. St. Thaddeus Jude is patron saint of the desperate and of lost or forgotten causes. The silver surface of the bust accentuates its spiritual, melancholic aura.  
The Provincial Museum in Olomouc owns a similar sculpture of a female figure with a ribbon in her hair. Presumably both busts are fragments of a larger series, the remainder of which are missing. Their “distant” inspiration may have been Bernini’s prestigious portraits.  
Zahner probably came to Olomouc via Vienna, after an apprenticeship to his father in Würzburg. In the 1740s he was assigned a particularly significant task, taking up the sculpted decoration of the Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc.  
With more demanding commissions, Zahner was assisted by Jan Kammereit, Wofgang Träger and Jan Michael Scherhauf. The work of this Bavaria-trained sculptor was received with great acclaim in Moravia.
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.short_description: This sculpture portrays the saint in a state of self-absorption and contemplation. The rich folds of the gown are partially obscured by a medallion with a profile of Christ and the iconography identifies the bust as St. Jude Thaddeus. A. Zahner also created the UNESCO monument, Holy Trinity Column in Olomouc.
bad4cf07-fa59-5807-ad90-cd911e6be4ac.method_for_datation: The attribution of this originally anonymous carving to Zahner was determined, in particular, by the characteristics of the saint: chiselled nose and sunken eyes, which resemble Zahner’s earlier works. His work is typified by an effort to transcribe the mental disposition of his figures.

bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.name: Fragment of wall decoration.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.description:
Fragment of wall-cladding made of *timchent* (local plaster) sculpted in the form of floral decoration spread over three registers separated by three frames formed of flat fillets that are themselves separated by a milled edge. In the lower register are four columns surmounted by arches in the form of rose pateras that are composed of nine very geometric palm leaves. The decoration of the second register employs symmetrical trefoil leaves that evoke a spread of vine leaves attached to their stems by large peduncles; the latter are perforated with circular holes forming lower lobes. The stems, linked to the perforated peduncles, recoil into hooks and join back on themselves to form rings.  
Only a small fragment of decoration remains to be seen on the upper register, composed of stylised leaves covering the whole surface.  
This fragment was discovered in three pieces and was then reconstructed.  
The sculpture was executed with the aid of an iron blade acting on the *timchent* while it was still soft. According to H. Saladin, this local plaster derived from limestone peculiar to the region was 'applied onto cob or roughstone walls'.  
This sculpted fragment is only one part of a wall-cladding that ornamented the wall of a room in a palace.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.short_description: Fragment of sculpted wall-cladding with floral decoration divided between three sections separated by flat or granulated lines. In the lower part, four columns support rosette-shaped arches, while in the upper part stylised leaves stretch up to the top section, of which little remains.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.dimensions: Length 71 cm, width 57 cm, thickness 5.5 cm.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.method_for_datation: From study of the inscription that features on a frieze found in the same palace. According to G. Marçais, the *kufic* characters of this inscription could date back to the '11th century and resemble those in Kairouan', which dates this fragment to the 5th / 11th century.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.method_for_provenance: The fragment was discovered in a palace in Sedrata following the report published in the *Comptes rendus de l'Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres* in 1952.

be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.name: Untitled
be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.description:
Sculpture of two blocks, designed for assembly and composed of horizontally-overlapping glass sheets. A signature of “TE85” appears on the upper part of the piece. Torres Esteban’s work is often characterized by this use of green, cut and cold-glued industrial plate glass. The form of the piece is also typical of the artist’s style. Here we see an interest in volume, with luminescent and kinetic effects that show the influence of Eusebio Sempere.  
  
The work of Joaquín Torres Esteban is associated with the Studio Glass Movement, which originated in the United States and spread internationally. Torres Esteban is one of the pioneers of laminated glass sculpture in Spain. Throughout his glassmaking career, he participated in numerous international events and organized VICOINTER’83, an international contemporary glass exhibition in Valencia.  
  
In 1986, the National Museum of Decorative Arts dedicated a monographic exhibition to Torres Esteban, after which the artist donated this piece.
be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.method_for_datation: Artist’s signature and accompanying reference to date of piece; donation record and artist’s monographic exhibition at the museum
be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.method_for_provenance: Donation record and artist’s monographic exhibition at the museum
be5014f2-b4bb-570b-94a8-c7b05ca72a9f.obtention: Donation of the artist following participation in a monographic exhibition at the National Museum of Decorative Arts

bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.name: Figurative architectural fragment.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.description:
An architectural fragment with figures made of limestone and carved in low relief. It is rectangular in shape, with two crowned arches on the bottom side. On the upper section there are various figures in rectangular cartouches. In order, these include symmetrically placed birds, human figures, peacocks, and winged lions (griffins). The birds are shown in profile; their upper parts each have a rosette motif. The human figures each hold a rosette in one hand and an object resembling a ball in the other. They are shown from the front, sitting cross-legged in the traditional Turkic posture of authority. The peacocks, shown in profile, have tails which end in volutes and bodies with rosettes on them. The griffins face each other in a walking stance and have the characteristics of Seljuq lions: their hind feet are on the ground, while one of their front feet is drawn back toward the body at chest level, and the other is extended forward. The upper part of each griffin's body has a wing motif which extends upward from the front leg. Their tails pass between their hind legs to end above the body. Two bird motifs (eagles) are seen at the tops of the arches. The eagles have thick beaks, pointed claws, and short tails; the one on the right is broken at body level.  
  
The arches are like those found in Artuqid architecture, with their crowns of sharp 'teeth' and the spiralling columns that support them. Between them, surrounded by a chain-motif border, is an inscription in *naskhi* script. The inscription reads, 'May the owner's honour and fortune continue. May God make his life and those of his *amirs* long'. Below the inscription are two kneeling figures holding spears in their hands and facing each other. Between them is a spiralling column. These figures, which we can identify as the guardians of the Tree of Life, are a symbolic expression rooted in shamanistic beliefs.  
  
The inscription suggests that the object may have come from a tomb or a charitable structure such as a fountain.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.short_description: Anatolian Seljuq stonework of the AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries displays extensive figurative decoration. Human and animal figures assuming symbolic meanings from pre-Islamic faiths are rendered exhibiting central Asian influences both in technique and style.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.dimensions: Height 55 cm, width 96.5 cm, depth 7 cm.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.method_for_datation: There is no documentary evidence indicating exactly where the object was produced or found, however, the composition, placement of figures, symbolic meaning, technique and architectural elements, as well as the fact that the craftsmanship exhibits all the characteristics of 7th / 13th century Artuqid work, allow us to date the object to that period.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.method_for_provenance: Inventory documents indicate that the object was initially brought to the Tiled Pavilion (çinili Köşk), from Diyarbakır. For this reason it is probable that the object was produced in southeastern Anatolia, in Diyarbakır or the region around it.
bf493827-b9c5-5274-9a0c-39fb761a93e1.obtention: The object was transferred from Diyarbakır to the Tiled Pavilion (çinili Köşk), Istanbul, in 1898 as part of the 19th-century initiative to collect artworks from across the country. The object was transferred to the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts in 1941.

c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.name: Parts of the St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces from Zagreb Cathedral
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.alternate_name: St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.description:
The museum's altarpiece composition comprises parts of two altarpieces, that of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus. It has a central niche from the altarpiece of St. Mary – decorated with acanthus leaves, putti and bunches of fruit – within which the statue of Mary with the Child Jesus in her arms is standing on a half-moon entwined by a serpent. In front of the niche stand the statues of St. Ladislaus, the King, and St. Emeric, the Duke, which belonged to the altarpiece of Ladislaus.      
The composition, flanked by carved consoles attached to the wall, has the same ornamental decoration as seen in the central niche of the altarpiece of St. Mary; the consoles used to support painted altarpiece wings. Above them are the statues of the four evangelists, which were originally in the niches of the predella panel of the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus.  
In a contract of 1686, the sculptor from Ljubljana, Ivan Komersteiner, agreed to make the altarpiece of St. Mary for the apse of the north aisle of Zagreb Cathedral. In another contract of 1688, he agreed to make its pair, the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus, for the apse on the south aisle. Komersteiner was already a citizen of Zagreb with a workshop in Zagreb's Kaptol.    
The two altarpieces were identical in design: winged altarpieces with painted panels showing scenes from the Life of Mary on the altarpiece dedicated to her, with statues distributed on two levels and in the attic. Painted panels depicting scenes from the Life of St. Ladislaus decorated the altarpiece dedicated to him, with appropriate statues. While the wings from the altarpiece of St. Mary were destroyed those from the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus are kept in Zagreb City Museum.     
St. Ladislaus, the King of Hungary, was responsible for the foundation of the Zagreb Diocese.  
Komersteiner was responsible for the statues and woodcarving. Ivan Eisenhort and Bernardo Bobić collaborated on the painting and gilding of the altarpieces, while Matijaž Erlman began the work on the architecture for the altarpiece of St. Mary.  
The arrival of the sculptor, Komersteiner, to Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque in the sculpture of continental Croatia. He brought with him as a novelty the ornamental decorative motif of Baroque acanthus, so-called Italian leaves, and his statues anticipate a new style expressed in the mobility of the slender figures of saints in characteristic counterpoise, freeing them from dependence on altarpiece niches.      
Komersteine's expression in his work has no direct analogies either in Croatia or in neighbouring territories, but the indirect influence of Italian art in his work is undeniable.  
During renovations in 1882, both altarpieces were removed from Zagreb Cathedral.
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.short_description:
A “composite” altarpiece composition comprising parts from the Altarpieces of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus originally designed for the apses of the north and south aisles of Zagreb Cathedral.  
During renovation of the cathedral in 1882, both altarpieces were removed and partially destroyed in the process. They were made by Ivan Komersteiner, a sculptor who worked first in Ljubljana and then in Zagreb. His arrival in Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque to continental Croatia.

c2f6e9fe-ab29-564b-aeb1-f14417f8e49c.name: *Pietà*
c2f6e9fe-ab29-564b-aeb1-f14417f8e49c.description:
With a preference for sculpture of enormous dimensions that entirely occupy the grand gilded altarpieces of the period, Frei Cipriano da Cruz is considered to be the most extraordinary representative of the National Baroque style.  
His sculpture was generally based on models that circulated throughout Europe and can be considered within the context of other depictions of the Crucifixion and Passion of Christ. A monk-sculptor, the *Pietà* is one of Frei Cipriano's greatest achievements. It exemplifies a theme widespread in Portuguese art in the 16th and 17th centuries, meeting most of the essential Tridentine ideals.  
The *Pietà* belongs to an ensemble of pieces made by Frei Cipriano for the S. Bento Church, which belonged to the college of the Benedictine order in Coimbra and was demolished in 1932.  
This ensemble features anatomical details that are typical of Frei Cipriano, in particular the hands and faces. In the *Pietà* Christ's hands are rough with square-shaped finger nails. His face is framed by abundant curly hair; the S-shaped curls are also present in the beard. The Virgin displays a heavy look; she has high symmetrical eyebrows, a long triangular-shaped nose, and thin defined lips.  
The heavy and pyramidal structure of the *Pietà* is accentuated by the drapery: the red, blue and gold cloak that completely wraps the figure. The drapery is notable in that its decorative motifs correspond with textiles of the period – elaborate brocades and oriental silks. The drapery and embroidery, generally designated as “upholstery”, were pre-made in resin-wax and were applied to the figure later after painting and finishing.  
The motif of the artichoke particularly stands out. It imitates the three-bordered brocade of Spanish and Italian origin and is strategically placed on the Virgin's knee to have the greatest visual impact.  
According to recent research (Alcoforado and Le Gac, 2003) Manuel da Costa Pereira, who was responsible for painting and gilding the *Pietà*, often worked with other painters. Further research about them will bring us closer to understanding the originality of Frei Cipriano da Cruz's sculpture.

The Pietà represents one of his greatest achievements.

c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.name: *Bust of a Saint*
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.description:
The bust, on an original volute pedestal, arises out of a relatively narrow base widening into a compact chest. The bearded head is that of an old man, with a cloak thrown loosely over the right shoulder. The figure might be St. Hieronymus, one of the church fathers. The pedestal shows that the object was a reliquary.  
*Bust of a Saint* demonstrates the artist's broad creativity seen not only his technical craft but also in his ability to capture mental states. The ecstatic expression of desire and submission to God is not rough-hewn, but has an elegant, court-like nature manifest in the figure's S-shaped movement and the soft shaping of the volume.  
Lengelacher may have familiarised himself with bust-making in his native Bavaria, or during a stay in Vienna through Giovanni Giuliani, who provided the gallery pews in the Heiligenkreutz Monastery, Lower Austria, with a whole series of busts. Lengelacher probably met Giuliani while working on the decorations of the Belveder in Vienna.  
In 1719 Lengelacher settled in Mikulov, where as sculptor to Walter František of Dietrichstein, he created sculpted interior decorations for several south Moravian churches. Lengelacher's *Bust of a Saint* is part of a series of original decorations for altar tables in the Church of St. Michael, Dolní Věstonice, which Lengelacher embellished with stuccoes and carvings. The artist worked there from the 1720s in relation to one of his first major commissions, the Benedictine church in Rajhrad (1727–1734).
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.short_description: *Bust of a Saint* demonstrates both the artist's skill as a sculptor and his ability to capture mental states. The ecstatic expression of desire and submission to God is not rough-hewn but has an elegant, court-like nature. The reliquary bust is part of the original altar decorations in Dolní Věstonice.

c38f62f6-12fe-51b9-8cb4-2373b6920841.name: *David*
c38f62f6-12fe-51b9-8cb4-2373b6920841.description:
This is the third group that Gian Lorenzo Bernini undertook for Scipione Borghese, around the same time that he was making *Apollo and Daphne*.  
It shows David, the young hero of the Old Testament (the Book of Kings), prophet of Christ, just before he slings his stone at the giant Philistine Goliath. David's attitude would be incomprehensible if we did not perceive our own space as part of the scene. The enemy Goliath is in the same space as the viewer, with Bernini removing the boundary between the sculpture and the space that surrounds it, a space that also encloses us, participants in the scene. The resultant theatrical effect is one of the recurring themes in Baroque art.  
The work reveals the influence of modern and ancient sculptural models as well as contemporary painting styles, but the artist affords the whole a new realism. The face, possibly a self-portrait, is concentrated in a moment of high drama. The tension of the imminent action is visible in every muscle of the face and body, suspended between stasis and motion, as well as in the detail of the foot jutting out over the plinth, giving a strong impression of gripping on to it.  
The sculpture was backed on to a wall so that the viewer, when entering the room, saw it from the angle intended by the artist: obliquely from the left. This effect was calculated to enhance the plastic tension of the hero and the pictorial value of the sculpture through development of the action by walking around to the front of the statue.    
The original base was lost when the work was moved around the Villa over the centuries. The plinth has been enlarged using plaster to suit a taste for greater regularity, but was removed in a recent restoration, restoring the Baroque effect rendered by the structure of the foot.
c38f62f6-12fe-51b9-8cb4-2373b6920841.short_description: Cardinal Borghese commissioned Bernini to sculpt the David when he was 25 years old. The artist had the intuition to stop the biblical hero just one second before the shot, placing Goliath’s presence in the viewer's space; perhaps a self-portrait of Bernini.
c38f62f6-12fe-51b9-8cb4-2373b6920841.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.name: Putto with a winged helmet blowing a horn
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.description: The small sculpture was assumedly used as a table decoration in the Augsburg Fugger Palace, the residence of the Fugger family. At the time, wealthy merchants may have felt the influence of Roman mythology and this reason chosen as their symbol the God of Commerce, Travel and Theft, Mercury, who is iconographically reflected by the winged helmet worn by the putto. The aeruginous black bronze figure has been placed in a standing, forward-stepping frontal position on a plinth. The nude body is partly covered by a fluttering cape. With his head raised and chubby cheeks, the Putto is about to sound the crumhorn and to recount the history of the Fugger family to his audience. The impression of effort and determination comes from the gesture of his left arm stretched out with a clenched fist. The front of the helmet has been decorated with the motif of a fire-spitting dragon, which might well represent a symbol of defence.
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.short_description: The small bronze figure of a nude Putto sounding a crumhorn and wearing a winged helmet can be regarded as an allusion to Mercury the antique God of Commerce and Travel with the helmet symbolising the world of wealthy merchants.
c3bdb147-116b-56ed-8b27-f2a31d87f80f.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis of Petel’s work.

c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.name: Stucco stained-glass window.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.description:
A stucco stained-glass window divided into 21 decorative units of vegetal and geometric motifs and inscriptions. The first unit is composed of a circular “flower” that complements and forms the arch, and which is adorned with a colourful geometric decoration in yellow, turquoise and dark-red glass. Adjacent to this area is a rectangular zone which contains the only inscription on the window. This is a verse from the Qur'an \[“al-Tawba”\] (“the Repentance”, 9: 18), which reads: “In the Cause of Allah, They are not comparable in the sight of Allah.” The inscription is carved in an interlaced script of white glass. The surrounding space is filled with simple squares of light-blue glass. Adjacent to the inscription are three squares of equal size. The two side squares are identical, and in the middle of each of them there is an eight-sided star. Both are divided into small pieces of dark-red, green and yellow glass. The middle square contains two polygons of yellow and blue glass; the decorative component transfers thereafter to three long rectangles. The two side rectangles are identical and are decorated with intertwining zigzag lines of blue, yellow and dark-red glass. The middle rectangle takes the form of a flower, out of which emerges an intertwining plant that wraps around three times to resemble a circle, and which is topped by a crown formed from vegetal motifs. The window terminates with three squares that are identical in size, and which resemble those mentioned earlier.  
The manufacture of stucco windows inset with stained glass requires a number of stages. The first stage is the preparation of a solid wooden frame to contain the finished window. Liquid plaster is then poured into the frame and left to dry completely. The window is then placed on an iron mount where an imprint of the decoration is made on the surface of the plaster. This can be done by transferring the design from a sheet of tracing paper with the use of a needle and lead filings, and then using a cutting tool. The carving is done directly on to the plaster by hand with the use of precision tools. The work is extremely exacting as the plaster is fragile, making the window vulnerable to damage. The carving is done at a level of deflection of 45 per cent, allowing light to fall at the centre of the mosque hall. The glass is slotted into the empty spaces from the back. Finally, the window is transferred from the workshop to the site where it is mounted. To produce a window such as this would take between nine and 12 months.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.short_description: This stucco window from al-Aqsa Mosque is divided into 11 decorative elements derived from vegetal, geometric and epigraphic forms. The independent elements appear as a collective unit within a wooden frame, which gathers a multiplicity of decorative forms in a number of colours.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by comparison of its style, decoration and form of production with other dated pieces, which are still *in situ*.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of the production of this piece in view of the presence of a permanent workshop for the production of such windows in the Haram al-Sharif. This workshop is still active at the Haram today and was re-established following a fire at al-Aqsa Mosque in 1969.
c3e4b4cd-933f-5d90-8421-12d6189be2e7.obtention: The piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum in around 1929 during renovation works that took place following an earthquake which struck Jerusalem in 1927.
