c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.name: *Bust of Cardinal Domenico Ginnasi*
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.description:
In 1911 the bust was found in the Carmelite Convent at the Church of Santa Maria della Vittoria, relocated from the Church of SS. Pietro e Marcellino, the seat of the Teresian Nuns. The nuns moved there in 1757, from the convent founded after the death of Domenico Ginnasi in Palazzo Ginnasi in 1639, and they took the bust with them, having always identified it as a portrait of the cardinal.  
The work was first attributed to both Bernini and Algardi, before being linked to Giuliano Finelli following comparison with the bust the sculptor made for the cardinal for his funeral monument at S. Lucia dei Ginnasi (the decoration is based on a design by Lanfranco, whose daughter married Finelli).  
The sculptor worked with Bernini on several occasions, notably on *Apollo and Daphne* in the Galleria Borghese and the baldachin (large sculpted bronze canopy over the altar) of Saint Peter's. He worked alone from 1629 and joined Rome's artistic circle thanks to the numerous contacts that he was able to make, notably Pietro da Cortona, who in turn introduced him to the Sacchetti family, well known patrons.  
His style is characterised by attention to detail, intense skill and psychological depth, but always retaining spontaneity and immediacy, a peculiarity of Bernini's so-called “talking portrait”. The partially unbuttoned *mozzetta* (a short elbow length cape worn by Catholic clergy), the kindly and informal face and the realistic lines are clear evidence of this style.  
In relation to this, a *Bust of Cardinal Scipione Borghese* made by Finelli and currently in the Metropolitan Museum of New York, was sculpted at the same time as the Bernini version (1632). In 1634 Finelli moved to Naples, where he developed a portrait style closer to Parthenopean and Spanish taste, preferring distant, official, commemorative portraits. However in the work undertaken at this time for Roman clients, he never completely abandoned his refined virtuosity and keen psychological study, as can be seen in the bust of Cardinal Ginnasi, sculpted in 1639.
c41a0993-462a-5165-a2e7-78834dccf500.short_description: A pupil of Bernini, Finelli focused his attention on the particular rather than the whole. This tendency prevented Finelli from being a great statuary artist, although it enabled him to evolve a striking flair for portraiture.

cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.name: Sacramento Monstrance
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.description:
An exceptional example of Baroque workmanship during the period of King João V, the Sacramento Monstrance – also called the *Anjo Custódia* “Angel Monstrance” – assumes the form of an Atlantis angel, a figure that is sometimes incorporated into the lower part of gilded wooden altarpieces. In this particular case the Atlantis angel appears free; instead of the usual representation as a pillar sustaining a globe the angel holds a radiant sun. Theatrical tension is undoubtedly achieved with the decoration of the piece itself, but the monstrance would have been surrounded by the gilded wood of the sacred space of the high altar and the aim would have been to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty.  
Symbol of the Church Triumphant, the monstrance is a splendid composition of contrasting effects: dynamic lines and imposing shape – the result of which sees the elegant sculptural angel in polychrome and gilded wood – and the resplendence of silver, colour and glinting of both the enamel and glass.  
The kneeling angel holds a spherical, smooth and polished monstrance enveloped in a corona of silver rays. Surrounding the *luna* – the space where the host is kept and exhibited – are Eucharistic symbols enhanced by brightly coloured enamel work, and mounted over a circular base with eight ornamental silver-gilt cherubs. Vegetal motifs and coloured glass form flowers to complete the decoration. The monstrance presents a municipal contrast between the silver from Lisbon (L), in use since 1690, and the incomplete hallmark of an unidentified goldsmith from Lisbon, whose initials were LRP, and who was active between the end of the 17th century and the first half of the 18th century.
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.short_description: Holding the solar sphere made out of silver – glowing with the true Word of God – the Atlantes angel is supposed to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty. This piece was probably the highlight of the gilded wood high altar at Sacramento Convent in Lisbon.
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.owner: Museu Nacional Machado de Castro, Coimbra
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.method_for_datation: This goldsmith’s hallmark first appeared in the early part of the decade of 1690 and continued to appear throughout the first decades of the 18th century. The technical and stylistic affinities of both the figure of the Atlantis angel and the polychrome allow the monstrance to be placed within the Baroque style during the reign of João V (1707–1750).
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.obtention: The monstrance came originally from the Santíssimo Sacramento Convent in Alcântara, Lisbon. Founded in 1612, the convent belonged to the female branch of the Dominican order and was closed after the death of the last nun in 1897. The monstrance was transferred to Coimbra in 1914 where it became part of the gold and silverware collection of the National Museum of Machado de Castro.

cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.name: *Proximus tuus* \[Latin: Your Neighbour\]
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.short_description: In 1880 Achille D’Orsi submitted two artworks, including *Proximus Tuus*, to the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in Brera. The sculpture of *Proximus Tuus* made D’Orsi famous as a member of the Italian “Verismo” school of painting. The misery and harshness of fieldwork is represented for the first time in sculpture to denounce the consequences of the brutalisation of the human beings. This clear social denunciation created the emergence of a huge debate over this issue. The body and the facial expression of the peasant exhausted by labour became a symbol of the working class. The sculpture makes a plea for sympathy and pity for the worker right from the work’s title, expressed in Latin. The subject of the painting has been reproduced and copied several times in order to produce greater awareness over these problems.

cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.name: Model for a male saint (St. Paul?)
cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.description: The small sculpture without a colour setting was originally used as a model for an assistant figure on an altar which is still unknown. Its strong impression, influenced by the sculptor J. B. Straub, resembles the laterally reversed large figure of *St. Joachim* which is part of the high altar of the monastery church of Fürstenfeld. The sculpture is considered to resemble the Apostle Paul, which iconographically is typified by the full beard and the large folio held on the left thigh. The dressed figure with a greatcoat has been placed in a standing position, with bare feet, right leg on the ground, and the left foot gaining a foothold on a rock. While the left arm is stretched out ahead and to the side with (the now lost) hand in an instructive attitude, the head is slightly raised and the lips are closed. The plinth is of modern origin.
cee9abc9-7697-5210-9e9a-510d6ec672a0.short_description: The small sculpture without a colour setting was originally used as a model for an assistant figure on an altar. Despite the small size of the figure its impression is astonishingly monumental.

cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.name: Head of St. Philip Neri
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.description:
This head modelled in wax is considered a replica of a bronze in the collection of the Rhode Island School of Design in Providence, made by Alessandro Algardi around 1640. Another bronze version is in the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica in Rome. These bronzes were made a few years before the artist was charged with the statue in marble of St. Philip Neri for the sacristy of Santa Maria in Vallicella, in Rome (1635–38). For this commission Algardi carefully studied the death mask of the saint, dead in 1595 and sanctified in 1622. The saint's face is strained by old age and suffering but shows deep humanity, humility and the extraordinary strength of a man near to God. Its classicising features make it similar to an antique portrait.  
Algardi, a pupil of Ludovico Carracci's, began a career as a sculptor and in 1625 moved to Rome where he spent nearly all his artistic life.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.short_description: This wax head is thought to be a replica of two bronze ones portraying the same saint, made by Alessandro Algardi around 1640. The sculptor previously carved a marble statue of St. Philip with an angel for the sacristy of Santa Maria in Vallicella in Rome (1635-38). In these head portraits which are strictly devotional, he deepens his analysis of the facial features, emphasising the strong humanity of the saint and his strong moral and spiritual strength.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.holder: Museo di Arte Industriale e Galleria Davia Bargellini
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.method_for_datation: The bronze head in Providence is nearly identical to the wax one, which bears a date. Critics think that heads like this were commissioned to sculptors after the success of the marble statue with St. Philip Neri and the angel for S. Maria in Vallicella, finished in 1638.
cfe04c10-c802-5c71-9567-60d035ba26a9.obtention: The work was probably purchased at the beginning of the twentieth-century; no documentation survives.

d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.name: Fragment of a female statue from Mushatta.
d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.description:
This fragment of the lower half of a female body is of a woman, whose robe has fallen, revealing her body from her hips to below her bottom. It is still possible to make out that the woman is holding the pleated robe with her right hand at her thigh, while remains of the robe are preserved at the left thigh. Her hips and buttocks remain uncovered. The thighs are intact up to a point just above the knee. The back part is covered in places by cloth, but the front of her legs is naked. The female figure, through its plump proportions and voluptuous forms, represents the aesthetic ideal of the Umayyad period for the representative arts. It belonged to the repertory of themes in the art of the court. Over the left thigh there is a deeply carved inscription in *kufic* script that runs vertically downwards, which would once have revealed the name of the woman. A satisfactory translation of the inscription has yet to be completed.  
The fragment belongs to a group of female figures that were displayed within various Umayyad castles. It can be said that these figures were based on the forms used both in Byzantine sculpture and painting and in Sassanid sculpture. The Umayyad Court developed its own thematic repertoire while borrowing from older examples. As well as in Mushatta, life-sized female figures were also found in Khirbat al-Mafdjar and Qasr al-Hair al-Gharbi. Near life-size paintings decorate the Palace in Qusayr ‘Amra.  
The question arises whether less dogmatic articles of faith obtaining during the earlier part of the Umayyad period favoured the creation of such sculptures. Undoubtedly, women were portrayed then as dancing girls and musicians, as members of harems or as goddesses. Given its incomplete condition, it is impossible to say whether this female figure was intended to represent a girl from the harem. Another female sculpture from Mushatta can be seen carrying an embossed container or cloth bag on her left side, for the purpose of sprinkling herself, or the ruler, with sweet-smelling perfume. Sculptures such as these demonstrate how powerfully pre-Islamic forms still exerted themselves over the art of this period. Nevertheless, the fact that this figure was then deliberately damaged shows how such freestanding sculptures were later disapproved of and rejected.
d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.short_description: In the Umayyad period Islamic caliphs and princes chose to adorn their palaces with a rich figural repertoire. This damaged female lower body with a vertical *kufic* inscription on the left thigh belonged to a partially clad, life-sized figure.

d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.initial_owner: Probably Caliph al-Walid II (r. AH 125–6 / AD 743–4).

d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.method_for_provenance: The provenance of the object has been affirmed through its discovery during the excavations in Qasr al-Mushatta in 1903.
d2379132-91f2-5a63-8508-ac615d5bf783.obtention: As a gift from the Ottoman Sultan Abd al-Hamid (Abdülhamid) II along with the façade of Mushatta in 1903.

d2e14578-6d14-5f7d-85be-43b1df94ecf2.name: Mary with child
d2e14578-6d14-5f7d-85be-43b1df94ecf2.description: The Madonna, originally from Zurich and reminiscent of antique statues in posture and clothing, was imported from Northern Italy. It is an example of the reinterpretation of a sacred sculpture after the Reformation. It was used to represent the Haus Zum grossen Weissen Fräulein (house of the large white maiden) at Obere Zäune 12 in Zurich. The collection of stone sculptures in the Swiss National Museum is modest. Whereas sculptures south of the Alps were mainly carved from stone, wood was the preferred material north of the Alps.

d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.name: *Judith and Holofernes*
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.description:
This carved panel depicting *Judith and Holofernes* in high relief is part of pair, the other panel is an image of *Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well*.  
During the Baroque era, Northern Europe experienced a revival of collecting precious ivory objects. The anonymous artist is very skilled in ivory carving technique and shows a deep knowledge of Italian classicism and baroque sculpture. The scene is well planned showing Judith with the sword in her hand, the beheaded body of Holofernes and an old servant holding the head of Holofernes. An angel is in the background holding a curtain. Clarity, narrative, theatricality and elegance join together to form a high quality work of art. These two bas-relieves have been frequently attributed to the French sculptor Pierre Puget; if this is correct, these panels are the only surviving ivory works of his.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.short_description:
This carved panel depicting *Judith and Holofernes* in high relief is part of a pair, its pendant showing *Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well*.  
In the seventeenth-century there was a revival in collecting precious carved ivory objects, especially in northern Europe. Clear and efficacious narrative, theatricality and elegance combine in this high quality piece which has all the main features of late seventeenth-century art.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.dates: Third quarter of the seventeenth century
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.method_for_datation: The carving is dated to around the second half of the seventeenth-century due to stylistic evidence.
d6415725-869b-5372-aaf8-ec6ca4131379.obtention: Petronio Matteucci, a professor of astronomy in Bologna University and assistant to the Specola donated both panels to the University Collections in 1740. With the creation of the Museo Civico di Bologna (1871), the two panels were given to the Municipality and exhibited in room XV in the new museum. In 1985 they became part of the ivory collection of the Museo Civico Medievale.

e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.name: *Portrait of Historian, Márton György Kovachich*
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.description:
Messerschmidt was born in south-west Germany. After studying in Munich and Graz, he matriculated at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1755. Having graduated, he was employed at the Imperial Arms collection. During the period 1760–69 his work followed the artistic style of the Late Baroque court, at that time under the determining influence of Balthasar Ferdinand Moll. From 1769, Messerschmidt's first Neo-Classical works appear and to which he applied the experiences of his study trip to Rome in 1765. In 1770–72, Messerschmidt began to work on his so-called *Character Heads*, obviously connected with certain paranoid ideas and hallucinations from which, at the beginning of the 1770s, the master began to suffer. After an unsuccessful application to the office of a leading professor at the Academy, in 1777, he settled down in Pozsony (Bratislava) where he dedicated himself primarily to his *Character Heads* and in addition made other portraits as well.  
The bust of Márton György Kovachich (1743–1821), a historian, a custodian of the Buda university library, and one of the most eminent scholars of the Enlightenment in Hungary, was the last of these commissions in Messerschmidt's oeuvre. Kovachich commissioned the portrait directly from the artist in Pozsony (Bratislava), a fact corroborated by a letter from Kovachich dated 1 May 1783, at which time the portrait was already standing in his room in Buda. Like the *Character Heads* the bust is made in the early Neo-Classical style preferred by Messerschmidt since 1769–70. His works of this period have an accentuated plainness, but nevertheless have a vigorous modelling and structure. The portraits have a timeless, monumental character enhanced by their firm portraiture, one marked by the face-on portrayal of his subject. These stylistic characteristics of the Neo-Classical aesthetic are, however, coupled with an exact portrayal of the sitter's features, so that Messerschmidt's portraits remain very close to a realistic appraisal of human individuality.
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.short_description: Messerschmidt moved to Vienna and later to Pozsony (Bratislava) from Bavaria. He made his famous *Character Heads* in Pozsony (Bratislava) when he was mentally ill. All of them portray the features of the artist. The bust of the historian, Kovachich, was made by the artist at a time when he his mental health was good.

e6f7eabb-fc4e-5c98-b6ca-f2544ae496d9.name: Model in plaster
e6f7eabb-fc4e-5c98-b6ca-f2544ae496d9.description: Following on the European fascination for the oriental world and for the famous Nasrid Palaces of the Alhambra (Granada, Spain), a lot of reproductions of its remarkable architectures and decorations were made and spread. José Contreras was commended as restorer and decorator and his son, Rafael (1824–1890), was the leading pioneer of this trend in 1847. His work was continued by the grandson and by a huge number of plaster-cast workshops in Granada, and very likely, in other cities. His plasterworks were very successful in the International Exhibitions and were kept in private collections and museums like South Kensington (London). This polychrome plaster cast res a window in the Mexnar Palace of Granada (Spain).

e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.name: Sphinx
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.description:
This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in AH 1343 / AD 1924 together with the cock (Isl 57) and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world.  
  
They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads. The North African historian al-Maqqari wrote that the Iberian Umayyad caliph Abd al-Rahman III had a fountain made with 12 figures: a lion with a gazelle, a crocodile, a serpent, an eagle, an elephant, a dove, a falcon, a peacock, a hen, a cock, a hawk and a vulture.
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

e78d7a24-9514-5540-ad77-b08982afe7c2.name: Bust of a female saint
e78d7a24-9514-5540-ad77-b08982afe7c2.description: The bust, thought to resemble St. Barbara or St. Katharine, was originally positioned on a plinth and might have been part of a family altar. Both saints were especially known as objects of worship in Bavaria, a fact that is iconographically typified by the figure’s crowned head. She wears a blouse with collar, brooch and breastplate, partly covered by a coat across her left shoulder and right arm. Bright-eyed, and her head slightly turned to the left, she looks on with the utmost attention. Her hair is parted in the middle and falls down in undulating tresses across the shoulders. The remainder of the original polychrome coating, which was possibly enriched by gold leaf on the crown and breastplate, is found on her lips and eyes. The pale greyish-yellow colour of lime-wood dominates.
e78d7a24-9514-5540-ad77-b08982afe7c2.short_description: The intimate bust of a female saint with long, undulating hair falling down to her shoulders and a crown on her head shows traces of the original polychrome coating, which remains on her eyes and lips, and gives the face a living attitude.

e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.name: High Choir, Organs
e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.description:
The dioceses of Braga and its archbishops was very important within the Catholic Church since the early Middle Ages, before the foundation of the Kingdom of Portugal, as well as throughout the Portuguese history namely in the Baroque period.  
In the North of Portugal during the 18th century there was an active workshop that provided important clients in accordance with the splendour and dignity of the court and religious life. Facing the need to replace the old choir stalls from the 16th century, Braga Cathedral commissioned Marceliano de Araújo and Miguel Francisco da Silva to design the monumental High Choir, the choir stalls and the gilded, carved wood organ cases in 1737.  
The whole set of the choir stalls made of carved and gilded wood includes two rows of seats, the cathedra for the Archbishop and in the centre a remarkable choir stand with the same decorative programme. Due to the major role of music within the Baroque Roman Catholic liturgy, Simão Fontanes was commissioned to build the mechanics of two impressive Baroque organs (1737-1738) with thousands of copper pipes, which are encased in magnificent cases made by Braga's woodcarver Marceliano de Araújo.  
The ceiling painting also belonging to this phase of the cathedral redecoration was executed by Manuel Furtado de Mendonça.  
The organs of the Braga Cathedral, commonly included within the category of the Iberian organs, are installed in two balconies over the central nave. The abundance of sculpture ornaments distributed from the base of the building to the top of the Cathedral allows us to include this artwork as one of the finest examples of the Baroque woodcarving in Portugal.
e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.short_description: The choir is located at the west end of the nave and includes two encased organs and choir stalls. They are an example of the work produced in the 18th century by the Northern Portuguese workshop to supply important clients in accordance with the dignity of the court and religious life.

eb6df6e0-21ee-543e-853b-04c21c09966f.name: *Sacred and Profane Love*
eb6df6e0-21ee-543e-853b-04c21c09966f.description:
Undeniably, the process of contact and conquest of the Portuguese Discoveries in the 15th and 16th centuries – through which Portugal came to dominate a large part of the world – was decisive in the creation of numerous and lasting cultural traditions. Peoples of Western and Eastern Cultures experimented with their limits of knowledge, customs and beliefs, a dynamic that was favorable to an artistic symbiosis.  
The Discovery of the New World promoted cultural exchange and hastened the decline of Islamic dominance. It permitted Trans-Asian trade to prosper and specifically encouraged an exchange of artistic knowledge, techniques and language.  
The allegory of *Sacred and Profane Love* is an interesting example of the artistic confluence of Christian Art in Asia. Probably the work of a Portuguese artist, this ivory plaque represents the strength and purity of Christian and Divine Love over what were perceived pagan beliefs like Hinduism and Islamism. Cupid and his arrows, symbol of Pagan Love, are smashed by the faithful spiritual love for Jesus Christ. In the background is a large group of Jesuits praying to the Triumph and Glory of Divine Love. The Jesuit, St. Francis Xavier, visited Ceylon in 1545 and again in 1548, before journeying to Japan in 1549.  
The representation of Divine or Sacred Love over pagan beliefs is well known in Asia, due to the fabulous Altar of St. Catherine made by the Portuguese painter Garcia Fernandes for Goa Cathedral (now in the sacristy). The plaque seen here reveals rare erudition in the organisation of the figures and in the iconography. Note for example the artist's sensibility in his rendering of the shadows around the main figures. Although the piece was produced by a local workshop it is clear that the *chiaroscuro* effects have been deliberately used to heighten the drama and give the piece the three-dimensionality made popular by the paintings of Caravaggio.
eb6df6e0-21ee-543e-853b-04c21c09966f.short_description: An ivory plaque depicting an allegory of Sacred and Profane Love. At the bottom is an inscription: “*Mostras de qvem he*” (“Show to whom you belong”). Divine Love steps over Cupid who has fallen to the floor with his arms tied. Holding an arrow in his right hand, he touches the wounded chest of Jesus Crucified. At the bottom of the Cross an inscription reads: “My Love was crucified”.

ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.name: Statue of Athlete – Ephesos
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.description: After competitions in the *palestra* (sports arena), it was customary for the athletes to clean the sand from their oiled bodies with a strigil, or scraping iron. The Ephesian athlete seen here has already finished this task and – with his hair still soaking in sweat – is cleaning the strigil itself. This statue cannot be attributed to any Greek artist with certainty, yet Roman reproductions in marble and depictions on pottery reliefs and engraved stones speak to a high degree of familiarity with the original.
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.dates: 2nd century AD (copy after a Greek original from the last quarter of the 4th century BC); found in 1895
keywords: Ephesos; Abdul Hamid II; Emperor Franz Joseph

ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.name: *Tomb statue of Prince Pál Esterházy and his first wife (Orsolya Esterházy?)*
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.description:
The four wooden statues representing the Esterházy brothers (Pál and Ferenc) and their wives were certainly commissioned by the Pál Esterházy family. The founder of the dynasty, Palatin Pál, built a family mausoleum in the Franciscan Church in Kismarton (Eisenstadt), within the residential area that formed part of his large estates. Although the crypt was completely rebuilt in 1856–57 its previous appearance can be reconstructed on the basis of a detailed description of the interior from 1835–36 and a plan of the building. As these documents prove, the Kismarton (Eisenstadt) Mausoleum consisted of a lower and an upper chapel. The rounded niches on the upper level were for the gilded-wood, kneeling figures of Pál and Ferenc Esterházy, Orsolya Esterházy and Kata Thököly. The statues in the Hungarian National Gallery, one of which also bears some marks of gilding, seem to be identical to these niche figures. The statues are composed on a frontal view. Their backs are grooved, and their feet are not perfectly carved, a sign that the statues were designed for wall-niches. Pál Esterházy is represented in somewhat historic clothes (coat-of-arms and a short skirt), with a wig, and the Order of the Golden Fleece, which he obtained in 1681. His wife wears Hungarian apparel, a shoulder corset decorated with flowers, a blouse with pleated shoulders, a girdle decorated with precious stones and a necklace.  
In the lower chapel is the still extant sarcophagus of Palatin Pál, which could be viewed from the upper level through the lattice window. There was an altar dedicated to the Virgin Mary in each chapel. Members of the Esterházy family kneeling in the niches of the upper chapel in gestures of eternal worship were, thus, turned to the Virgin Mary mourning her son, suggesting therefore that they committed themselves to her patronage not only in life but even in death.  
The design of Pál Esterházy's sepulchral chapel represents an organic part of his art patronage, in which the cult of the Virgin Mary was determinative.
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.short_description: The sculptures represent the founder of the Esterházy dynasty, Pál Esterházy, and his first wife, Orsolya Esterházy (together with the figures of his brother and sister-in-law) kneeling in prayer. The works originate from the Kismarton (Eisenstadt) family vault and are representative examples of 17th-century portrait sculpture of the region.
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.initial_owner: Esterházy family or the Franciscan Order
ef74c9ed-a4dc-57df-a3a1-c5538d838390.obtention: Purchased through art dealers from Pozsony (Bratislava) for the collection of the Museum of Applied Arts, Budapest; transferred in 1950 to the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest and in 1974 to the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest.

ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.name: Basin.
ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.description:
This small basin consists of three elements: a socle (plinth) with a sculpted shaft and a basin fixed to the socle. The socle is divided into two, acting as a base and a shaft. The cubic base is crowned with a step moulding. The lower part of the cylindrical shaft, which widens at the top, is sculpted with two toruses like the base of a column. This section is followed by a smooth surface engraved with four rows of superposed arches crowned with gadroons sculpted in low relief. The upper part, which narrows towards the top, is engraved with two horizontal grooves.  
The hemispheric basin has deep flutes hollowed out of the inside and a circular aperture at its centre for the provision of water. It is sculpted on the outside with gadroons in high relief.  
This small font, designed in the image of the large basins that stand in the centre of the courtyards of sanctuaries and *madrasas*, was found in the ablutions room of the Buinaniya.
ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.short_description: This small ablutions room font was designed in the image of the great basins that stood in the centre of sanctuary courtyards. The outside of the bowl is decorated with regular gadroons in high relief, and the inside with flutes.
ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.dimensions: Height 41.6 cm, shaft height 21.5 cm, basin diameter 35 cm.
ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.method_for_datation: From the date of construction of the Buinaniya, where the basin came from.
ef7b97e5-69b3-517c-bb7c-4c9c0bd06850.obtention: Salvaged during the restoration of the monument.

f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.name: *Mashrabiyya* window.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.description: A stucco and coloured glass *mashrabiyya* window, which belongs to a set of openwork windows in the Kelvingrove Collection, each with a different design in the centre of the niche. This one shows a cypress tree surrounded by flower stems under a niche. The green, red, and yellow coloured-glass pieces have been imbedded in the stucco openwork from the back. During the Ottoman period in Cairo both mosques and private houses were adorned with such windows from as early as the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The tradition of setting coloured-glass in stucco has endured since its earliest days in the Abbasid capital of Samarra (AH mid-2nd / AD 9th century) to the present day.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.short_description: This stucco and coloured glass window is decorated with a cypress tree and floral arrangements, typical of AH 13th- / AD 19th-century Ottoman art. The cypress tree symbolises a true Muslim as it stands tall and bows in the wind gracefully. Windows such as this adorned both homes and mosques in Cairo.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the style and technique of this window resembles many 13th- / 19th-century stucco windows still in place in Cairo today.
f066d3bf-136b-5661-b693-1a11ebfeb55e.obtention: Purchased by Glasgow Museums / Kelvingrove Art Gallery in 1896.

keywords: Architectural features; floral decoration; religious symbol; religious object; palatial architecture

f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.name: *Portrait of Felice Zacchia Rondanini*
f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.description:
Domenico Guidi, nephew of the sculptor Giuliano Finelli, with whom he worked in Naples (1639–49), moved to the workshops of Algardi in Rome in 1649. He stayed there until the death of his master, from whom he learned the classicism that is a fundamental part of his style, although he was not as skilled in its execution.  
The bust was acquired by the Italian state from an antique market in 1907. It was initially attributed to the Berninian school on account of the elliptical shape enclosing the female figure and the “unfinished” back, a trait peculiar to Bernini on unseen surfaces. It was later attributed to 17th- and 18th-century sculptors (such as Bracci on account of the stylistic analogies with the sculptor's bust of Clement XII in the Borghese collection). It was finally attributed to Guidi, who was summoned by Bernini in 1668 to decorate the Ponte Sant'Angelo, although his style was more classical and less elaborate in form.  
The woman is probably Felice Zacchia Rondanini, daughter of Laudivio Zacchia who, once widowed, gave his life to religion and was made a cardinal in 1626. Algardi made a portrait of the father, having already made several busts for the Rondanini family. For his part, Guidi was responsible for the Rondanini tomb in S. Maria del Popolo, Rome in 1657. In 1683, in the same church, he sculpted the funerary monument to Vincenza Danesi, who some scholars connect to the Borghese portrait, although there is no documentation to support the theory. A ring is fixed under the cloak, which suggests it was originally intended to be placed in a niche, and the measurements coincide with the anchor points of the Danesi monument.  
The old lady wears a large veil forming a convex shape, on which shadows accentuate the face in the foreground, which is struck by light. The detail on the face is particularly interesting, especially the deep lines on the face and neck and the wart on the right cheek, emphasising the realism of the portrait.  
Guidi was so well regarded by the French for his classicism that by the end of his career he was a synonym for French taste. Nonetheless, a sculptural group made for Louis XIV failed to please the king and it ended up in the same place as Bernini's: the gardens of Versailles.
f4070107-bd84-5299-8132-72ae7c8a76e8.short_description:
A portrait of an old lady who wears a veil. The detail on the face is particularly interesting, especially the deep lines on the face and neck and the wart on the right cheek, emphasising the realism of the portrait.  
Guidi produced a few works for Bernini (such as the *Angel with a Lance* on Ponte Sant'Angelo) most of his collaborative work was, however, with Algardi.

f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.name: Human head.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.description:
The face is that of an apparently fine-featured man but the damage to the nose and mouth is very serious. He wears a turban in the Oriental manner. It reminds us of certain pictures of human figures on pottery of the Samanid era of Nishabour (Iran). The turban is V-shaped and a deep fold extends right across its width. The face is covered with a veil, like several other images of heads from Fatimid Egypt and Umayyad Spain in the AH 4th and 5th / AD 10th and 11th centuries. The man's eyes are quite prominent and seem originally to have been covered by two pieces of glass indicating the irises, like other images found on site at Sabra.  
The head's discovery in the Fatimid capital gives weight to the opinion that the Shi'ites, unlike the very iconoclastic Malikites, tolerated human representation in their sculptures.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.short_description: The discovery of this piece in Sabra al-Mansuriyya, the Fatimid capital, supports the idea that Shi'ite Muslims tolerated sculptures of human forms, unlike the very iconoclastic Malikites. This image is similar to others originating from Spain and Egypt at that time.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.dimensions: Height 11.5 cm, width 11.5 cm, thickness 7.5 cm.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.method_for_datation: This stucco head was found, among other human and animal carvings, in the excavations carried out at Sabra al-Mansuriyya in 1978. It was found in a very ploughed-up area with no clear archaeological layering. The objects were scattered around in a random manner. One has the impression that someone had tried to eradicate or hide these figurative objects for no obvious reason except that there could be a connection with the changing religious mentality in Ifriqiya. This action could indeed coincide with the persecution of the Shi'ites during the troubles in 407 / 1016 or following the split between the Zirid emirate and the Fatimid caliphate in 440 / 1048–9. This date could be a *terminus post quem*. The *terminus ante quem* is just after the founding of Sabra in 337 / 948. Any further precision is rendered impossible due to the lack of a definite archaeological layer.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.method_for_provenance: The manufacture of these objects, which is unique in Ifriqiya and in the Maghreb, appears to have taken place in Sabra al-Mansuriyya and to have been commissioned by the Shi'ites.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.obtention: After its discovery at Sabra al-Mansuriyya, this piece was placed in the site storehouse. It was acquired in 1992 by the Museum at Raqqada. It will be displayed in the second section of the Museum, currently under construction.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.bibliography: *Tunisie, terre de rencontres et de civilisation* (Seville exhibition catalogue), Tunis, 1992, p.229.
f5c68eab-37f6-5a2c-b181-f87cfef70a15.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Figurative decoration; human figure

f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.name: *Conversion of St. Paul* Altarpiece
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.description:
A Rococo type of *reredos* (retable) with ornamental pilasters instead of columns, and a wealth of Rococo ornamentation in compact form. At the centre is the *Conversion of St. Paul*, flanked by two female saints without attributes. Two angels kneel at the corners of the cornice. The central, upper section of the altarpiece holds the coat of arms of the Halper-Sigetski family.  
Initially, the altarpiece stood in St. Mark's Church in Zagreb, near the triumphal arch. Like most altarpieces in the church, this one was commissioned by a particular guild, the boot-makers' guild. Its production was part funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich in 1760, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
The altarpiece is by an accomplished master, showing a high level of design and technical skill. The influence of Vid Königer (one of the greatest Styrian sculptors of the second half of the 18th century) is apparent, seen in the female saints in particular.  
During restoration of St Mark's at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.short_description:
A richly carved Rococo altarpiece: two saints stand either side of twisted pilasters and two angels decorate the attic, while the central scene of the *Conversion of St Paul* is in high relief.  
Commissioned for St Mark's Church by the boot-makers' guild in 1760, it was part-funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
During restoration of the church at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.dimensions: H: 226 cm; w: 258 cm; depth 70 cm
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.method_for_datation:
By stylistic analysis and research.  
During restoration and conservation work an older painted layer was discovered under the coat of arms revealing letters next to the frame and the year: "S. D. M. ANNA SAN(C) NATA DE GERLICHISCH 1760". Anna Gerličić, whose name appears on the coat of arms, probably sponsored some of the work for this altarpiece, such as the gilding.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.provenance: Boot-Makers’ Guild altarpiece, Church of St. Mark, Zagreb
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.obtention: During restoration of St. Mark’s Church by architects Schmidt and Bollé (1876–1882), in 1880, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of the former Patačić Manor in Zajezda. It is probable that the coat of arms of the Halper-Sigetski family was applied to the altarpiece while at Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, from where it was transferred to Zagreb.

f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.name: Relief of a lute player.
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.description:
The origin of this roughly worked marble block is unknown. Only through comparing it to fragments on other similarly decorated buildings are we able to give it both a date and a social context. It depicts a musician with his legs crossed, playing a lute. He is wearing trousers and a wide-sleeved shirt.  
The musician’s hair is long, which is in keeping with the fashion of the day. The man is shown in a front-facing pose. He clutches the lute’s neck with his left hand, and with his right holds a plectrum, which is used to pluck the instrument’s strings. Stylistically, the relief is very basic. No details are included. The surface is crudely cut, which may be an indication that the relief was never completed. Another possibility might be that the surface was covered by painted stucco. Stone reliefs were incorporated into the city walls of Konya, among other places, during the Seljuq period.  
Throughout the centuries, music has featured at the magnificent royal courts of Eastern princes. Court celebrations and their musical entertainment had already been written about since the Middle Ages, with much admiration. These sources also relate how much the sultan or prince enjoyed this musical entertainment. Not only were meals consumed at these events, but wine was drunk too. One listened to songs and watched dancers of both sexes perform. Music was felt as the enjoyment of a beauty that was not merely visible. The authors of these historical sources include Ibn Khaldun and al-Ghazzali among others. The harmony between different religious communities is illustrated by the fact that even an Iraqi Christian chronicler, Bar Hebraeus, describes with admiration a feast thrown by the Seljuq Sultan ‘Ala’ al-Din Kay Qubadh (Alaaddin Keykubad) I in 1237.
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.short_description: The musician on this marble relief plays a lute. It may have belonged to a group of similar reliefs which decorated a palace with scenes from court life. In Seljuq Anatolia, reliefs were often assembled to decorate different buildings including city walls such as those in Konya.
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.initial_owner: R. Nadolny, German Ambassador to Turkey 1924–33.
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.method_for_datation: Lute players were frequently represented in Islamic art. This stone relief is characteristic of Seljuq Anatolia, as only there have similar reliefs been found remaining.
f968ffa7-16a4-52b6-80b2-1fcd031e5841.method_for_provenance: The previous owner stated that the relief was of Turkish provenance when the object was acquired. This information as well as the style in which it was made testify to its Anatolian Seljuq origin.

f9783fd3-09a2-5548-be22-593259d96e06.name: Fragment of the Parthenon frieze
f9783fd3-09a2-5548-be22-593259d96e06.description: The climax of the Greater Panathenaia, the chief festival of Athens, held in honour of Athena, was a procession which ended with the presentation of the newly woven peplos (a woman’s garment) to the tutelary goddess of the city. This is the subject of the frieze around the cella of the Parthenon, the temple on the Athenian Acropolis. This fragment shows two bearded elder citizens of Athens in conversation.
f9783fd3-09a2-5548-be22-593259d96e06.holder: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities
keywords: Athens; Acropolis; Franz Ferdinand

fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.name: Lion from a fountain.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.description:
A sculpture such as this hollow lion – standing erect with its uplifted tasselled tail in the shape of a handle – is testament to the variety of Fatimid art. The open jaw of the lion once held a water pipe. The lion’s shape is based on a composition of very abstract forms. Thus its paws are flat, its ribs drawn out linearly, and the lines to describe both the extension of its ears and its bulging eyebrows are simple. The surface of its body along its back, chest and upper legs, is decorated with a spiral pattern that reinforces the sculpture’s stylised form. The engraved inscription found on both sides of the neck can be seen clearly and may date from the AH 7th / AD 13th century. It refers to bi-rasem al-amir Shams al-Din wali Misr, who was probably the governor of ‘Misr’ (Lower Egypt and Cairo).  
A fully modelled sculpture of a living creature is of interest, as it does not conform to the specifications of Islamic dogma. However, such sculptures emerged from the Egyptian Court because, within its circles, the prohibition of the representation of living forms was not always enforced or adhered to, and also because the Fatimid Shi’ites adopted a liberal view. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo holds a sitting lion figure. The Berlin lion could have formed part of a sculptured fountain that featured a variety of figures. Thus, it would correspond to the lions of the well-known, bigger lion fountains of the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. Given its small size, the lion could have been part of a larger construction featuring a number of sculptures such as those represented in Iraqi manuscripts from the AH 7th / AD 13th century onwards. Bronze figures like this lion were widespread across the Mediterranean, and especially across Spain. One of these Spanish lions can be seen in the Louvre Museum in Paris. One can assume that most of these bronze lions did not survive the test of time and were melted down.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.short_description: This lively little lion with an open mouth and upturned tail was used as a fountain spigot during the Fatimid period in Egypt. It is made of cast bronze that has been decorated with scrolls on the back and the legs. Fountains with animal decoration were widespread in Mediterranean countries.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_datation: Similar figures, cast in bronze, were made especially in Fatimid Egypt. Both the design and the decoration of the lion fountain demonstrate parallels to similar pieces that were created during the Fatimid period. Additionally, it features an inscription that names an apparent governor of Egypt.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_provenance: The inscription appears to name a governor of Egypt. Furthermore the stylistic markings testify to having originated from the Egyptian Fatimid period.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1911.

fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.name: Fountain spout
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.description:
Small gilded bronze sculpture in the form of a hind. The figure is fragile and disproportionate. Almost all of the surface is covered with delicate oriental plant decoration (lotus flowers inscribed in circles) which make it look as if it is swathed in a rich fabric. Judging from the remains left in the grooves of the engraving and various parts of the body, the piece would have been completely gilded.  
The simple forms of the body, its facial characteristics and its legs, which end with discs and are extremely short in relation to its body, are reminiscent of representations of animals that appear in Fatimid ceramics.  
This sculpture undoubtedly served as a fountain spout because, apart from the legs, its body is hollow and there is a hole in its belly to allow water to pass through and cascade out of its mouth.  
The presence of water in Umayyad gardens was a sign of wealth, luxury and well-being. Fountains were an important aesthetic element in Islamic palaces in the West and in al-Andalus in particular. This hind would probably have been accompanied by other bronze animals.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.short_description: Its cloven hoofs, the base of its horns and its short pointed tail suggest that this animal is a fawn. It would undoubtedly have been used as a spout in a basin or fountain in a Córdoban palace, with the water entering through a duct beneath the belly and coming out through the mouth.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis. Although the Madrid hind is smaller and less stylised, it is clearly similar to other pieces found in the 10th / 16th century among the ruins of the Madinat al-Zahra palace, one of which can be found in the Archaeological Museum of Córdoba. The second disappeared at the start of the 19th centuryfrom the Monastery of Guadalupe, where it was being stored, but has recently been recovered and has been in the Qatar National Museum since 1997.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_provenance: Some researchers believe that this piece could have been imported from Fatimid Egypt. However, its discovery in the province of Córdoba and the similarities to the deer of Córdoba and Qatar suggest that the three sculptures were produced, if not in the same workshop, at least in the same geographical area of al-Andalus, where metalwork workshops developed.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.obtention: The hind was bought by the National Archaeological Museum on 3 February 1940.

fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.name: El transparente Universo (The Transparent Universe)
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.description:
Originally from Segovia, Torres Esteban represents one of the first exponents who worked with studio glass in Spain. From the late 70s, his presence in international forums enabled him to contact sculptors from around the world and make propositions to the representatives of CEVIDER in Valencia, the organizer of the VICOINTER ‘83 exhibition.  
The glasswork by Torres Esteban is characterised by the construction of monumental geometric shapes, which is owed to both constructivism and kinetic art. His playfulness led him to work with geometry and the shapes he created, all of which were generally of a changeable nature. His works facilitate different arrangements that move away from the solidity of the closed to the open, the passive space that surrounded the cube, becomes dynamic and plays with the light that is projected on the interior surfaces of the piece, in which certain cuts in glass sheets that compose it have developed spherical cavities.
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.method_for_datation: Author archives and conversations with his son in order to create the exhibition: “Torres Esteban. A passion for glass”.
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.method_for_provenance: Temporary exhibition at the Royal Glass Factory. Museo Tecnológico del Vidrio, 1998
fc579321-e275-5fe1-8dd0-ec1b2c450394.bibliography: González Vicario, Mª Teresa, de Pablos, Eliseo, Gómez, Javier and García, Pedro, *Torres Esteban. Una pasión por el vidrio*, San Ildefonso, Segovia: Fundación Centro Nacional del Vidrio, 1998.
